drivers.name: Paris Agreement
drivers.logic: The Paris Agreement establishes the global framework for limiting climate change, driving governments, financial institutions and markets toward decarbonization, climate resilience and alignment of capital flows with climate objectives. For banks, this increases expectations to manage climate-related portfolio risks and direct financing toward the transition.

drivers.name: UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
drivers.logic: The SDGs establish a global framework for sustainable development that influences banks' sustainability strategies, impact priorities, responsible banking commitments and allocation of capital toward sustainable development.

drivers.name: Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF)
drivers.logic: The GBF increases expectations for financial institutions to identify and manage nature-related dependencies, impacts, risks and opportunities within lending and investment portfolios and to direct finance toward nature-positive activities.

drivers.name: COP 29 Decisions
drivers.logic: COP decisions increasingly shape the policy and investment environment for banks by increasing demand for climate finance, transition finance, adaptation finance and private capital mobilisation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: COP29: USD 300bn/year by 2035 in climate finance to developing countries and efforts to scale total finance to USD 1.3tn/year by 2035.

drivers.name: IFRS S1
drivers.logic: IFRS S1 creates a global baseline for disclosure of sustainability-related financial risks and opportunities, increasing expectations for banks to connect ESG issues with strategy, risk management, financial position and access to capital.

drivers.name: IFRS S2
drivers.logic: IFRS S2 strengthens climate-related financial disclosure and increases expectations for banks to identify, assess and disclose physical and transition climate risks and opportunities, including implications for portfolios and strategy.

drivers.name: GRI Standards
drivers.logic: GRI provides a widely used impact-reporting framework, increasing expectations for banks to disclose their material economic, environmental and social impacts and how they are managed.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Universal, Sector and Topic Standards; 
revised biodiversity standard effective 2026 and revised climate/energy standards effective 2027.

drivers.name: SASB – Commercial Banks
drivers.logic: The SASB Commercial Banks standard provides industry-specific sustainability information relevant to investors, encouraging banks to identify and report financially material sustainability topics specific to banking.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Commercial Banks is an identified SASB industry standard; SASB standards are incorporated into the ISSB framework and provide industry-based information for IFRS S1/S2 application.

drivers.name: TNFD
drivers.logic: TNFD creates a framework for banks and other financial institutions to identify, assess and disclose nature-related dependencies, impacts, risks and opportunities across portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 14 recommended disclosures across governance, strategy, risk & impact management, and metrics & targets.

drivers.name: GHG Protocol
drivers.logic: GHG Protocol provides the underlying accounting architecture for measuring greenhouse-gas emissions, supporting consistent corporate and value-chain emissions data that banks increasingly need to assess borrowers and financed emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Scope 1, 2 and 3 accounting; Scope 3 Category 15 covers investments. Financial-sector guidance supports financed-emissions measurement.

drivers.name: CDP
drivers.logic: CDP creates demand for standardized environmental disclosure and provides environmental data used by banks and investors in credit, investment and engagement decisions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CDP capital-market signatories include banks and insurers; data covers climate change, deforestation and water security.

drivers.name: TCFD (legacy/reference)
drivers.logic: TCFD established the four-pillar structure that continues to underpin climate-related disclosure and has been incorporated into IFRS S2. It remains useful as a reference when assessing legacy reporting frameworks and existing bank disclosures.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 4 pillars: governance, strategy, risk management, metrics & targets. TCFD completed its remit in 2023 and monitoring transitioned to the IFRS Foundation.

drivers.name: ESRS (conditional on EU exposure)
drivers.logic: ESRS creates sustainability reporting requirements for entities within the EU reporting perimeter and can affect internationally active banks and banks financing/reporting on EU-exposed groups.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ESRS covers environmental, social and governance matters; revised ESRS were adopted by the European Commission in July 2026.

drivers.name: Science-Based Climate Targets for Financial Institutions
drivers.logic: Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) frameworks provide financial institutions with methodologies for setting science-based near-term and net-zero targets covering financed emissions and investment/lending portfolios. This increases expectations for banks to measure portfolio emissions, establish credible decarbonisation targets and align financing with climate pathways.
drivers.evidenceKpi: SBTi's Financial Institutions Net-Zero Standard provides requirements for financial institutions to set science-based net-zero targets, while its Near-Term Criteria establish requirements for near-term targets. The framework covers financial institutions' financed emissions and portfolio alignment.

drivers.name: Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI)
drivers.logic: PRI drives ESG integration and responsible-investment practices among institutional investors and asset owners, influencing banks involved in investment, asset management and capital markets.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
6 Principles for incorporating ESG into investment and ownership practices: 
1. Incorporation
2. Active ownership
3. Appropriate disclosure
4. Promote acceptance
5. Work together 
6. Report activities

drivers.name: Net-Zero Banking Alliance (NZBA) (legacy/reference)
drivers.logic: NZBA guidance established a banking-specific approach to setting financed-emissions and sectoral decarbonization targets, influencing banks' transition planning and climate strategies. Although the alliance's membership structure was under transition from 2025, its guidance and methodologies remain relevant as a reference for banks' net-zero target-setting and transition planning.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Sectoral financed-emissions targets; 2030 interim targets; transition plans; portfolio alignment; financed-emissions reduction

drivers.name: Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF)
drivers.logic: PCAF provides a standardized methodology for banks to measure and disclose financed emissions, making portfolio-level GHG accounting increasingly actionable for climate strategy and risk management.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Standard covers financed emissions, facilitated emissions and insurance-associated emissions; built on GHG Protocol.

drivers.name: Equator Principles
drivers.logic: The Equator Principles establish an environmental and social risk-management framework for financial institutions financing large infrastructure and industrial projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
10 Principles; applies globally to project finance and related products.
Principle 1: Review & Categorisation;
Principle 2: E&S Assessment;
Principle 3: Applicable E&S Standards;
Principle 4: E&S Management System & EP Action Plan
Principle 5: Stakeholder Engagement 
Principle 6: Grievance Mechanism
Principle 7: Independent Review 
Principle 8: Covenants
Principle 9: Independent Monitoring & Reporting 
Principle 10: Reporting & Transparency

drivers.name: ICMA Green Bond Principles
drivers.logic: GBP provide voluntary market standards for green bonds, increasing expectations for transparent use of proceeds, project selection, management of proceeds and reporting.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Four core components (Use of Proceeds; Process for Project Evaluation and Selection; Management of Proceeds; Reporting); used by issuers, banks, investors and arrangers.

drivers.name: ICMA Social Bond Principles
drivers.logic: SBP support transparent financing of projects with positive social outcomes and strengthen the integrity of the social bond market.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2025 edition; use-of-proceeds framework with transparency and reporting recommendations.

drivers.name: ICMA Sustainability Bond Guidelines
drivers.logic: Sustainability Bond Guidelines support issuance combining eligible environmental and social projects, expanding banks' sustainable debt-product capabilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Combines green and social project categories; follows ICMA's four core green/social bond components.

drivers.name: ICMA Sustainability-Linked Bond Principles
drivers.logic: SLBP increase demand for credible sustainability KPIs and targets in debt financing, creating opportunities for banks as arrangers, lenders and sustainability-linked finance providers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2024 SLBP; focuses on KPI selection, target calibration, disclosure and reporting.

drivers.name: Climate Bonds Standard
drivers.logic: Climate Bonds Standard provides a certification framework for climate-aligned investments and bonds, strengthening credibility and comparability of climate finance products.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Voluntary certification; alignment with 1.5°C goal; current framework requires 95% of proceeds to align with climate goals.

drivers.name: GFANZ (Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero)
drivers.logic: GFANZ develops transition-finance and transition-planning guidance that helps financial institutions align strategies and capital allocation with the real-economy transition.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Financial-institution transition planning; private-sector capital mobilisation.

drivers.name: Sustainable Banking and Finance Network (SBFN)
drivers.logic:
SBN/SBFN is a voluntary community of financial sector regulators and industry associations from emerging markets, who are committed to advancing sustainable finance to support national development priorities, deepen financial markets, and promote financial stability.

The World Bank Group (WBG) serves as SBFN’s Secretariat and knowledge partner, helping members share insights, access capacity-building resources, and design and implement national sustainable finance initiatives.
drivers.evidenceKpi: As of July 2026, SBFN brings together 105 member institutions from 74 countries including 7 regional members covering an additional 32 countries in emerging markets, representing US$79.5 trillion—96 percent of total banking assets in emerging markets.

drivers.name: IFC Performance Standards on Environmental and Social Sustainability
drivers.logic: IFC Performance Standards provide a widely used environmental and social risk framework for project and corporate finance, particularly relevant to banks financing infrastructure and large projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
8 IFC Performance Standards covering environmental and social risks and impacts.
Performance Standard 1: Assessment and Management of Environmental and Social Risks and Impacts
Performance Standard 2: Labor and Working Conditions
Performance Standard 3: Resource Efficiency and Pollution Prevention
Performance Standard 4: Community Health, Safety, and Security 
Performance Standard 5: Land Acquisition and Involuntary Resettlement
Performance Standard 6: Biodiversity Conservation and Sustainable Management of Living Natural Resources 
Performance Standard 7: Indigenous People
Performance Standard 8: Cultural Heritage

drivers.name: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct
drivers.logic:
OECD responsible-business-conduct expectations strengthen human-rights, environmental and governance due diligence considerations relevant to banks financing multinational clients and projects.

They establish expectations for banks to conduct risk-based due diligence, ensuring their lending, investment, and underwriting services do not cause, contribute to, or link directly to human rights abuses, environmental damage, or corruption.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2023 Guidelines cover responsible business conduct, climate change, biodiversity, technology and due diligence.

drivers.name: Sustainability Disclosure and Cost of Capital
drivers.logic: Comprehensive, comparable and reliable sustainability disclosure can reduce a company’s cost of capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Empirical research from the University of Oxford found that ‘90% of the studies on the cost of capital show that sound sustainability standards lower the cost of capital for companies.
drivers.keySources: University of Oxford and Arabesque Partners, ‘From the Stockholder to the Stakeholder: How Sustainability Can Drive Financial Outperformance,’ March 2015.

drivers.name: Sustainability Information and Earnings Stability
drivers.logic: Sustainability information can be a strong signal of share price volatility.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Based on historical data, Bank of America Global Research found that companies in the top quintile of sustainability performance experienced the lowest volatility in earnings per share (EPS) in a subsequent five-year period. By contrast, ‘companies with the worst environmental, social and governance records averaged 92% volatility.

The researchers also found that sustainability information was the only reliable signal for predicting EPS volatility, providing better insight than traditional measures such as return on equity.
drivers.keySources: Bank of America, ‘Equity Strategy Focus Point,’ 18 December 2016.

drivers.name: Sustainable Bond Market Development
drivers.logic: The continued growth of sustainable bond markets increases demand for ESG strategies, sustainability frameworks, transparent disclosures, and impact reporting. Companies issuing sustainable bonds are expected to align with internationally recognized market principles and demonstrate the environmental and/or social use of proceeds or sustainability performance commitments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2026: Total sustainable bond issuance reached USD 357.6 billion. Green bonds remained the largest segment, with USD 229.2 billion issued (64.08% of total issuance), followed by Sustainability bonds with USD 60.3 billion (16.88% of total issuance).

drivers.name: Net-Zero Banking Alliance (NZBA)
drivers.logic: The Net-Zero Banking Alliance (NZBA) establishes voluntary international best practices for banks to measure financed emissions, align lending and investment portfolios with net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, set science-based interim targets, strengthen climate transition planning, and enhance climate-related disclosures.
drivers.evidenceKpi: NZBA members commit to aligning financed emissions with net-zero by 2050, establishing 2030 interim targets using science-based pathways, measuring and disclosing financed emissions, and integrating transition planning into banking strategies. The 2023 Progress Update reports that over two-thirds of member banks had established targets aligned with 1.5°C scenarios and nearly nine in ten banks met their initial target-setting commitments.

drivers.name: The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS)
drivers.logic: The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) develops climate macro-financial scenarios that support banks, central banks and financial supervisors in assessing physical and transition climate risks, conducting climate stress testing, and integrating climate risk into financial decision-making.
drivers.evidenceKpi: NGFS publishes long-term climate macro-financial scenarios incorporating updated transition pathways, physical risks and macroeconomic impacts to support climate risk assessment and financial resilience.

drivers.name: FSB Climate-Related Financial Risk
drivers.logic: The Financial Stability Board (FSB) coordinates international efforts to strengthen financial stability by promoting consistent approaches to identifying, assessing and managing climate-related financial risks across the global financial system.
drivers.evidenceKpi: FSB develops international recommendations and coordinates supervisory work on climate-related financial risks, supporting consistent regulatory approaches, financial stability monitoring and climate-related disclosures.

drivers.name: Environmental Code
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's Environmental Code classifies economic activities by environmental impact and establishes EIA, environmental permitting, emissions and waste requirements, BAT requirements and remediation liabilities. For banks, these requirements create environmental and credit-risk exposure through borrowers, particularly clients operating in high-impact sectors such as mining, oil & gas, metallurgy and power.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Facility environmental category: I / II / III / IV
% of lending exposure to Category I borrowers
% of borrowers requiring environmental permits
% of high-risk borrowers subject to environmental due diligence
Exposure to borrowers with environmental fines/liabilities
Environmental/BAT capex requirements of borrowers

drivers.name: Green taxonomy
drivers.logic: The Kazakhstan Green Taxonomy provides eligibility criteria for green projects and enables banks to classify and finance activities that contribute to environmental objectives.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Applies to green financing including green bonds and green lending; methodology developed for financial institutions and other stakeholders.
drivers.keySources:
1. Green Finance Platform
2. Adilet Website
3. AIFC GFC

drivers.name: ESG disclosure requirements
drivers.logic: Growing ESG disclosure expectations increase banks' need for sustainability data, governance and transparent reporting on material ESG risks and impacts.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2023, the Agency of the Republic of Kazakhstan for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market (ARDFM) introduced ESG Disclosure Guidelines and subsequently established mandatory sustainable development disclosure requirements for banks beginning in 2025.

drivers.name: Climate-risk management requirements
drivers.logic: Emerging climate-risk requirements increase banks' need to identify physical and transition risks and incorporate them into governance, risk assessment and portfolio management.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2024, ARDFM introduced Environmental and Social Risk Management (ESRM) Guidelines to support the integration of environmental and social risks into financing decisions and internal governance processes.

drivers.name: NDC 3.0
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's enhanced NDC strengthens national decarbonization commitments, increasing transition risks and financing needs across borrowers and creating demand for climate and transition finance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2026–2035 implementation period; 2035 emissions target; national climate-policy alignment.

drivers.name: Carbon Neutrality Strategy 2060
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's long-term decarbonisation pathway creates transition and financing implications for banks through borrowers and demand for capital for renewable energy, energy efficiency, industrial modernization and other low-carbon investments.
drivers.keySources: UNFCCC - Strategy of the Republic of Kazakhstan on Achieving Carbon Neutrality

drivers.name: Kazakhstan Emissions Trading System (ETS)
drivers.logic: Carbon pricing increases transition risk for emissions-intensive borrowers, potentially affecting operating costs, capital expenditure, creditworthiness and financing needs.

drivers.name: Best Available Techniques (BAT)
drivers.logic: BAT requirements increase transition and capex requirements for major industrial borrowers, creating credit-risk implications and demand for modernization finance.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
According to the Environmental Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, from 1 January 2025, Category I facilities are required to obtain comprehensive environmental permits (CEPs) based on the application of BAT and compliance of facilities with the emission levels specified in BAT reference documents.

When implementing BAT, industry is exempted from paying environmental tax payments on emissions, and for enterprises that do not switch to CEP, environmental payments will be gradually increased by 2, 4 and 8 times.

drivers.name: CBAM
drivers.logic: CBAM creates indirect transition and market-access risks for banks financing Kazakhstan exporters of covered products, particularly where carbon costs affect borrowers' competitiveness and investment needs.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Definitive CBAM regime began 1 January 2026; covered sectors initially include cement, iron & steel, aluminium, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen.

drivers.name: Water/environmental regulation
drivers.logic: Water-use permits, withdrawal limits, wastewater requirements and water-efficiency obligations can increase compliance and investment costs for water-intensive borrowers, creating credit and transition risks for banks and demand for water-efficiency financing.
drivers.keySources:
Adilet - Water Code 
Adilet - Kazakhstan Ecological Code

drivers.name: Green lending & preferential financing programmes
drivers.logic: Public and development-finance programmes reduce financing barriers for eligible green projects, creating opportunities for banks to expand green lending.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC). Cumulative green bonds and loans have surpassed KZT 150 billion. Funding primarily targets renewable energy, industrial energy efficiency, and sustainable infrastructure.

10% interest-rate subsidy; up to 25% principal subsidy; guarantees up to 85% of loan amount; USD 2m UNDP–Damu RES programme
drivers.keySources:
AIFC Green Finance Centre
Damu Fund - Cooperation with UNDP

drivers.name: Green bonds
drivers.logic: Development of Kazakhstan's green bond market creates opportunities for banks as issuers, arrangers, investors and lenders to sustainable projects.

drivers.name: Sustainability-linked financing
drivers.logic: Sustainability-linked financing allows banks to link financing terms to a borrower's measurable sustainability performance, creating a financing mechanism for companies undertaking ESG/transition improvements.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Sustainability-linked loans and bonds are recognized among ESG financing instruments in Kazakhstan; transactions require measurable sustainability KPIs/targets, reporting and verification.

AIFC's State of Sustainable Finance in Central Asia reports USD 10 million of sustainability-linked bonds for Kazakhstan as of May 2024.

drivers.name: Exposure to carbon-intensive sectors
drivers.logic: Banks with significant exposure to fossil fuels, electricity and heavy industry face transition risks from carbon pricing, climate policy, technological change and declining demand for emissions-intensive products. These risks can increase borrowers' probability of default and reduce collateral values.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ~50% of corporate loan books of Kazakhstan's banks were exposed to electricity, fossil energy and heavy industry in 2021; banks with high emissions-intensive exposure could experience up to 30% additional losses under a disorderly 1.5°C scenario over 5–7 years; energy sector = 80% of Kazakhstan's GHG emissions.
drivers.keySources: IMF–World Bank FSAP, Climate-Related Risks and Financial Stability in Kazakhstan (2024)

drivers.name: Physical climate risks to borrowers
drivers.logic: Increasing floods, droughts, heat and other climate hazards can damage borrowers' assets, disrupt operations and reduce debt-servicing capacity, creating credit and collateral risks for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Floods and droughts caused ~KZT 350bn in losses over the past 3 decades; their intensity and frequency are expected to increase. Climate risks include heatwaves, droughts, floods, glacier melt, mudflows and landslides.
drivers.keySources: IMF–World Bank FSAP, Climate-Related Risks and Financial Stability in Kazakhstan (2024)

drivers.name: Water scarcity
drivers.logic: Water stress can affect agricultural, mining, industrial and energy borrowers, increasing operating costs, production risks and financing needs.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Kazakhstan's surface-water flows have declined ~27%; agriculture accounts for ~70% of water abstractions; water stress ratio is 0.23–0.30, with significant regional differences. 
According to IMF, 62% of agricultural land could be exposed to water stress under a moderate-emissions scenario, while droughts are expected to intensify.
drivers.keySources:
1. World Bank – General Country Assessment: Kazakhstan
2. IMF

drivers.name: Extreme flooding
drivers.logic: Flooding can damage borrowers' assets and collateral, disrupt operations and reduce debt-servicing capacity, increasing credit losses for banks, particularly in real estate, agriculture, infrastructure and SME portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2024 floods: ~USD 877m estimated losses and 118,000 people displaced; USD 419m average annual flood losses; under SSP2-4.5, high-hazard flood risk could triple by 2100.

drivers.name: Agricultural climate exposure
drivers.logic: Drought, heat and changing precipitation patterns can reduce agricultural productivity and borrower cash flows, affecting agricultural and rural lending portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Spring wheat yields could decline by up to 50% by mid-century without adaptation; 62% of agricultural land could face water stress under a moderate-emissions scenario; agriculture accounts for ~5% of GDP and 25% of employment.
drivers.keySources:
1. IMF – Climate-Related Risks and Financial Stability in Kazakhstan 
2. World Bank – Water, Agriculture & Rangelands Diagnostic

drivers.name: EU CBAM
drivers.logic: CBAM can increase transition costs and competitiveness pressure for borrowers exporting covered goods to the EU, affecting cash flows, investment needs and credit risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Definitive regime from 1 Jan 2026; covers cement, iron & steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen; EU importers >50 tonnes of CBAM goods are subject to the definitive regime; Kazakhstan's aluminium exports to the EU were historically ~US$200m/year, with ~30% of Kazakhstan's aluminium exports going to the EU; Kazakhstan aluminium production intensity ~615 tCO₂e/US$1m, vs EU ~122. Bank KPIs: % lending to CBAM-exposed exporters; borrower EU export share; embedded emissions; estimated CBAM cost.

drivers.name: Supply-chain ESG & Responsible Sourcing Requirements
drivers.logic: International customers, investors and regulators increasingly require suppliers to demonstrate environmental, climate, human-rights and responsible-sourcing practices. This can affect borrowers' market access, costs and competitiveness, creating credit risk for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Supplier ESG due diligence; GHG/emissions data; mineral traceability; human-rights due diligence; % portfolio exposed to export-oriented/high-risk supply chains. OECD Guidelines recommend risk-based due diligence across operations, supply chains and business relationships.
drivers.keySources: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct

drivers.name: Climate-related financial risk management
drivers.logic: Climate change is recognized as a financial-stability risk, requiring banks to identify, assess and manage climate-related financial risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CBU has an explicit mandate to develop recommendations and requirements for banks on climate-related financial risk management; climate-risk indicators, risk maps and stress testing are being incorporated into financial-stability analysis.
drivers.keySources:
1. Central Bank of Uzbekistan - Regulation of Credit Organizations
2. Central Bank of Uzbekistan - Financial Stability Department

drivers.name: ESG integration in banking
drivers.logic: ESG considerations are increasingly being incorporated into banks' risk management and sustainable-finance practices, increasing expectations for ESG assessment in lending.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CBU conducted an ESG regulation seminar with commercial banks in 2024, covering ESG controls, international standards and green financing; ESG criteria in lending/risk assessment.

drivers.name: Green finance / green lending development
drivers.logic: Government policy and financial incentives are expanding green financing and creating opportunities for banks to originate green loans.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan - On the state program for the implementation of the "Uzbekistan 2030" strategy in the Year of Environmental Protection and Green Economy

drivers.name: IFRS adoption for financial institutions
drivers.logic: IFRS-based accounting and reporting increases comparability, transparency and quality of financial information used by investors, regulators and lenders.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Commercial banks have been required to transition to IFRS-based accounting; CBU continues implementation and alignment of bank reporting with IFRS.

drivers.name: National Green Economy Taxonomy
drivers.logic: The taxonomy establishes criteria for identifying eligible green activities and directly affects banks' classification and financing of green projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Adopted 25 Oct 2023; applies to green projects financed through green bonds, loans and other funding; includes energy efficiency, renewables, green buildings, water/resource efficiency, etc.

drivers.name: NDC 3.0
drivers.logic: National climate targets increase transition expectations for borrowers and create demand for climate and transition financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 50% reduction in GHG emissions intensity per GDP by 2035 vs. 2010; sectoral 2035 emissions projections included in NDC.

drivers.name: Green Economy Transition Strategy 2019–2030
drivers.logic: The national transition strategy drives investment in energy efficiency, renewables, resource efficiency and low-carbon development, creating financing demand for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Strategy establishes 2030 green-economy targets covering energy efficiency, renewables, resource efficiency and emissions intensity.

drivers.name: Green Finance System Development
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan is developing a national green-finance system, including mechanisms to attract concessional and private capital for decarbonization and climate adaptation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: National green-finance programme; concessional funding mobilized; green-finance volumes
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan - Green Economy Transition Strategy

drivers.name: Green bonds and sustainable bonds
drivers.logic: Growth of green and sustainable debt markets creates opportunities for banks to act as issuers, arrangers, underwriters, investors and financing intermediaries for eligible projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: USD 660m sovereign green bonds issued in 2023; Uzbekistan has also developed a national framework for green bonds and green loans;

drivers.name: Climate Finance Gap
drivers.logic: Large climate-investment needs create financing demand for banks, while mobilization of private capital creates opportunities to participate in climate projects through lending, project finance and investment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: USD 9.5bn mitigation financing gap by 2030; USD 7.2bn adaptation gap; USD 2–3bn/year potential private financing for decarbonization of energy and industry.

drivers.name: Transition Risk in Bank Portfolios
drivers.logic: Decarbonisation policies, technology changes and shifts in market demand can reduce the profitability and asset values of carbon-intensive borrowers, affecting banks' credit quality.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 42% of bank lending was exposed to high-emission-prone sectors in 2022, mainly fossil fuels, utilities and energy-intensive sectors; this exposure was growing during 2021–2022.

drivers.name: Water Stress
drivers.logic: Water scarcity can reduce production and cash flows of water-dependent borrowers, particularly agriculture, increasing credit risk for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 90% of national water use is attributable to irrigated agriculture; ~95% of crop production depends on irrigation; agricultural yields could decline 10% by 2050 without major water-efficiency measures. Around US$8.7bn is estimated to be needed through 2030 to fully modernize irrigation and adapt to climate impacts.

drivers.name: Drought & Heat Stress
drivers.logic: Increasing drought and heat can reduce agricultural productivity, livestock output and labor productivity, weakening borrower cash flows and increasing credit risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan is already experiencing prolonged droughts and extreme heat. Climate change could make the economy ~10% smaller by 2050 than without climate damages; adaptation needs are estimated at US$46.7–59.8bn through 2060, depending on the climate scenario.

drivers.name: Extreme weather and flooding
drivers.logic: Floods and other climate-related hazards can damage borrower assets and infrastructure, disrupt operations and reduce repayment capacity and collateral values.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The CCDR identifies floods, landslides and other natural hazards as contributors to climate/land-degradation risk. 30% of Uzbekistan's land (13.7m ha) is severely degraded, with risk concentrated in areas including the Fergana Valley, Samarkand, Karshi and Tashkent.

drivers.name: EU CBAM
drivers.logic: Banks financing exporters to the EU may face indirect transition risk as CBAM increases carbon-related costs and competitiveness pressure for exposed borrowers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Definitive CBAM regime from 1 Jan 2026; covers cement, iron & steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. KPIs: bank exposure to CBAM-covered exporters; EU export share; embedded emissions; estimated CBAM cost.

drivers.name: Supply-chain ESG & Responsible Sourcing Requirements
drivers.logic: International buyers increasingly require suppliers to demonstrate environmental, climate, social and responsible-sourcing practices. Failure to meet these requirements can affect borrowers' market access, costs and competitiveness, creating indirect credit risk for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Supplier ESG due diligence, GHG/emissions data, mineral traceability, human-rights due diligence and environmental certifications.

drivers.name: UAE Net Zero by 2050 Strategic Initiative
drivers.logic: The national net-zero pathway increases transition expectations for banks and their borrowers and creates demand for transition and low-carbon finance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Net zero by 2050; economy-wide decarbonization pathway;

drivers.name: UAE NDC 3.0
drivers.logic: The strengthened national emissions target increases transition pressure across corporate portfolios and financing needs for mitigation and adaptation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 47% GHG reduction by 2035 vs. 2019, equivalent to reducing emissions from 196.3 MtCO₂e to 103.5 MtCO₂e.

drivers.name: CBUAE Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation (C 8/2025)
drivers.logic: Establishes mandatory minimum standards for banks to identify, assess, manage and disclose climate-related financial risks and integrate them into risk-management and capital processes.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In force since 14 Oct 2025; applies to banks and insurance companies; requires climate-risk integration into risk management, data systems, strategy and ICAAP/capital adequacy.

drivers.name: CBUAE Sustainability-related Disclosure Principles
drivers.logic: Establishes expectations for sustainability disclosures, increasing banks' need for reliable ESG data, governance, metrics and targets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Principles cover governance, strategy, risk management, metrics & targets; require systems for sustainability reporting and addressing data gaps.

drivers.name: UAE Sustainable Finance Working Group (SFWG) Frameworks
drivers.logic: SFWG initiatives establish common sustainable-finance and transition-planning expectations across UAE financial regulators and market participants.
drivers.evidenceKpi: SFWG established in 2019; has issued sustainable-finance principles, climate-risk principles, sustainability-disclosure principles and climate transition-planning principles.

drivers.name: AED 1 Trillion Sustainable-Finance Mobilization Target
drivers.logic: The UAE's sustainable-finance target creates substantial demand for banks to originate, arrange, underwrite, invest in and distribute sustainable-finance products.
drivers.evidenceKpi: AED 1 trillion sustainable finance mobilization target by 2030

drivers.name: Green Bonds & Green Sukuk
drivers.logic: Expansion of green debt markets creates opportunities for banks to act as arrangers, issuers, investors and financiers of eligible green projects; green sukuk additionally connects sustainable finance with the UAE's Islamic-finance market.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPI: annual green bond/sukuk issuance; outstanding volume; bank underwriting/investment; proceeds allocated to eligible projects.

drivers.name: Sustainability-linked financing
drivers.logic: Sustainability-linked loans and bonds allow banks to connect financing terms to borrowers' measurable sustainability performance, expanding ESG-linked corporate financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPI: SLL/SLB volume; number of transactions; sustainability KPIs and targets; margin adjustments linked to performance.

drivers.name: Transition finance
drivers.logic: UAE decarbonization objectives create demand for financing companies in emissions-intensive sectors that require capital to reduce emissions rather than immediately exit high-carbon activities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE SFWG has issued Principles for Climate Transition Planning

drivers.name: UAE as Regional Sustainable-Finance Hub
drivers.logic: The UAE's established financial centres and sustainable-finance infrastructure create opportunities for banks to attract international capital and provide regional ESG financing and structuring services.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPI: sustainable-finance transactions involving UAE financial centres; international capital mobilized; regional green/sustainable issuance; cross-border sustainable-finance activity.

drivers.name: Extreme heat
drivers.logic: Extreme temperatures can reduce labour productivity, increase cooling and operating costs, damage infrastructure and weaken borrower cash flows, creating physical credit risk for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE faces extreme heat as a key physical climate hazard. KPIs: portfolio exposure to heat-sensitive sectors/assets; operating-cost impacts; heat-related business interruption; climate-related credit losses.

drivers.name: Water scarcity
drivers.logic: Water stress can increase costs and constrain production for water-dependent borrowers, particularly utilities, agriculture, industry and real estate, transmitting physical risk to banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Water scarcity is identified as a major climate vulnerability; KPI: portfolio exposure to water-intensive sectors/locations; borrower water intensity; exposure to water-stressed assets.

drivers.name: Flooding / extreme rainfall
drivers.logic: Extreme rainfall and flooding can damage borrower assets and collateral, interrupt operations and increase insurance and financing costs, creating credit risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2024 UAE floods caused significant disruption and infrastructure damage; CBUAE identifies flooding and extreme weather among physical climate risks. KPIs: portfolio/collateral exposure to flood-prone areas; uninsured exposure; expected credit losses.
drivers.keySources: CBUAE Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation

drivers.name: Sea-level rise and coastal exposure
drivers.logic: Sea-level rise and coastal hazards can damage property, infrastructure and other collateral, increasing credit and valuation risks for banks with coastal exposure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPI: % loan/collateral exposure in coastal/high-risk zones; property values at risk; insured vs. uninsured exposure. Particularly relevant to UAE real estate, infrastructure and tourism portfolios.
drivers.keySources: UAE NDC 3.0 + CBUAE Climate Risk Regulation

drivers.name: Physical risks to real estate portfolios
drivers.logic: Climate hazards can reduce property/infrastructure values, increase maintenance and insurance costs and disrupt project cash flows, affecting mortgage, corporate and project-finance portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPI: portfolio exposure to climate-sensitive real estate/infrastructure; collateral value at risk; insurance coverage; project-level climate-risk assessments.
drivers.keySources: CBUAE Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation

drivers.name: Transition risk from oil & gas exposure
drivers.logic: Global decarbonization, changing energy demand, technology and carbon policies can reduce profitability and asset values of oil & gas borrowers, affecting banks' credit exposure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Oil & gas remains highly material to the UAE economy and emissions profile. KPIs: bank exposure to oil & gas; financed emissions; borrower carbon intensity; concentration risk; exposure to transition-sensitive assets.
drivers.keySources: UAE NDC 3.0 + CBUAE Climate Risk Regulation

drivers.name: Energy-transition risk across corporate portfolios
drivers.logic: Changes in energy technologies, carbon policies, customer demand and financing conditions can affect borrowers across sectors, creating broader portfolio-level transition risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPI: financed emissions; portfolio carbon intensity; exposure to transition-sensitive sectors; portfolio alignment with UAE climate targets.
drivers.keySources: CBUAE Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation

drivers.name: CBAM exposure of UAE exporters
drivers.logic: Banks financing UAE exporters may face indirect transition risk as CBAM increases carbon-related costs and competitiveness pressure for borrowers exporting covered goods to the EU.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Definitive CBAM regime from 1 Jan 2026; covers cement, iron & steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. KPIs: bank exposure to CBAM-covered exporters; EU export share; embedded emissions; estimated CBAM cost.

drivers.name: Supply-chain ESG, Responsible Sourcing & Emissions Requirements
drivers.logic: International customers and value-chain partners increasingly require suppliers to demonstrate ESG performance, responsible sourcing and emissions management. Failure to meet requirements can affect borrowers' market access, costs and competitiveness, creating indirect credit risk for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Supplier ESG due diligence; GHG/Scope 3 data; mineral/material traceability; human-rights due diligence; supplier emissions targets. KPIs: % portfolio exposed to export-oriented/high-risk supply chains; borrowers subject to buyer ESG requirements; supply-chain emissions.

drivers.name: Saudi Arabia NDC / Second NDC
drivers.logic: National emissions targets increase transition pressure on corporate borrowers and create financing demand for decarbonization and climate-resilient investment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Second NDC target: 278 MtCO₂e annual emissions reduction by 2030 through the Circular Carbon Economy approach; sectoral mitigation measures and investment needs.

drivers.name: Saudi Green Initiative
drivers.logic: SGI translates national climate objectives into large-scale emissions-reduction, renewable-energy and environmental investment programmes, affecting bank sector exposure and creating financing opportunities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 278 MtCO₂e/year emissions reduction by 2030; 50% renewable electricity target by 2030; >SAR 705bn investment across 86 initiatives reported in 2024.

drivers.name: Net Zero 2060 Commitment
drivers.logic: The long-term net-zero commitment increases transition expectations for banks and borrowers and supports demand for transition finance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Net zero by 2060

drivers.name: Sustainable Finance Framework & Regulatory Development
drivers.logic: Saudi financial authorities are progressively developing sustainable-finance practices and frameworks, increasing expectations for financial institutions to integrate climate and sustainability considerations into financing and risk management.
drivers.evidenceKpi: SAMA has incorporated climate-related financial-risk assessment into its financial-stability work; Saudi banks have established ESG structures and developed green-finance activities.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) – Financial Stability Report 2023

drivers.name: Climate-related financial risk management
drivers.logic: Physical and transition risks can affect borrowers, collateral and financial stability, requiring banks to identify, assess and manage climate-related financial risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: SAMA has assessed banks' exposures to high-GHG-emitting sectors, including credit exposures and investment activities, and continues to assess climate-related financial risks.

drivers.name: Saudi Green Financing Framework
drivers.logic: The framework establishes a formal basis for financing eligible green expenditures and issuing green bonds, creating opportunities for banks to arrange, invest in and finance eligible green projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Framework issued March 2024; Saudi Arabia completed its first international green bond issuance in February 2025, including a EUR 1.5bn (SAR 5.9bn) green tranche; order book reached ~EUR 10bn.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Ministry of Finance / SAMA Financial Stability Report 2025

drivers.name: Green Bonds & Green Sukuk
drivers.logic: Green debt issuance creates opportunities for banks to act as arrangers, investors, underwriters and financiers of eligible green projects; sukuk adds a strong Islamic-finance channel.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EUR 1.5bn green tranche issued in 2025 as part of Saudi Arabia's first international green bond; order book reportedly reached ~EUR 10bn.

drivers.name: Sustainability-linked financing
drivers.logic: Sustainability-linked loans and bonds allow banks to link financing terms to measurable borrower sustainability performance, supporting transition across corporate portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPI: SLL/SLB volume; number of transactions; sustainability KPIs and targets; margin adjustments linked to performance.

drivers.name: Transition Finance
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's decarbonization pathway creates demand for financing companies in emissions-intensive sectors that require capital to reduce emissions while continuing their transition.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Green Financing Framework includes transition-related financing considerations
drivers.keySources: Saudi Ministry of Finance – Green Financing Framework

drivers.name: Climate & Sustainable Infrastructure Investment
drivers.logic: Large-scale renewable-energy, transport, water and other infrastructure programmes create demand for bank project finance, corporate lending and capital-market financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPI: sustainable-infrastructure financing volume; project-finance exposure; renewable-energy/project pipeline; private capital mobilized.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Ministry of Finance – Budget / Infrastructure Investment

drivers.name: Extreme heat
drivers.logic: Extreme heat can reduce labour productivity, increase cooling and operating costs, damage infrastructure and weaken borrower cash flows, creating physical credit risk for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia identifies extreme heat and rising temperatures as critical climate challenges. KPIs: exposure to heat-sensitive sectors/assets; heat-related operating losses; cooling costs; climate-related credit losses.

drivers.name: Water scarcity
drivers.logic: Severe water scarcity can constrain production and increase costs for water-dependent borrowers, particularly agriculture, utilities and industry, transmitting physical risk into bank portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia has very low annual rainfall, no permanent rivers/lakes and heavy dependence on groundwater; water scarcity is identified as one of the Kingdom's most pressing climate concerns.

drivers.name: Drought & Desertification
drivers.logic: Drought and land degradation can reduce agricultural productivity, damage land-based assets and increase operating costs, affecting borrowers' cash flows and collateral values.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Over 80% of Saudi Arabia's land is desert; the government identifies drought and desertification as major climate vulnerabilities, with implications for agriculture, biodiversity and land productivity.

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall & Flash Flooding
drivers.logic: Heavy rainfall and flash floods can damage borrower assets and collateral, interrupt operations and reduce repayment capacity, creating credit and operational risks for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's climate-risk assessment identifies heavy rainfall and flash flooding among relevant hazards.

drivers.name: Coastal and sea-level risks
drivers.logic: Sea-level rise and coastal hazards can affect real estate, ports, tourism, industrial facilities and infrastructure, creating collateral and project-finance risks for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's adaptation framework explicitly considers coastlines and seas as climate-sensitive assets/ecosystems.

drivers.name: Physical risk to infrastructure and real estate
drivers.logic: Heat, flooding, water stress and other hazards can damage infrastructure and property, increase maintenance/insurance costs and disrupt project cash flows, affecting banks' collateral and project-finance portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi adaptation priorities explicitly cover infrastructure and urban development. KPIs: climate-sensitive infrastructure exposure; real-estate collateral at risk; insurance coverage; project-level climate-risk assessments.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Arabia – BTR1; SAMA Financial Stability Report

drivers.name: Transition risk from oil & gas exposure
drivers.logic: Global energy-transition policies, technology changes and shifts in energy demand can reduce profitability and asset values of oil & gas borrowers, creating concentration and credit risks for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: SAMA has already conducted a preliminary assessment of Saudi banks' exposures to high-GHG-emitting sectors, including both credit exposures and investment activities.

drivers.name: Energy-transition risk
drivers.logic: Changes in energy technologies, climate policies, carbon constraints and market demand can affect borrowers across sectors, creating broader portfolio-wide transition risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: SAMA identifies credit and market risks as potential financial-stability transmission channels and has assessed banks' exposure to high-emission sectors.

drivers.name: Climate risks to agriculture and food security
drivers.logic: Heat, drought and water scarcity can reduce agricultural productivity and increase food-system costs, affecting agricultural and food-related borrowers and banks' rural/agri portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia identifies agriculture, water and food security as climate-sensitive areas; water scarcity and drought directly threaten agricultural production.

drivers.name: EU CBAM Exposure of Saudi Exporters
drivers.logic: Banks financing Saudi exporters to the EU may face indirect transition risk through borrowers exposed to CBAM-related carbon costs and competitiveness pressures.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CBAM definitive regime applies from 1 Jan 2026 and covers cement, iron & steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen.

drivers.name: International Supply-chain ESG & Due-diligence Requirements
drivers.logic: International customers and business partners increasingly expect suppliers to demonstrate environmental, social and responsible-business practices. Failure to meet these requirements can affect borrowers' market access, costs and competitiveness, creating indirect credit risk for banks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Supplier ESG assessments; emissions data; environmental/social due diligence; human-rights due diligence; supplier codes of conduct.
drivers.keySources: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct

drivers.name: Supply-chain Decarbonization & Scope 3 Requirements
drivers.logic: Requirements from customers, investors and value-chain partners to measure and reduce value-chain emissions can increase data, technology and decarbonization costs for corporate borrowers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Scope 3 emissions; supplier emissions data; emissions-reduction targets; % of suppliers with emissions reporting.

drivers.name: Oil & Gas Supply-chain Emissions Requirements
drivers.logic: Increasing methane and emissions-management expectations across the oil & gas value chain can increase measurement, reporting and abatement requirements for Saudi energy-sector borrowers and their suppliers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Methane intensity; Scope 1–3 emissions; methane measurement/reporting; emissions-reduction targets; flaring intensity.

drivers.name: Paris Agreement
drivers.logic: Global temperature goals accelerate decarbonisation of electricity systems, affecting generation mix, asset economics and long-term investment decisions for energy companies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Well below 2°C / pursue 1.5°C; portfolio alignment; Scope 1–3 emissions; % low-carbon generation; transition capex.

drivers.name: National Climate Targets & NDCs
drivers.logic: National climate commitments translate global climate objectives into renewable deployment, coal/gas transition, efficiency and grid-investment policies that directly affect energy-sector assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: National GHG targets; renewable-capacity targets; coal/gas phase-down plans; power-sector emissions targets.

drivers.name: IFRS S2 Climate Disclosure
drivers.logic: Climate-related disclosure makes transition risks, physical risks and climate opportunities financially visible to investors and lenders, increasing data and governance requirements for energy companies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Scope 1–3; climate targets; scenario analysis; transition plans; climate-related capex; internal carbon price.

drivers.name: Industry-based Guidance
drivers.logic: Power utilities and generators face increasing pressure to reduce GHG emissions while managing the transition of their generation portfolios and energy resources. IFRS S2 industry-based guidance identifies GHG emissions and energy-resource planning as material climate-related disclosure topics for the electricity generation and utility sector, including Scope 1 emissions, emissions associated with power deliveries, and strategies and targets for emissions reduction.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Scope 1 GHG emissions (tCO₂e); GHG emissions associated with power deliveries (tCO₂e); emissions intensity of electricity generation/deliveries (tCO₂e/MWh); % renewable generation; generation capacity by energy source (MW); emissions-reduction targets and progress against targets; capital expenditure/investment in low-carbon generation and grid infrastructure
drivers.keySources: IFRS S2 Industry-based Guidance – Volume B32, Electric Utilities & Power Generators

drivers.name: GHG Emissions Measurement & Accounting
drivers.logic: Standardised GHG accounting enables energy companies, investors and lenders to measure emissions intensity, set targets and compare generation technologies and portfolios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Scope 1–3; tCO₂e/MWh; tCO₂e/GWh; emissions by generation technology; methane where relevant.

drivers.name: Science-Based Net-Zero Targets for the Power Sector
drivers.logic: SBTi's Power Sector Net-Zero Standard establishes sector-specific requirements for electricity companies to set and achieve near-term and net-zero targets. The draft covers a broader range of power-sector activities and emissions, introduces activity-specific metrics and target-setting approaches, and uses regionally differentiated pathways based on the IEA NZE scenario. This increases expectations for power companies to align generation, transmission, distribution and other relevant activities with science-based decarbonisation pathways.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The draft states that power-sector emissions represented nearly 40% of global energy-related GHG emissions in 2023, while electricity's share of final energy consumption is projected to rise from 20% in 2023 to >50% by 2050.

drivers.name: Renewable Energy Expansion
drivers.logic: Rapid growth of renewables is changing the global generation mix and redirecting investment toward renewable assets, grids and flexibility while increasing pressure on higher-carbon generation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 5,149 GW renewable capacity at end-2025; 692 GW added in 2025; 85.6% of global power additions were renewable. Company KPIs: renewable capacity; % generation from renewables; renewable capex.

drivers.name: Solar PV Expansion
drivers.logic: Rapid solar deployment is increasing competition for generation investment and changing the economics and utilisation of conventional power assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Solar capacity additions; installed solar GW; % generation; capacity factor; LCOE; company solar pipeline.

drivers.name: Wind Energy Expansion
drivers.logic: Growth in wind generation creates investment opportunities but increases requirements for grid capacity, balancing and flexible generation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Installed wind GW; annual additions; capacity factor; % generation; curtailment; grid-connection capacity.

drivers.name: Grid Modernisation & Expansion
drivers.logic: Rising electricity demand and rapid renewable deployment are making transmission and distribution capacity a critical constraint, increasing investment needs for utilities and grid operators.
drivers.evidenceKpi: More than 2,500 GW of projects are stalled in grid-connection queues; annual grid investment needs to rise ~50% from today's USD 400bn by 2030. Grid losses; transmission capacity; congestion; connection queues.

drivers.name: Energy Storage Expansion
drivers.logic: Increasing variable renewable generation creates demand for batteries and other storage to provide flexibility, balancing and grid stability.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Global storage capacity needs to increase sixfold to 1,500 GW by 2030; battery storage to ~1,200 GW in the IEA NZE scenario. MW/MWh installed; storage duration; utilisation; storage pipeline.
drivers.keySources: IEA – Batteries and Secure Energy Transitions

drivers.name: Electrification & Rising Electricity Demand
drivers.logic: Electrification of transport, buildings and industry is increasing electricity demand and creating opportunities for generation, networks, storage and flexibility providers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Global electricity demand forecast to grow 3.6% annually in 2026–2030; variable renewables' share of generation projected to rise to 27% by 2030. Electricity demand growth; EV load; industrial load; peak demand.

drivers.name: Energy Efficiency
drivers.logic: Efficiency improvements can moderate electricity-demand growth and alter investment requirements for generation and networks, while creating opportunities for efficiency-service businesses.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Energy intensity; electricity avoided; efficiency investment; kWh saved; % reduction in energy intensity.

drivers.name: Coal Phase-down
drivers.logic: Climate policies, renewable competition and changing power economics increase transition risk for coal-fired assets, potentially accelerating retirement, impairment and stranded-asset risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Coal capacity/generation; retirement pipeline; remaining asset life; utilisation rate; % generation from coal; impairment/stranded-asset exposure.

drivers.name: Natural Gas Transition
drivers.logic: Gas can provide flexibility and reliability during renewable expansion, but longer-term decarbonisation creates risks for new gas investment, utilisation and asset life.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Gas capacity/generation; utilisation; remaining asset life; LNG exposure; methane intensity; scenario-based demand.

drivers.name: Energy Security & Supply Diversification
drivers.logic: Fuel-price volatility and geopolitical disruptions increase the value of diversified generation, domestic renewable resources, storage and resilient infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Fuel-import dependency; generation concentration; reserve margin; fuel-price exposure; domestic renewable share.

drivers.name: Climate Physical Risk to Energy Infrastructure
drivers.logic: Heat, drought, floods and storms can reduce generation efficiency, damage power infrastructure and cause outages, creating operational and financial risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Assets exposed to physical hazards; outage hours; heat days; flood exposure; adaptation capex; expected annual physical loss.

drivers.name: Water Stress & Energy-Water Nexus
drivers.logic: Water availability can constrain thermal generation and hydropower, making water stress a material operational and location-specific risk for energy assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: m³/MWh water withdrawal/consumption; % assets in high-water-stress areas; cooling-water dependence; reservoir levels.

drivers.name: Biodiversity & Land-use Constraints
drivers.logic: Renewable energy and grid infrastructure can create land-use and biodiversity impacts, potentially increasing permitting, development and stakeholder risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Land footprint; protected-area exposure; biodiversity-sensitive sites; mitigation/restoration expenditure; permitting delays.

drivers.name: Just Energy Transition
drivers.logic: Energy-system transformation can affect workers, communities and regions dependent on fossil-fuel industries, creating workforce, social-licence and project-development risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Fossil-fuel employment exposure; workforce affected; reskilling expenditure; community investment; regional economic exposure.

drivers.name: Sustainability Disclosure and Cost of Capital
drivers.logic: Comprehensive, comparable and reliable sustainability disclosure can reduce a company’s cost of capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Empirical research from the University of Oxford found that ‘90% of the studies on the cost of capital show that sound sustainability standards lower the cost of capital for companies.
drivers.keySources: University of Oxford and Arabesque Partners, ‘From the Stockholder to the Stakeholder: How Sustainability Can Drive Financial Outperformance,’ March 2015.

drivers.name: Sustainability Information and Earnings Stability
drivers.logic: Sustainability information can be a strong signal of share price volatility.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Based on historical data, Bank of America Global Research found that companies in the top quintile of sustainability performance experienced the lowest volatility in earnings per share (EPS) in a subsequent five-year period. By contrast, ‘companies with the worst environmental, social and governance records averaged 92% volatility.

The researchers also found that sustainability information was the only reliable signal for predicting EPS volatility, providing better insight than traditional measures such as return on equity.
drivers.keySources: Bank of America, ‘Equity Strategy Focus Point,’ 18 December 2016.

drivers.name: Sustainable Bond Market Development
drivers.logic: The continued growth of sustainable bond markets increases demand for ESG strategies, sustainability frameworks, transparent disclosures, and impact reporting. Companies issuing sustainable bonds are expected to align with internationally recognized market principles and demonstrate the environmental and/or social use of proceeds or sustainability performance commitments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2026: Total sustainable bond issuance reached USD 357.6 billion. Green bonds remained the largest segment, with USD 229.2 billion issued (64.08% of total issuance), followed by Sustainability bonds with USD 60.3 billion (16.88% of total issuance).

drivers.name: Carbon Neutrality Strategy 2060
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's long-term carbon-neutrality pathway drives structural changes in the energy system, including decarbonisation of generation, changes in the energy mix and investment in low-carbon technologies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Carbon neutrality by 2060; national net GHG emissions targeted at 324.4 MtCO₂e in 2030, 209.9 MtCO₂e in 2040, 95.4 MtCO₂e in 2050 and 0 MtCO₂e in 2060; energy sector accounted for 77.6% / 272.5 MtCO₂e of national GHG emissions in 2020; coal contributed >55.7% of national net emissions despite representing 29.4% of domestic fuel-energy consumption; renewable share of electricity generation was 3.6% in 2021 under the Strategy baseline.
drivers.keySources: Strategy for Achieving Carbon Neutrality of Kazakhstan until 2060, approved by Presidential Decree No. 121 (2023). Adilet — Carbon Neutrality Strategy 2060

drivers.name: NDC 3.0 – National Climate Commitment
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's latest NDC establishes its current international mitigation commitment and provides the national framework for reducing emissions, with direct implications for electricity generation and the wider energy system.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Economy-wide GHG reduction of 17% by 2035 vs 1990 unconditionally, up to 25% with international support; at least 35% of electricity generation from renewable and nuclear sources by 2035; energy-intensity reduction target of 20% vs 2021 by 2035.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan NDC 3.0, submitted to UNFCCC in November 2025

drivers.name: GHG Emissions Trading System (ETS)
drivers.logic: Covered installations face regulatory requirements for GHG monitoring, reporting and emissions quotas, creating direct carbon-cost and compliance exposure for carbon-intensive generation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ETS operating since 2013; approximately 50% of Kazakhstan's CO₂ emissions covered in 2024; 229 installations covered; 167.4 MtCO₂ 2025 cap including reserve; 2025 average secondary-market price KZT 455.48/tCO₂; draft 2026–2030 allocation plan envisages annual cap reductions of 10.4–23% vs 2025.

drivers.name: Renewable Energy Support Framework
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's RES framework provides regulated mechanisms for renewable deployment, changing the investment economics and competitive position of conventional generators.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
169 RES facilities / 3,749.62 MW operating as of Q2 2026; 8.621 TWh RES generation in 2025, equal to 7% of total generation; 20-year guaranteed purchase at auction price; annual auction-price indexation; grid-transmission fee exemption; investment preferences.

97 contracted/planned RES projects / 3,013.9 MW; 2,077 MW wind, 707.52 MW hydro, 220.0 MW solar, 9.4 MW biogas; at least 8.4 GW RES capacity targeted by 2035; ~4.8 GW of large-scale projects being developed with strategic international investors.
drivers.keySources: Law No. 165-IV “On Support of the Use of Renewable Energy Sources”. Adilet — RES Support Law

drivers.name: RES Auctions & Capacity Allocation
drivers.logic: Competitive auctions determine the selection and pricing of new renewable projects, creating a regulated pipeline of low-carbon capacity and increasing competition for conventional generation.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
6,935 MW of RES capacity auctioned during 2018–2025; 4,540 MW auctioned under the 2024–2027 plan as of December 2025; 915 MW offered for auction in 2026 (450 MW wind, 265 MW solar, 200 MW hydro); ~260 companies from 14 countries participated in 2018–2025 auctions.

On 15 April 2025, Kazakhstan held its first auction for large-scale RES projects incorporating electricity storage, selecting a 1 GW wind + storage project at an auction price of KZT 18.72/kWh.

drivers.name: Renewable Energy & Energy Storage Integration
drivers.logic: The policy framework is moving beyond renewable capacity additions toward integrating variable renewable generation with storage, increasing the need for system flexibility and changing the technical requirements for new generation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: First large-scale RES + storage auction held 15 Apr. 2025; 1 GW wind + storage selected; winning auction price KZT 18.72/kWh. Large projects under development include 1 GW Masdar + storage, 1 GW TotalEnergies + storage, 1 GW CPIH + storage and 800 MW China Energy wind/solar + storage; total storage capacity in large renewable projects exceeds 3 GWh.

drivers.name: RES Deployment & Capacity Targets
drivers.logic: The scale of contracted and planned renewable capacity indicates a structural expansion of low-carbon generation and creates a growing market for renewable infrastructure, technology and financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 97 projects / 3,013.921 MW planned under signed agreements: 2,077 MW wind, 707.52 MW hydro, 220.001 MW solar, 9.4 MW biogas; at least 8.4 GW RES capacity planned by 2035; approximately 4.8 GW of large projects under development with strategic international investors.

drivers.name: Electricity Market & Investment-Tariff Regulation
drivers.logic: Electricity-market and tariff regulation affects the revenue model and investment attractiveness of generators, while tariff-for-investment mechanisms are being used to finance modernisation and new capacity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Under the updated “Tariff in Exchange for Investment” programme, the annual investment-recovery limit increased from KZT 32bn to KZT 428bn; 25 investment agreements concluded. In 2024–2025, 16 investment agreements with power producers covered approximately 2.78 GW in aggregate.

drivers.name: Balancing Market & Generation Flexibility
drivers.logic: Balancing-market requirements create financial and operational exposure from deviations between scheduled and actual generation/consumption. This is increasingly important as variable RES penetration grows.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Approximately 31.4% of new capacity is planned for load regulation/system flexibility; includes 1.17 GW hydro and 5.6 GW CCGT; 1.5 GW of Ekibastuz GRES-3's 2.64 GW planned for balancing functions; large RES projects include >3 GWh storage.
drivers.keySources: Rules for functioning of the balancing electricity market, Ministry of Energy

drivers.name: Energy Efficiency & Energy Intensity
drivers.logic: Energy-efficiency regulation creates requirements and incentives to reduce energy consumption and improve efficiency, affecting utilities, generators and energy-intensive consumers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 20% reduction in GDP energy intensity vs 2021 by 2035 under NDC 3.0; plant heat rate; generation efficiency; network losses; MWh/unit output; energy-efficiency CAPEX.
drivers.keySources: Law “On Energy Saving and Energy Efficiency Improvement”

drivers.name: BAT & Integrated Environmental Permitting
drivers.logic: Large Category I facilities are subject to integrated environmental permitting and BAT-related requirements, potentially requiring modernization of thermal-generation assets and tighter control of pollutants.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Integrated environmental permit mandatory for Category I facilities; requirements became applicable from 1 Jan. 2025 for relevant facilities; BAT-associated emission levels; SOx/NOx/PM; modernization CAPEX; permit compliance.

drivers.name: Generation Modernisation & Environmental Upgrade
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's modernization policy is driving investment into aging generation assets to improve reliability, efficiency and environmental performance. This creates significant CAPEX and technology-transition requirements for existing generators.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KZT 411bn allocated to the 2025 repair campaign; 10 power units, 63 boilers and 39 turbines repaired; 17,000 km of networks renewed; CHP wear reduced from 64% to 61%; 2026 plans include 9 power units, 55 boilers and 51 turbines and 17.1 thousand km of electricity networks.
drivers.keySources: Ministry of Energy - 2025 results / 2026 energy-sector plan.

drivers.name: Grid Modernisation & Renewable Integration
drivers.logic: Increasing electricity demand and RES deployment require transmission and distribution upgrades. Network capacity and connection availability can constrain new generation and increase investment requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2025 electricity consumption 124.6 TWh (+3.8%) vs generation 123.1 TWh (+4.4%); peak demand 17.724 GW; Southern-zone peak deficit at the 2025 peak required 1.941 GW North–South transit; 2026–27 winter peak forecast 18.2 GW; 2026 plans include 17.1 thousand km of electricity-network modernisation.

drivers.name: Energy Security & Capacity Adequacy
drivers.logic: Rising electricity demand, aging infrastructure and regional supply-demand imbalances create regulatory pressure to maintain sufficient reliable generation and reserve capacity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2025 consumption 124.6 TWh, generation 123.1 TWh; absolute peak demand 17.724 GW, including 209 MW load shedding in the Southern Zone; 2026 generation target 126.5 TWh; approximately 2.6 GW new capacity planned for 2026; Government expects electricity demand to be fully met by Q1 2027 and a sustained surplus by 2029.
drivers.keySources: Ministry of Energy / KEGOC - national power-system and capacity data

drivers.name: Coal Generation Transition & Modernisation
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's continued reliance on coal creates a specific transition exposure. Current policy simultaneously seeks energy security and modernization of coal generation while the 2060 strategy requires long-term decarbonisation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2025 electricity generation: 74.4% from thermal power plants; Carbon Neutrality Strategy identifies coal as contributing >55.7% of national net emissions; current clean-coal development programme includes projects totaling 7.6 GW; Ekibastuz GRES-3: 2.64 GW, with 1.5 GW planned for balancing; Kurchatov coal plant: 700 MW; 2026 major overhauls planned for 9 units.
drivers.keySources: Carbon Neutrality Strategy 2060 + Ministry of Energy energy-sector plans

drivers.name: Renewable Energy Investment Pipeline
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's expanding renewable project pipeline creates growing demand for project finance and long-term infrastructure capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 3.5 GW installed RES capacity; 7% of electricity generation in 2025; at least 8.4 GW RES capacity planned by 2035; ~4.8 GW of large projects under development with international investors.

drivers.name: International Renewable-Energy Capital
drivers.logic: Participation of international developers and investors increases cross-border capital flows into Kazakhstan's renewable-energy sector and provides evidence of international investor appetite.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ~260 companies from 14 countries participated in RES auctions in 2018–2025; major projects include 1 GW Masdar, 1 GW TotalEnergies, 1 GW CPIH and 800 MW China Energy projects.

drivers.name: Energy Storage Financing
drivers.logic: Increasing deployment of variable renewable generation creates a new financing segment for battery storage and hybrid renewable projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: First large-scale RES + storage auction in April 2025 selected a 1 GW wind + storage project at KZT 18.72/kWh; major RES + storage pipeline exceeds 3 GWh.

drivers.name: Grid & Transmission Financing
drivers.logic: Electricity-demand growth and system constraints are increasing financing requirements for transmission and network infrastructure, creating opportunities for infrastructure and institutional capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2025 consumption 124.6 TWh; peak demand 17.724 GW; ~17.1 thousand km of electricity networks planned for modernisation in 2026; KPIs: grid CAPEX, financing raised, transmission capacity, network assets financed.

drivers.name: Generation Modernisation Financing
drivers.logic: Aging power assets require significant rehabilitation and replacement capital, creating financing demand across the electricity sector.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KZT 411bn allocated to 2025 repair campaign; 10 power units, 63 boilers and 39 turbines repaired; CHP wear reduced from 64% to 61%; KPIs: modernisation CAPEX, units upgraded/retired, asset age, efficiency.

drivers.name: Green Bond Financing for Energy
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's green-bond market provides a dedicated capital-market channel for financing renewable-energy and energy-efficiency projects, increasing relevance of ESG-labelled debt.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Samruk-Energy issued KZT 18.4bn debut green bonds on AIX in 2021; proceeds designated for green projects; KPIs: green-bond issuance, outstanding green debt, proceeds allocated to RES/efficiency, investor demand.

drivers.name: Transition Finance / Decarbonisation CAPEX
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's carbon-neutrality pathway creates long-term capital requirements for replacing or modernising carbon-intensive generation and financing lower-carbon capacity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Carbon neutrality target 2060; thermal generation represented 74.4% of electricity generation in 2025; KPIs: transition CAPEX, coal exposure, financed emissions, emissions intensity, low-carbon CAPEX share.
drivers.keySources: Ministry of Energy / Carbon Neutrality Strategy

drivers.name: New Generation Capacity Financing
drivers.logic: Rising demand and capacity constraints are generating a large pipeline of new power projects requiring long-term debt and equity financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Government programme targets 68 projects adding ~6.7 GW by 2029; KPIs: project pipeline, committed CAPEX, debt/equity financing, new MW, financial close.

drivers.name: Extreme Heat & Thermal-Generation Stress
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures can increase cooling demand while reducing thermal-power efficiency and stressing grid infrastructure during peak periods.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's median heat-risk projections show increasing exposure to extreme heat; World Bank identifies potential grid strain, outages and reduced generation efficiency from extreme heat. KPIs: cooling-degree days; peak demand; maximum temperature; thermal efficiency; heat-related outages.

drivers.name: Water Scarcity & Thermal-Cooling Exposure
drivers.logic: Water availability is a material physical risk for thermal generation because reduced water resources can constrain cooling and increase competition with other users.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank identifies Kazakhstan as water-constrained and notes potential vulnerability of fossil-fuel generation to cooling-water constraints. KPIs: water withdrawal/consumption (m³/MWh); water-stressed capacity (%); cooling-water availability; reservoir levels.

drivers.name: Drought & Hydropower Variability
drivers.logic: More frequent/severe droughts can reduce river runoff and hydropower availability while increasing competition for water resources.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank projects more frequent severe droughts under most emissions pathways; KPIs: hydropower generation; inflow/runoff; reservoir levels; drought duration; generation lost due to water constraints.

drivers.name: Flood & Glacier-Melt Exposure
drivers.logic: Changes in precipitation and accelerated glacier melt can increase near- and medium-term flood risks, exposing generation and transmission assets to physical damage and outages.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank projects glacier retreat to increase river flow and flood risk through the middle of the century, followed by longer-term decline in river flows. KPIs: assets in flood zones; flood events; affected MW; outage hours; repair costs.

drivers.name: Extreme Wind & Transmission Exposure
