drivers.logic: Severe wind events can damage overhead transmission and distribution infrastructure, causing outages and increasing maintenance and resilience costs.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan has documented exposure to high wind speeds, particularly near the Russian border. KPIs: wind-speed exceedances; affected line-km; weather-related outages; repair costs; infrastructure reinforcement CAPEX.

drivers.name: Climate-Driven Electricity Demand & Peak-Load Risk
drivers.logic: Increasing temperatures can shift electricity demand upward during hot periods, increasing peak-load pressure and reserve requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's electricity generation reached 123.1 TWh in 2025, with a 126.5 TWh generation plan for 2026; World Bank identifies increased cooling demand and potential grid outages under extreme heat. KPIs: summer peak demand; cooling-degree days; reserve margin; peak-load growth; demand-response capacity.

drivers.name: Climate-Related Infrastructure Damage & Resilience Costs
drivers.logic: Increasing frequency or severity of floods, droughts, heat and other hazards can increase physical damage, maintenance and resilience expenditure across aging energy infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's electricity/heat infrastructure already requires substantial renewal: KZT 210bn allocated to 75 modernisation projects in 2025. KPIs: climate-related repair costs; asset exposure; resilience CAPEX; outage duration; insured losses.

drivers.name: Renewable Equipment Import Dependence
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's rapid renewable-energy expansion creates exposure to imported equipment and associated environmental, social and supply-chain risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan had 169 RES facilities / 3,749.62 MW as of Q2 2026; official investment data reports that all wind-turbine components were imported from China and Russia with zero localisation at the time of reporting.

drivers.name: Critical Minerals & Responsible Sourcing
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's energy transition increases exposure to critical-mineral value chains for batteries, grids and renewable technologies, making environmental, social and governance conditions in mineral supply chains relevant to energy companies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan and EU established a strategic partnership covering critical raw materials, batteries and renewable hydrogen value chains, including sustainable value-chain integration and resilience. KPIs: critical-mineral exposure; supplier-country concentration; traceability coverage; ESG due-diligence coverage.

drivers.name: Supply-Chain ESG Due Diligence
drivers.logic: Procurement of equipment, materials and services exposes energy companies to upstream environmental, labour, human-rights and governance risks, particularly where international supply chains are involved.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: % suppliers ESG-screened; % high-risk suppliers assessed; supplier environmental/social incidents; corrective actions; human-rights due diligence coverage.

drivers.name: Critical-Mineral Traceability
drivers.logic: Increasing reliance on critical minerals makes traceability of origin, custody and processing relevant to responsible sourcing and supply-chain resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA/OECD survey covered 80+ companies across six critical-mineral supply chains; IEA identifies traceability as increasingly important amid concentrated supply chains.

drivers.name: Renewable Equipment Localisation & Sustainable Manufacturing
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's rapid renewable deployment creates pressure to develop domestic manufacturing and more sustainable local value chains for renewable-energy equipment, reducing dependence on imported components while creating environmental and social implications from industrial development.
drivers.evidenceKpi: As of March, all wind-farm components were imported from China and Russia with zero localisation; Kazakhstan imported >24,000 tonnes worth $990m of wind-energy products in 2018–2022.

drivers.name: Sustainable Critical-Raw-Material Value Chains
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's role as a supplier of critical raw materials creates ESG exposure across mining, processing and downstream energy-transition supply chains, including environmental performance, responsible sourcing, traceability and resource efficiency.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan produces 21 of the EU's 34 critical raw materials; Kazakhstan–EU partnership explicitly targets sustainable raw-material, battery and renewable-hydrogen value chains and alignment with high ESG standards.

drivers.name: NDC 3.0 – Climate Commitment
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's updated NDC strengthens the national decarbonisation trajectory, creating regulatory pressure on the energy sector to reduce emissions intensity and improve efficiency.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 50% reduction in GHG emissions per unit of GDP by 2035 vs. 2010; raised from the previous 35% target; net-zero target 2055.

drivers.name: Renewable Energy Deployment & Generation-Mix Targets
drivers.logic: Government targets are rapidly changing Uzbekistan's generation mix, increasing regulatory and investment pressure on conventional generation while expanding renewable capacity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 30% of electricity from green energy in 2025; target 54% by 2030. Installed generation capacity at end-2025: 25.8 GW, including 5.6 GW solar/wind and 2.4 GW hydro.

drivers.name: Energy-Efficiency & Energy-Intensity Reduction
drivers.logic: National energy policy targets lower energy intensity and more efficient use of energy, creating modernization requirements for generation and networks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: energy intensity; MWh/GDP; generation efficiency; network losses; energy-efficiency CAPEX.

drivers.name: Energy Storage & System Flexibility
drivers.logic: Increasing variable renewable generation is driving deployment of storage and flexibility capacity to maintain system reliability.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 1,245 MW of storage facilities included in projects launched/planned for 2025; 10 storage facilities.

drivers.name: Renewable Energy Investment Pipeline
drivers.logic: Rapid renewable deployment is creating a substantial pipeline of bankable generation projects and increasing demand for private and institutional capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 25 GW RES target by 2030; 5 GW Aral wind IPP agreement worth $4.85bn; renewable capacity additions; PPA capacity; investment volume.

drivers.name: Energy Infrastructure Financing Need
drivers.logic: Expansion of generation and ageing networks creates substantial demand for infrastructure and project finance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: $40.5bn / 58 major energy projects planned for 2025; includes 1,413 MW solar, 752 MW wind, 168 MW hydro and 1,245 MW storage.

drivers.name: PPP-Based Private Capital Mobilisation
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's PPP model is becoming a major channel for private investment in energy infrastructure, particularly renewables.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ~$28bn PPP projects signed by 1 Jan. 2025; ~90% in energy, predominantly renewable energy.

drivers.name: Foreign Direct Investment in Energy Transition
drivers.logic: International investors are providing substantial capital for Uzbekistan's generation and clean-energy expansion, increasing the sector's access to cross-border financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: $8.8bn FDI in fuel & energy in Jan–Nov 2025, including $6.3bn electricity and $4.7bn green energy; cumulative energy FDI over recent years reported at ~$35bn.

drivers.name: Grid Modernisation Financing
drivers.logic: Ageing distribution infrastructure and renewable integration requirements create significant financing needs for grid upgrades, providing opportunities for infrastructure and sustainable-finance capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
$100m World Bank financing + $50m co-financing; distribution losses ~13%; >50% of facilities >30 years old; grid CAPEX; upgraded network assets.
69,000 km of transmission networks and 14,000 transformer substations built in 2021–2025; another 45,000 km, 43 substations and 9,700 transformer points planned for 2026–2030.

drivers.name: Small-Hydropower Project Finance
drivers.logic: Development-finance programmes are creating financing structures for smaller renewable projects and mobilising private-sector capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: $150m World Bank concessional financing; project targets small hydropower and involves local developers and banks; electricity demand expected to exceed 120 TWh by 2030, with ~10% currently unmet.

drivers.name: Private-Capital Mobilisation for Energy Transition
drivers.logic: Increasing private participation and international investment in Uzbekistan's power sector is expanding the role of private capital in generation and energy-transition infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Private sector reached 24% of generation by Jan. 2025; $11bn energy investment in 2025; international IPP projects; private investment volume.

drivers.name: Extreme Heat & Rising Cooling Demand
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures increase cooling demand and peak electricity loads while heat can reduce thermal-generation efficiency and strain grids.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's annual cooling-degree days are projected to increase to approximately twice their historical level by the 2090s under RCP8.5. Research cited in the World Bank/ADB climate profile indicates that a 1°C increase in ambient temperature can increase electricity demand by 0.5–8.5%.
drivers.keySources: World Bank / ADB Climate Risk Country Profile – Uzbekistan (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Increasing Temperature Exposure
drivers.logic: Rising average and extreme temperatures increase operational risks for generation assets, grids and electricity demand.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan is projected to experience a 1.2°C–1.9°C temperature increase during this century; UNEP reported that temperatures have already risen at nearly three times the global average, with increases of up to 2.5°C in the Aral Sea region.
drivers.keySources: IMF Uzbekistan Article IV – Climate Risks; UNEP Uzbekistan Environmental Change Atlas (IMF eLibrary)

drivers.name: Drought & Water Availability Risk
drivers.logic: More frequent droughts and water scarcity can constrain hydropower and increase competition for water used by thermal generation and other sectors.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UNEP recorded six dry years between 2019 and 2024. Uzbekistan's official climate reporting identifies long periods of low river flows as a risk to water resources needed for hydropower generation.
drivers.keySources: UNEP – Climate Change and Drought in Uzbekistan; Uzbekistan Biennial Transparency Report (UNEP - UN Environment Programme)

drivers.name: Water Scarcity & Energy-System Exposure
drivers.logic: Water scarcity affects energy reliability through hydropower availability and competition for water resources across thermal generation, agriculture and other users.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's official reporting states that water resources required for drinking water, agriculture, industry and hydropower generation are under threat. World Bank analysis identifies water scarcity as a major climate risk, while the national risk assessment rates water scarcity risk as high.
drivers.keySources: World Bank Uzbekistan Climate and Development Report; Uzbekistan Climate Risk Assessment (World Bank)

drivers.name: Flooding & Extreme Precipitation
drivers.logic: Floods and increasingly variable rainfall can damage generation, substations and transmission and distribution infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's climate-risk assessment gives river flooding a high hazard probability and reports an INFORM flood risk score of 6.3/10. UNEP reports average natural-disaster losses of approximately US$92 million per year.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Climate Risk Assessment; UNEP – Climate Change and Drought in Uzbekistan (World Bank)

drivers.name: Dust Storm & Aral Sea Environmental Exposure
drivers.logic: Dust storms associated with the Aral Sea ecological crisis can affect energy infrastructure, increase maintenance requirements and expose workers and communities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The highest observed increase in maximum temperature was 2.9°C in the Aral Sea region. Uzbekistan's climate reporting identifies dust storms among the particularly dangerous climate phenomena affecting the country.

drivers.name: UAE Energy Strategy 2050
drivers.logic: The national energy strategy drives structural decarbonisation of the power and water system through renewable and nuclear deployment, efficiency improvements and lower-carbon electricity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: By 2030: triple renewable-energy contribution; increase clean-energy capacity from 14.2 GW to 19.8 GW; achieve 30% clean-energy capacity share and 32% clean electricity generation; improve energy-consumption efficiency by 42–45% vs 2019; grid-emissions factor target of 0.27 kg CO₂/kWh.
drivers.keySources: UAE Government / Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure

drivers.name: Net Zero 2050 & Power-Sector Transition
drivers.logic: The UAE's legally and strategically established net-zero pathway creates long-term transition expectations for electricity and energy companies, requiring progressive decarbonisation of generation and energy infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The UAE targets net zero by 2050. The updated Net Zero Strategy includes 25+ programmes across six sectors, including energy and power, providing a national framework for economy-wide emissions reduction.

drivers.name: UAE NDC 3.0 – 2035 Emissions Target
drivers.logic: The UAE's NDC establishes a quantified national decarbonisation pathway with direct implications for the energy sector, which accounts for the majority of national emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Economy-wide target: 47% reduction by 2035 vs 2019, reducing net emissions from 196.3 MtCO₂e to 103.5 MtCO₂e. The IPCC-defined energy sector is targeted to fall from 171.4 MtCO₂e in 2019 to 87.6 MtCO₂e in 2035.

drivers.name: Power & Water Sector Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: The NDC specifically identifies the power and water system as a major mitigation sector, increasing pressure to decarbonise gas-fired generation and energy-intensive water infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Power and water sector emissions were 78.9 MtCO₂e in 2019. The NDC identifies decarbonisation of power and water as a major mitigation priority within the national emissions pathway.

drivers.name: Energy & Water Efficiency Requirements
drivers.logic: National efficiency targets create incentives for utilities and energy companies to reduce electricity and water demand, network losses and energy intensity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE Energy Strategy 2050 targets a 42–45% improvement in energy-consumption efficiency by 2030 versus 2019. Dubai's Demand Side Management Strategy targets 30% reduction in energy and water consumption by 2030 and 50% by 2050 versus business-as-usual.

drivers.name: Clean Energy Attribute Certification
drivers.logic: The UAE's clean-energy certificate framework creates a regulated mechanism for verifying and monetising claims regarding renewable and nuclear electricity consumption.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Abu Dhabi Clean Energy Certificates represent 1 MWh of certified clean electricity and can be issued for eligible renewable and nuclear generation.

drivers.name: Carbon Credits & Carbon-Market Regulation
drivers.logic: Development of the UAE carbon-credit market creates a new carbon-related compliance and financial infrastructure relevant to energy companies developing emission-reduction or carbon projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Cabinet Resolution No. 67 of 2024 establishes the regulatory framework for the National Carbon Credits Registry. UAE capital-market regulation recognises carbon credits as tradable financial instruments.

drivers.name: Emirate-Level Clean-Energy & Demand-Side Targets
drivers.logic: Dubai and Abu Dhabi maintain additional energy-transition targets that can affect utilities and energy developers operating within those markets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Dubai Clean Energy Strategy 2050 targets 100% clean energy production capacity by 2050. Dubai's DSM Strategy targets 30% reduction in energy and water consumption by 2030 and 50% by 2050 versus business-as-usual.
drivers.keySources: UAE Government / Dubai Supreme Council of Energy

drivers.name: Nuclear Energy Integration
drivers.logic: Nuclear power is a structural component of the UAE's low-carbon electricity transition and affects the future generation mix, system planning and competitiveness of conventional generation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant has 5.6 GW of total capacity across four units. Full operation of the four units materially increases the share of low-carbon baseload electricity in the UAE generation mix.

drivers.name: National Clean-Energy Investment Pipeline
drivers.logic: UAE policy targets create a large pipeline for private and public investment in renewable generation, nuclear, grids and low-carbon infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE Energy Strategy 2050 envisages AED 150–200 billion of investment by 2030 and AED 100 billion in financial savings from the strategy's implementation.

drivers.name: Sustainable Finance Mobilisation
drivers.logic: UAE financial institutions are increasingly mobilising capital toward sustainable and climate-aligned activities, expanding financing availability for low-carbon energy infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE banks have committed to mobilise AED 1 trillion (approximately USD 272 billion) in sustainable finance by 2030 under the UAE Sustainable Finance Framework.

drivers.name: Green Bonds & Sukuk for Energy Infrastructure
drivers.logic: The UAE's sustainable debt framework provides financing channels for renewable generation, energy efficiency, clean infrastructure and other eligible green projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE regulatory requirements for green bonds and sukuk establish eligible-project, use-of-proceeds and reporting requirements for environmentally beneficial activities, including renewable energy and energy efficiency.

drivers.name: Solar & Utility-Scale Renewable Investment
drivers.logic: Utility-scale solar remains a major capital deployment opportunity because of the UAE's high solar resource and national clean-capacity targets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: National clean-energy capacity is targeted to increase from 14.2 GW to 19.8 GW by 2030. The target represents approximately 5.6 GW of additional clean-energy capacity within the strategy period.

drivers.name: Grid, Storage & System-Flexibility Investment
drivers.logic: Higher renewable and nuclear penetration increases the need for transmission, storage and system-flexibility investment to maintain reliability and integrate low-carbon electricity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The UAE targets 32% clean electricity generation by 2030. Abu Dhabi's 2026 round-the-clock renewable-energy project combines 5.2 GW of solar PV with 19 GWh of battery storage, demonstrating the scale of emerging storage investment.

drivers.name: Energy-Efficiency & Demand-Side Investment
drivers.logic: National efficiency targets create investable opportunities in building efficiency, district cooling, demand management and energy-service models.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE Energy Strategy 2050 targets 42–45% improvement in energy-consumption efficiency by 2030 versus 2019. Dubai's DSM Strategy targets 30% demand-side savings by 2030 and 50% by 2050 versus business-as-usual.
drivers.keySources: UAE Government / Dubai Supreme Council of Energy

drivers.name: Extreme Heat & Cooling Demand
drivers.logic: Extreme heat and humidity increase air-conditioning demand, peak loads and grid stress while reducing generation efficiency and increasing thermal stress on energy infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank identifies extreme heat as a material risk to UAE energy and utility systems, including increased electricity demand, grid stress and reduced generation efficiency. UAE temperatures can exceed 50°C during summer, while air conditioning represents a major component of electricity demand.
drivers.keySources: World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Water Scarcity & Energy–Water Nexus
drivers.logic: Severe water scarcity creates interconnected risks because electricity generation, cooling and desalination are closely linked in the UAE.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The UAE has extremely low natural freshwater availability and relies heavily on desalination for municipal water supply. The IEA identifies the Middle East as the world's largest desalination market and highlights the energy-intensive nature of desalination, creating a strong energy–water interdependency.

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall & Flash Flooding
drivers.logic: Extreme rainfall can disrupt substations, transmission corridors, solar facilities and other infrastructure designed historically for an arid climate.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank's UAE climate-risk data identify extreme precipitation and flooding as relevant physical climate hazards. The exceptional April 2024 rainfall event caused widespread flooding across the UAE and demonstrated the potential for severe disruption from extreme precipitation.
drivers.keySources: World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Coastal Exposure & Sea-Level Rise
drivers.logic: A significant share of UAE energy and water infrastructure is located in coastal areas, creating long-term exposure to sea-level rise and coastal flooding.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank/IPCC projections provide UAE-specific sea-level-rise scenarios through 2150 under multiple SSP pathways. The UAE's concentration of major electricity-generation and desalination facilities along the coast increases the relevance of long-term coastal exposure.

drivers.name: Compound Heat–Humidity Risk
drivers.logic: High temperature combined with humidity can intensify cooling demand and increase operational and workforce stress beyond temperature alone.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank's UAE heat-risk assessment incorporates combined temperature and humidity thresholds and identifies substantial exposure to compounded heat conditions.
drivers.keySources: World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Clean-Energy Technology Supply-Chain Dependence
drivers.logic: Rapid deployment of solar PV, battery storage and other clean-energy technologies increases the UAE power sector’s dependence on global equipment manufacturers and logistics networks. Concentration in manufacturing and potential trade or logistics disruptions can create equipment shortages, project delays and cost pressure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE targets an increase in installed clean-energy capacity from 14.2 GW to 19.8 GW by 2030, alongside a tripling of renewable energy capacity. The scale-up implies substantial procurement requirements for solar modules, inverters, storage systems and associated equipment.

drivers.name: Critical Minerals Supply Concentration & Price Exposure
drivers.logic: Expansion of solar, battery storage and grid infrastructure increases indirect exposure to concentrated global supply chains for copper, lithium, graphite, nickel and rare earth elements. Supply disruptions or export restrictions can increase the cost and reduce the availability of clean-energy equipment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, the average share of the top refined supplier across key energy minerals reached 70%. IEA projects a potential 25% copper supply deficit in 2035 under its 2026 outlook. Lithium demand has grown by around 25% annually over the past two years.

drivers.name: Grid Equipment & Infrastructure Bottlenecks
drivers.logic: Accelerating renewable deployment and rising electricity demand require significant expansion of transmission and distribution infrastructure. Global shortages of transformers, cables and other grid components can constrain connection of new generation and increase project costs and delivery times.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA estimates that procurement of large power transformers can take up to four years, while cable and transformer lead times have almost doubled since 2021. Global supply-chain constraints are becoming a limiting factor for grid expansion.

drivers.name: Energy Storage & Flexibility Dependence
drivers.logic: The UAE’s rapid expansion of solar generation increases the need for storage and other flexibility resources to manage intermittency and maintain system reliability. This creates growing dependence on battery technologies, storage equipment and associated supply chains.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The UAE targets 19.8 GW of clean-energy capacity by 2030 and its long-term decarbonisation pathway identifies storage as necessary to manage solar intermittency. Abu Dhabi’s 2026 round-the-clock project combines 5.2 GW of solar PV with 19 GWh of battery storage, illustrating the increasing scale of storage deployment.

drivers.name: Natural Gas Dependence & Fuel-Supply Exposure
drivers.logic: Despite the rapid expansion of clean energy, gas-fired generation remains an important source of dispatchable power in the UAE. Continued reliance on gas exposes power producers to fuel availability, gas infrastructure reliability and fluctuations in fuel economics during the transition toward a lower-carbon generation mix.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Natural gas remains a major component of the UAE’s electricity system, alongside nuclear and rapidly expanding solar generation. The UAE’s 2030 strategy targets 32% clean-energy generation, implying continued reliance on conventional generation for the remainder of the power mix.

drivers.name: Conventional Generation Transition & Stranded-Asset Risk
drivers.logic: Increasing renewable and nuclear generation, together with tighter national decarbonisation objectives, may alter the utilisation and long-term economics of existing gas-fired assets. Assets designed for baseload operation may increasingly need to provide flexible or balancing capacity, potentially affecting utilisation, revenues and economic life.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE Energy Strategy 2050 targets 32% clean-energy generation by 2030, while NDC 3.0 commits the UAE to a 47% reduction in economy-wide GHG emissions by 2035 from 2019 levels, reducing emissions from 196.3 MtCO₂e to 103.5 MtCO₂e. (u.ae)

drivers.name: Saudi Vision 2030 – Electricity-Mix Diversification
drivers.logic: Vision 2030 and the Kingdom's electricity-sector strategy are restructuring generation away from oil and other liquid fuels toward natural gas and renewable energy. This changes the long-term generation mix and the economics of conventional generation assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Ministry of Energy's Optimal Energy Mix Program targets approximately 50% natural gas and 50% renewable energy in electricity generation by 2030, with liquid fuels progressively displaced.
drivers.keySources: Ministry of Energy / Saudi National Platform

drivers.name: National Renewable Energy Program (NREP)
drivers.logic: NREP establishes the national framework for competitive procurement and development of utility-scale renewable generation, creating a structured pipeline for private-sector renewable projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: NREP targets 50% renewable electricity generation by 2030. In 2024, Saudi Arabia announced plans to tender 20 GW of renewable projects annually, with the objective of reaching 100–130 GW of renewable capacity by 2030, depending on electricity-demand growth.
drivers.keySources: Ministry of Energy / Saudi Press Agency

drivers.name: Liquid-Fuel Displacement in Power Generation
drivers.logic: The replacement of crude oil and other liquid fuels with natural gas and renewable generation is a structural policy priority. For generators, this changes fuel economics, operating profiles and emissions intensity while reducing the domestic use of valuable liquid hydrocarbons.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The electricity-sector strategy explicitly prioritises phasing out liquid fuels in power plants and replacing them with natural gas and renewable energy. The Ministry's target is approximately 50% gas / 50% renewable generation by 2030.
drivers.keySources: Saudi National Platform / Ministry of Energy

drivers.name: Saudi Arabia Second NDC – 2040 Emissions Target
drivers.logic: The updated NDC establishes a national emissions-reduction pathway covering the energy, industrial, agricultural, land-use and waste sectors. The target directly increases the importance of decarbonisation across electricity generation and energy infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's Second NDC, submitted in December 2025, aims to reduce, avoid and remove 335 MtCO₂e annually by 2040, using a dynamic baseline and 2019 as the base year. The target covers Energy, IPPU, Agriculture, LULUCF and Waste.

drivers.name: Net Zero 2060 Commitment
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's long-term net-zero commitment establishes a structural decarbonisation direction for the energy system while allowing the Kingdom to pursue its Circular Carbon Economy approach and economic diversification strategy.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia announced a net-zero carbon emissions target for 2060. The target is pursued through the Circular Carbon Economy framework and national mitigation initiatives.

drivers.name: Energy Efficiency & Demand Management
drivers.logic: High cooling demand and rapid electricity-demand growth make energy efficiency a central component of Saudi Arabia's energy strategy. Efficiency measures can reduce generation requirements, peak-load pressure and associated emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi energy-efficiency programmes were reported by the Ministry of Energy as having reduced emissions by 48 MtCO₂ annually, with additional reductions targeted through industry, transport and buildings.

drivers.name: Circular Carbon Economy Framework
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's climate policy incorporates the Circular Carbon Economy model, which seeks to reduce, reuse, recycle and remove carbon emissions rather than relying solely on fuel switching. This creates a policy basis for CCUS, efficiency and carbon-removal investments within the energy sector.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The CCE framework was endorsed by the G20 in 2020 and forms a core element of Saudi Arabia's climate-policy approach. Saudi Arabia's 2025 NDC continues to incorporate emissions reduction, avoidance and removal measures.

drivers.name: Grid Reliability & Electricity-Sector Modernisation
drivers.logic: Renewable expansion and rising electricity demand require a more flexible and digitally enabled electricity system. Saudi electricity policy therefore places emphasis on strengthening the national grid, automation, smart-grid technologies and reliable electricity supply.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi electricity-sector policy explicitly includes reinforcement of the national electricity grid, smart-grid technologies, automation and improved reliability as sector-development priorities.
drivers.keySources: Saudi National Platform / Ministry of Energy

drivers.name: International Carbon-Policy & Export Competitiveness
drivers.logic: Saudi energy and industrial companies increasingly operate in markets where carbon intensity, methane emissions and product-level emissions can influence market access, financing and customer preferences. This creates transition pressure even where domestic regulation remains less stringent.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's 2025 NDC covers economy-wide emissions and targets 335 MtCO₂e of annual reductions, removals and avoided emissions by 2040. The NDC also links climate action to economic diversification and sustainable development.

drivers.name: Large-Scale Renewable Investment Pipeline
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's renewable-energy targets are creating one of the largest utility-scale renewable investment pipelines in the region, increasing opportunities for IPPs, infrastructure investors, lenders and equipment providers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Ministry of Energy announced plans to tender approximately 20 GW of renewable projects annually from 2024, targeting 100–130 GW by 2030, subject to electricity-demand growth.

drivers.name: Renewable Energy Auctions & IPP Financing
drivers.logic: Competitive renewable procurement enables private-sector participation through long-term project structures, creating a scalable financing model for utility-scale solar and wind projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: NREP uses competitive procurement and private-sector participation. The programme's 2030 objective is approximately 50% renewable electricity generation, creating a large pipeline of IPP-scale projects.

drivers.name: Grid & System-Flexibility Investment
drivers.logic: Rapid renewable deployment requires additional transmission, distribution, storage and system-balancing infrastructure. This creates a parallel infrastructure-investment opportunity beyond generation assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi electricity policy identifies grid reinforcement, smart-grid technologies and automation as strategic priorities. The national renewable target of approximately 50% of generation by 2030 increases the scale of required system-flexibility infrastructure.
drivers.keySources: Saudi National Platform / Ministry of Energy

drivers.name: Green & Sustainable Finance Mobilisation
drivers.logic: National climate and renewable-energy objectives are creating demand for labelled financing and transition-oriented capital, particularly for renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable water infrastructure and other eligible projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: PIF's Green Finance Framework supports financing through green bonds, sukuk and loans. PIF's 2025 euro-denominated green bond raised €1.65 billion and was more than six times oversubscribed, with proceeds eligible for renewable energy, energy efficiency and sustainable water projects. (PIF)

drivers.name: Renewable-Energy Localisation & Domestic Manufacturing
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia is pursuing localisation of renewable-energy technologies and energy-sector supply chains, creating investment opportunities in domestic manufacturing, services and technology development while reducing dependence on imported equipment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi electricity policy explicitly identifies maximising local content in electrical goods and services, localising jobs and supporting energy-related R&D as sector priorities.
drivers.keySources: Saudi National Platform / Ministry of Energy

drivers.name: Green Hydrogen Investment
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's renewable-resource base and large-scale renewable pipeline support investment in green hydrogen and derivative fuels, creating new demand for renewable generation, electrolysers, transmission and export infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The NEOM Green Hydrogen facility is designed to integrate up to 4 GW of solar and wind capacity and produce up to 600 tonnes of green hydrogen per day. The project secured SAR 22.9 billion in financing from 23 financial institutions. (NEOM)

drivers.name: CCUS Infrastructure Investment
drivers.logic: CCUS is a central component of Saudi Arabia's Circular Carbon Economy strategy and creates investment opportunities in capture, transport and storage infrastructure, particularly around industrial and energy clusters.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia targets 44 MtCO₂/year of CCUS capacity by 2035, including the Jubail CCUS hub. Aramco identifies an 11 MtCO₂/year Jubail capture target by 2035. (Aramco)

drivers.name: Clean-Energy & Energy-Technology Industrial Diversification
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia is using the energy transition not only to decarbonise electricity but also to create new domestic industries in renewable energy, hydrogen, CCUS and related technologies. This creates opportunities for energy companies to diversify revenue and build new technology capabilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's renewable programme targets 100–130 GW of renewable capacity by 2030; the NEOM green-hydrogen project integrates up to 4 GW of renewable capacity and targets 600 tonnes/day of hydrogen production; Saudi Arabia targets 44 MtCO₂/year of CCUS capacity by 2035. (Saudi Press Agency)
drivers.keySources: Saudi Ministry of Energy / NEOM / Aramco

drivers.name: Extreme Heat & Cooling Demand
drivers.logic: Extreme heat increases air-conditioning demand and electricity peaks while reducing thermal-generation and equipment efficiency. This can increase grid stress and the need for additional reserve and generation capacity during extreme conditions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The IEA identifies extreme heat and cooling as major drivers of electricity demand across MENA. Cooling currently accounts for nearly half of peak electricity demand and around one-quarter of annual electricity demand in MENA; cooling is projected to remain the largest source of electricity-demand growth through 2035. (IEA)

drivers.name: Compound Heat & Operational Stress
drivers.logic: High temperatures combined with humidity increase heat stress for workers and can constrain outdoor construction, maintenance and emergency-response activities. The same conditions can increase cooling requirements and operational stress across power infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank heat-risk analysis evaluates Saudi Arabia using thresholds up to 45°C daytime temperature and heat-index thresholds up to 41°C, and identifies strained grids, potential outages and reduced power-generation efficiency as energy-sector consequences of extreme heat. (climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org)
drivers.keySources: World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Water Scarcity & Energy–Water Nexus
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's extreme water scarcity creates a direct dependency between electricity and water systems. Desalination is energy-intensive, while power generation and industrial facilities also depend on water availability, creating mutual exposure between water security and energy reliability.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Desalination supplies the majority of daily water needs in Saudi Arabia. IEA estimates desalination typically requires more than 1 kWh/m³, while Saudi Arabia's desalination system includes facilities producing more than 1 million m³/day. (IEA)

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall & Flash Flooding
drivers.logic: Despite its predominantly arid climate, intense rainfall events can produce flash flooding capable of disrupting power plants, substations, transmission infrastructure, access roads and other energy assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank's Saudi Arabia climate portal identifies extreme precipitation events as a country-specific climate hazard and provides historical and projected extreme-event datasets under multiple climate scenarios.
drivers.keySources: World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Coastal Exposure & Sea-Level Rise
drivers.logic: Major energy, industrial and desalination infrastructure is concentrated along Saudi Arabia's Red Sea and Arabian Gulf coastlines. Sea-level rise and coastal flooding therefore create long-term physical risks to strategically important infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank/NASA sea-level datasets provide historical coastal-flooding indicators for Saudi Arabia's EEZ, including thresholds of 40 cm, 60 cm and 80 cm above average high tide for minor, moderate and major high-tide flooding. (climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org)

drivers.name: Climate-Driven Electricity Demand Growth
drivers.logic: Beyond individual heatwaves, persistent warming, population growth and urbanisation increase structural electricity demand, particularly for cooling. This creates a long-term requirement for additional generation, grid capacity and demand-side efficiency.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA projects MENA electricity demand to increase by around 50% by 2035 from current levels, with around 40% of projected growth coming from cooling and desalination. (IEA)

drivers.name: Solar & Wind Equipment Supply-Chain Dependence
drivers.logic: The scale-up of solar and wind generation increases dependence on global manufacturers of PV modules, turbines, inverters, transformers and other specialised equipment. Concentrated manufacturing capacity creates exposure to trade disruptions, logistics bottlenecks and equipment-price volatility.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia plans to tender 20 GW of renewable projects annually and reach 100–130 GW of renewable capacity by 2030, substantially increasing demand for imported and domestically manufactured renewable-energy equipment. (Saudi Press Agency)

drivers.name: Critical-Mineral Supply Concentration
drivers.logic: Large-scale solar, wind, storage and grid deployment increases indirect exposure to global supplies of copper, lithium, nickel, graphite and rare-earth elements. Supply concentration or price volatility can affect renewable and grid-equipment costs.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA identifies significant global concentration in the supply of key energy-transition minerals and highlights growing demand from clean-energy technologies. This is particularly relevant to Saudi Arabia given the planned 100–130 GW renewable-capacity pipeline.

drivers.name: Grid Equipment & Transformer Availability
drivers.logic: Renewable expansion and electricity-demand growth require large volumes of transformers, cables and other specialised grid equipment. Global manufacturing constraints can delay grid expansion and renewable connections.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA identifies transformers and high-voltage cables as critical grid-supply bottlenecks, with procurement lead times increasing significantly as grid investment accelerates globally.

drivers.name: Energy-Sector Localisation
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's energy strategy increasingly emphasises domestic manufacturing and local content, reducing exposure to imported equipment while creating new domestic industrial and supplier ecosystems around electricity and renewable energy.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi electricity-sector policy explicitly targets maximising local content in electrical goods and services, localisation of jobs and development of domestic R&D capabilities.
drivers.keySources: Saudi National Platform / Ministry of Energy

drivers.name: Natural-Gas Supply & Infrastructure Dependence
drivers.logic: As liquid fuels are displaced by gas in electricity generation, the reliability and expansion of domestic gas production, processing and distribution infrastructure become increasingly important to the power system.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Optimal Energy Mix Program targets approximately 50% natural gas and 50% renewable generation by 2030, increasing the strategic role of gas as firm generation capacity.

drivers.name: Paris Agreement & Global Decarbonisation Pathways
drivers.logic: Alignment with the Paris Agreement is driving long-term changes in energy demand, national climate policy, technology deployment and capital allocation. For oil and gas companies, this creates transition exposure through potential changes in fossil-fuel demand, emissions regulation and investment preferences.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Paris Agreement aims to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. Global climate scenarios imply materially different trajectories for oil and gas demand, investment and asset utilisation.

drivers.name: National Climate Commitments (NDCs)
drivers.logic: National climate commitments increasingly translate international climate objectives into domestic emissions policies affecting hydrocarbon production, methane emissions, flaring, energy efficiency and industrial decarbonisation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 194 Parties had submitted NDCs under the Paris Agreement by the 2025 NDC cycle. NDCs increasingly include energy-sector mitigation measures and methane-related policies.

drivers.name: Oil Demand Transition
drivers.logic: Electrification, energy efficiency, alternative fuels and deployment of low-carbon technologies can reduce long-term oil demand growth. This can affect production economics, reserve valuations, project economics and the utilisation of oil-related infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA's World Energy Outlook 2025 shows oil demand trajectories diverging substantially across scenarios, with demand peaking before 2030 in the Stated Policies Scenario and declining more rapidly in scenarios aligned with stronger climate action.

drivers.name: Natural Gas & LNG Demand Transition
drivers.logic: Gas may retain an important role in the energy transition, but increasing renewable generation, electrification, energy efficiency and decarbonisation policies can alter long-term gas demand and utilisation of gas infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA scenarios show materially different long-term gas-demand trajectories depending on climate and energy-policy assumptions. LNG demand and infrastructure utilisation therefore remain exposed to transition scenarios.

drivers.name: Stranded Asset & Reserve Risk
drivers.logic: Long-lived upstream, midstream and downstream assets may become economically impaired if fossil-fuel demand, commodity prices or operating conditions change faster than expected. The risk is particularly relevant for high-cost or carbon-intensive projects with long payback periods.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Reserve life, project breakeven price, asset utilisation, impairment charges and capital expenditure exposure to long-lived hydrocarbon assets are key financial indicators. IEA transition scenarios demonstrate significant divergence in future fossil-fuel demand.

drivers.name: Carbon Pricing & Emissions Costs
drivers.logic: Carbon pricing increases the cost of GHG-intensive operations and can affect the relative economics of different oil and gas assets, particularly high-emissions production, processing and refining facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: As of 2025, 80 carbon pricing instruments were implemented globally, covering approximately 28% of global GHG emissions and generating more than USD 100 billion in government revenue in 2024.

drivers.name: Methane Emissions
drivers.logic: Methane emissions from oil and gas production, processing and transportation have a disproportionately high short-term climate impact. Increasing methane regulation, investor scrutiny and abatement technology can increase operational requirements and create differentiation between producers based on methane intensity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Global energy-related methane emissions were approximately 124 Mt CH₄ in 2025, with oil operations accounting for approximately 45 Mt and natural gas operations approximately 36 Mt.

drivers.name: Routine Gas Flaring
drivers.logic: Flaring wastes valuable hydrocarbon resources and generates CO₂ and methane emissions. International initiatives and regulatory pressure increasingly favour elimination of routine flaring and greater utilisation of associated gas.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Global gas flaring reached approximately 151 bcm in 2024, generating around 381 MtCO₂e of emissions. The World Bank's Zero Routine Flaring initiative targets elimination of routine flaring by 2030.

drivers.name: Climate-Related Financial Disclosure (IFRS S2)
drivers.logic: IFRS S2 increases the consistency and comparability of climate-related financial disclosures, making transition risks, physical risks, emissions and climate-related opportunities more visible to investors and lenders. Oil and gas companies are particularly exposed because of their emissions profile and long-lived assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IFRS S2 requires disclosure of Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 GHG emissions, climate-related risks and opportunities, and information on transition plans and targets where applicable.

drivers.name: Sector-Specific Sustainability Disclosure (SASB Oil & Gas)
drivers.logic: Sector-specific disclosure standards increase comparability of financially material sustainability information across oil and gas companies, including emissions, reserves, water, safety and operational risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: SASB Oil & Gas standards cover metrics including Scope 1 emissions, methane emissions, proved and probable reserves, water management and operational safety across oil and gas activities.

drivers.name: Value-Chain Emissions Accounting (GHG Protocol)
drivers.logic: Standardised GHG accounting increases transparency over operational and value-chain emissions and enables comparison of emissions performance across companies and activities. This is particularly material for oil and gas because downstream combustion can represent a significant portion of lifecycle emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: GHG Protocol provides standards for Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions. For oil and gas, relevant Scope 3 categories include use of sold products.

drivers.name: Investor Climate Disclosure & CDP
drivers.logic: Investor and customer expectations for climate disclosure increase pressure on oil and gas companies to provide transparent information on emissions, targets, governance and transition strategies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CDP's corporate questionnaire covers Scope 1–3 emissions, climate targets, transition planning, governance and risk management.

drivers.name: CCUS & Carbon Management
drivers.logic: CCUS can reduce emissions from refineries, gas processing, hydrogen production and other hard-to-abate operations. It can therefore become an important component of transition strategies for companies with large concentrated CO₂ sources.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Global CO₂ capture capacity reached approximately 50 MtCO₂/year in 2024, with the announced project pipeline potentially increasing capacity to more than 430 MtCO₂/year by 2030.

drivers.name: Transition Finance
drivers.logic: As conventional green-finance frameworks generally exclude unabated fossil-fuel activities, oil and gas companies increasingly face demand for credible transition financing for methane abatement, efficiency, CCUS and lower-carbon projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ICMA's Climate Transition Finance Handbook provides guidance for financing an issuer's transition toward a low-GHG economy, including transition-focused use of proceeds and sustainability-linked structures.

drivers.name: Water Stress & Operational Dependence
drivers.logic: Oil and gas production, refining and petrochemical operations require water for processing, cooling and other activities. Increasing water stress can increase competition for water resources, operating costs and physical disruption risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Oil and gas operations can require substantial water inputs, while water availability is declining in many producing regions. Relevant sector metrics include water withdrawal/consumption per barrel, freshwater use and water-stressed asset exposure.

drivers.name: Nature & Biodiversity Impacts
drivers.logic: Exploration, drilling, pipelines, offshore infrastructure and spills can affect terrestrial and marine ecosystems. Increasing nature-related disclosure and regulation can therefore create operational, permitting and financial risks for oil and gas companies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: TNFD recommends assessment of dependencies, impacts, risks and opportunities related to nature. Oil and gas activities can involve land disturbance, habitat fragmentation, marine impacts and pollution incidents.

drivers.name: Oil Spill & Environmental Liability
drivers.logic: Offshore production, pipelines, tankers and storage infrastructure create risks of accidental releases that can result in environmental damage, remediation costs, regulatory penalties and reputational impacts.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IPIECA identifies oil-spill preparedness and response as a material environmental-management issue for the industry. Relevant indicators include spill volume, number of significant spills, affected area and remediation costs.

drivers.name: Sustainability Disclosure and Cost of Capital
drivers.logic: Comprehensive, comparable and reliable sustainability disclosure can reduce a company’s cost of capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Empirical research from the University of Oxford found that ‘90% of the studies on the cost of capital show that sound sustainability standards lower the cost of capital for companies.
drivers.keySources: University of Oxford and Arabesque Partners, ‘From the Stockholder to the Stakeholder: How Sustainability Can Drive Financial Outperformance,’ March 2015.

drivers.name: Sustainability Information and Earnings Stability
drivers.logic: Sustainability information can be a strong signal of share price volatility.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Based on historical data, Bank of America Global Research found that companies in the top quintile of sustainability performance experienced the lowest volatility in earnings per share (EPS) in a subsequent five-year period. By contrast, ‘companies with the worst environmental, social and governance records averaged 92% volatility.

The researchers also found that sustainability information was the only reliable signal for predicting EPS volatility, providing better insight than traditional measures such as return on equity.
drivers.keySources: Bank of America, ‘Equity Strategy Focus Point,’ 18 December 2016.

drivers.name: Sustainable Bond Market Development
drivers.logic: The continued growth of sustainable bond markets increases demand for ESG strategies, sustainability frameworks, transparent disclosures, and impact reporting. Companies issuing sustainable bonds are expected to align with internationally recognized market principles and demonstrate the environmental and/or social use of proceeds or sustainability performance commitments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2026: Total sustainable bond issuance reached USD 357.6 billion. Green bonds remained the largest segment, with USD 229.2 billion issued (64.08% of total issuance), followed by Sustainability bonds with USD 60.3 billion (16.88% of total issuance).

drivers.name: Science-Based Transition Targets for Oil & Gas
drivers.logic: SBTi's oil-and-gas-sector pathways provide sector-specific metrics and transition pathways for assessing the alignment of oil and gas companies with net-zero objectives. This increases expectations around emissions reductions, production-related emissions, methane and the credibility of corporate transition strategies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: SBTi's oil-and-gas pathway document establishes sector-specific pathways and metrics for assessing the net-zero transition of oil and gas companies.

drivers.name: Carbon Neutrality Strategy 2060
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's long-term carbon-neutrality pathway creates structural transition pressure for oil and gas producers, refiners and infrastructure operators. The sector is exposed both through its own emissions and through potential changes in the country's energy and economic structure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan adopted the Carbon Neutrality Strategy to 2060 by Presidential Decree No. 121 in February 2023. The strategy establishes the national policy framework for transforming the economy toward carbon neutrality.

drivers.name: Updated NDC – 2030 GHG Target
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's NDC translates international climate commitments into a national emissions-reduction pathway, creating longer-term policy pressure on carbon-intensive sectors including oil and gas.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 15% reduction in GHG emissions by 2030 vs. 1990 unconditionally; 25% reduction conditionally subject to international investment, technology transfer and other support. The target applies economy-wide.

drivers.name: Kazakhstan Emissions Trading System (ETS)
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's ETS creates a direct carbon-cost mechanism for covered installations and increases the economic value of emissions reductions and lower-carbon technologies. This is particularly relevant for large upstream, processing and refining facilities with significant combustion and process emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's ETS operates under the Environmental Code and covers regulated GHG emissions from designated installations. Relevant financial exposure includes verified tCO₂e emissions, allowance allocation, carbon price and compliance costs.

drivers.name: Environmental Code & Integrated Environmental Permits
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's Environmental Code strengthens environmental requirements for major industrial facilities. Category I facilities face enhanced permitting and technological requirements, increasing compliance and modernization requirements for large oil, gas and refining assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Category I facilities are subject to environmental permitting requirements and emission limits. The Code establishes technological emission norms and permissible emission standards as part of environmental regulation.

drivers.name: Best Available Techniques (BAT)
drivers.logic: BAT requirements can require major industrial facilities to modernize production processes and deploy technologies that reduce emissions and environmental impacts. This creates regulatory-driven capex requirements for large oil and gas processing facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: BAT-based technological standards form part of the environmental regulation framework for relevant Category I installations. Financial exposure arises through modernization CAPEX, technology upgrades and compliance with technological emission norms.

drivers.name: Methane & Fugitive-Emission Management
drivers.logic: Methane is particularly material to oil and gas because production, processing, storage and transportation can generate fugitive and vented emissions. Kazakhstan's environmental framework increasingly incorporates GHG measurement and emissions management, creating pressure for improved methane control.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Relevant indicators include methane emissions, methane intensity, venting and fugitive emissions, leak-detection coverage and emissions from oil and gas facilities.

drivers.name: Gas Flaring & Associated-Gas Utilisation
drivers.logic: Restrictions on flaring increase the economic and environmental incentive to capture and utilise associated gas rather than combusting it. This is directly relevant to upstream producers operating oil fields with associated gas.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Relevant indicators include flared gas volume, flare intensity, associated-gas utilisation and recovered gas volumes.

drivers.name: Subsoil Use & Hydrocarbon Licensing
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's subsoil regime determines access to hydrocarbon resources and establishes contractual, investment and environmental obligations for exploration and production. Changes in licensing and subsoil policy can therefore affect reserve access and project economics.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan had 345 subsoil-use contracts as of 2024; 14 subsoil blocks were awarded through auctions in 2024, with USD 72.5 million committed to geological exploration.

drivers.name: Gas Industry Development Plan 2025–2029
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's gas policy is shifting toward expanding the domestic resource base, gas processing and transmission infrastructure. This supports investment in gas infrastructure while increasing the strategic importance of gas utilisation and domestic supply security.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The 2025–2029 plan targets a 17% increase in the commercial-gas resource base to 34.4 bcm, an additional 5 bcm of gas-processing capacity by 2029, and development of new gas-processing facilities including the Kashagan GPP (1 bcm/year) and Karachaganak GPP (4 bcm/year).

drivers.name: Local-Content Requirements
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's local-content policy affects procurement and supplier selection across major oil and gas projects, increasing incentives for domestic manufacturing and supplier development while potentially changing procurement economics.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's local content in subsoil-user procurement was 61.9% in 2024, equivalent to KZT 3.8 trillion, with a government target of 62% in 2025 and plans to localise 10 new oil and gas manufacturing facilities.

drivers.name: Upstream Production & Investment Expansion
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan remains a major hydrocarbon producer and continues investing in large fields, creating substantial capital requirements but also increasing long-term exposure to commodity cycles and transition risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan produced 87.7 Mt of oil in 2024. Government plans initially targeted 96.2 Mt in 2025, with the increase driven principally by the Tengiz expansion.

drivers.name: Tengiz Expansion
drivers.logic: The Tengiz expansion materially increases Kazakhstan's upstream production capacity and therefore represents significant long-duration capital exposure to oil markets, export infrastructure and transition scenarios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Tengiz expansion was the principal driver of the increase in Kazakhstan's 2025 oil production and exports. The Ministry reported that the project was fully completed in 2025.

drivers.name: Gas Processing Infrastructure Investment
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's gas-processing deficit creates a substantial investment pipeline for converting raw gas into commercial gas and supporting domestic supply.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Government plan targets +5 bcm/year of gas-processing capacity by 2029. Planned projects include 1 bcm/year Kashagan GPP and 4 bcm/year Karachaganak GPP.

drivers.name: Refinery Modernisation & Downstream Investment
drivers.logic: Modernisation and expansion of Kazakhstan's refineries create capital requirements for increasing processing capacity, improving product quality and strengthening environmental performance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan processed approximately 17.9 Mt of crude in 2024. The government's 2026 programme envisages 18.2 Mt of crude processing and 15.5 Mt of petroleum products.

drivers.name: Oil Export Revenue & Commodity-Price Exposure
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's dependence on hydrocarbon exports makes oil and gas companies and the broader sector sensitive to global oil prices, refining margins, export volumes and geopolitical disruptions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan exported 78.7 Mt of oil in 2025, an 11.6% increase over the government's annual plan. Hydrocarbon export volumes therefore remain a major determinant of sector revenues and capital-generation capacity.

drivers.name: Extreme Heat
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures can affect worker safety, equipment performance, cooling requirements and operating efficiency across upstream, refining and transportation assets. Heat can be particularly material for outdoor oilfield operations and infrastructure exposed to prolonged summer extremes.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank climate projections show increasing exposure to extreme heat thresholds across Kazakhstan, with heat risk expanding geographically and seasonally under higher-emissions scenarios. Relevant indicators include days above 35°C/40°C, heatwave duration and heat-related operational disruption.
drivers.keySources: World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Water Stress & Drought
drivers.logic: Water scarcity can constrain upstream production, refining and processing where water is required for drilling, cooling and other industrial processes. Drought can also increase competition for water between industrial, agricultural and municipal users.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's climate-risk profile identifies drought as a significant natural hazard, while future climate conditions can increase water stress in vulnerable regions. Relevant indicators include water withdrawal/consumption, water intensity per barrel, freshwater dependence and assets located in water-stressed basins.

drivers.name: Flooding & Extreme Precipitation
drivers.logic: Flooding can damage wells, roads, pipelines, storage facilities, power infrastructure and processing assets and can interrupt transport links connecting production sites with export infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank identifies flooding as one of Kazakhstan's major climate-related natural hazards, alongside drought and other extreme events.

drivers.name: Caspian Sea Level Decline
drivers.logic: Declining Caspian Sea levels can affect offshore oil operations, marine logistics, port accessibility and coastal infrastructure. For Kazakhstan's western oil-producing region, this creates a distinctive physical climate risk that is not captured by generic flood or heat drivers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank identifies changes in the Caspian Sea as a regional climate risk. Lower water levels can affect port access, navigation depth and coastal/offshore infrastructure.

drivers.name: Extreme Weather & Infrastructure Disruption
drivers.logic: Increasing climate variability can disrupt transport corridors, electricity supply, roads and other infrastructure supporting remote oil and gas operations. Because upstream assets depend on extensive supporting infrastructure, disruption can propagate across the value chain.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's climate-risk profile identifies floods, droughts, heatwaves and other natural hazards as relevant physical risks.

drivers.name: CPC Export Route Concentration & Cross-Border Infrastructure Dependence
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's oil exports are highly concentrated in the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) route, creating material exposure to cross-border infrastructure disruptions, geopolitical events, operational incidents and restrictions affecting the corridor.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, Kazakhstan exported 78.7 Mt of oil, of which 64.8 Mt moved through CPC — approximately 82% of total exports.

drivers.name: Export Route Diversification
drivers.logic: High dependence on CPC increases the importance of alternative export routes through the Caspian and Azerbaijan. However, diversification depends on sufficient port, tanker, rail and downstream pipeline capacity, creating a Kazakhstan-specific infrastructure and supply-chain resilience challenge.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan transported approximately 1.2 Mt/year through BTC in 2025, while Azerbaijan indicated capacity to receive up to 2.2 Mt/year of Kazakh oil.

drivers.name: Localisation of Oil & Gas Supply Chains
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's industrial policy increasingly seeks to localise oil and gas equipment manufacturing and increase domestic procurement, reducing external supply dependence while creating obligations and opportunities for operators and suppliers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's local content in subsoil-user procurement was 61.9% in 2024 (KZT 3.8 trillion), with a 62% target for 2025 and plans to localise 10 new oil and gas manufacturing facilities.

drivers.name: Gas Processing & Infrastructure Capacity Constraints
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's ability to monetise associated and raw gas depends on adequate processing and transportation capacity. Insufficient processing infrastructure can constrain production utilisation and increase flaring or reinjection requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The 2025–2029 government plan identifies gas-processing expansion as a priority and targets 5 bcm of additional processing capacity by 2029, including Kashagan and Karachaganak facilities.

drivers.name: Caspian Marine Logistics Dependence
drivers.logic: Oil transported through the Caspian depends on port, tanker and marine infrastructure. Changes in Caspian water levels can therefore create both a climate risk and a supply-chain/logistics risk for alternative export routes.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The combination of Kazakhstan's western oil production, Aktau/Caspian logistics and declining Caspian water levels creates exposure to navigation depth, port accessibility and marine transport capacity.

drivers.name: Uzbekistan NDC 3.0 – Economy-wide Decarbonisation Pathway
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's updated NDC establishes a stronger national decarbonisation pathway, increasing transition expectations for the energy sector and emissions-intensive oil and gas operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan commits to reducing GHG emissions intensity per unit of GDP by 50% by 2035 compared with 2010. The NDC identifies the energy sector as the country's largest source of emissions and includes further decarbonisation of energy production and consumption as a core mitigation pathway. Relevant company indicators include Scope 1–2 emissions, emissions intensity and emissions reductions from operational efficiency and fuel switching.

drivers.name: Methane-Emission Reduction Commitment
drivers.logic: Methane is a particularly material ESG and climate issue for Uzbekistan because natural gas dominates the country's energy system and emissions can arise throughout production, processing, transmission and distribution infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan has committed to reducing methane emissions as part of its participation in the Global Methane Pledge, supporting the global objective of reducing anthropogenic methane emissions by at least 30% by 2030 from 2020 levels. Relevant indicators include methane emissions, methane intensity, fugitive emissions and methane-abatement performance.

drivers.name: National Green Economy Transition Strategy 2019–2030
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's green-transition strategy integrates energy efficiency, resource efficiency and lower-carbon development into national economic policy, creating pressure to improve the efficiency of energy-intensive industrial and hydrocarbon infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The 2019–2030 strategy prioritises energy efficiency in basic sectors and originally targeted a doubling of energy efficiency. The subsequent 2030 Green Growth Programme targets at least a 20% improvement in industrial energy efficiency and a 30% reduction in GDP energy intensity.

drivers.name: Energy Efficiency and Energy-Saving Policy
drivers.logic: High energy intensity and losses across Uzbekistan's energy system create regulatory and economic pressure to improve efficiency in gas production, processing, transport and industrial consumption.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The national green-growth programme targets at least a 20% improvement in industrial energy efficiency and includes energy-saving measures and efficiency improvements across industrial infrastructure. Relevant indicators include energy consumption per unit of output, fuel use, compressor efficiency and operational emissions intensity.

drivers.name: Associated Gas Utilisation and Flaring Reduction
drivers.logic: Reducing associated-gas flaring improves resource efficiency and lowers CO₂ and methane emissions from hydrocarbon production.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's updated subsoil legislation permits flaring or cold discharge of produced hydrocarbons only in specified circumstances, including safety requirements and commissioning activities. Relevant performance indicators include flaring volume, flaring intensity and associated-gas utilisation.
drivers.keySources: World Bank Global Gas Flaring Tracker

drivers.name: Subsoil Use and Hydrocarbon Licensing Framework
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's Law on Subsoil establishes the legal framework for hydrocarbon exploration and production and integrates environmental, social and operational obligations into subsoil-use activities. Oil and gas operators require authorisation to use subsoil plots and must comply with environmental assessment, environmental management, decommissioning and rehabilitation requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Under Law No. ZRU-987 (2024), hydrocarbon activities require permits for subsoil use. Before hydrocarbon exploration and production, operators must obtain required environmental assessments and approvals. Hydrocarbon producers must implement an approved environmental and social management plan, comply with environmental requirements for waste storage and disposal, and make contributions to a decommissioning fund for facility closure and land restoration.

drivers.name: Gas Infrastructure Modernisation Investment
drivers.logic: Ageing gas transmission infrastructure creates a significant investment requirement for pipeline rehabilitation, leak detection and repair, compression, metering and network modernisation. For Uzbekistan's oil and gas sector, these investments have both commercial and ESG value because they reduce gas losses, methane emissions and supply disruptions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank estimates that, without repairs, gas losses from Uzbekistan's transmission network could reach 1.75 bcm by 2030, equivalent to approximately USD 228 million in lost revenue. A World Bank-supported leak-repair programme is expected to recover around 47,500 tonnes of gas annually by 2029 and generate approximately USD 18 million in financial savings. This provides a direct quantitative investment case for methane monitoring, pipeline rehabilitation and leak-repair technologies. Relevant investment indicators include infrastructure CAPEX, gas losses, methane emissions, recovered gas volumes and avoided revenue losses.

drivers.name: Gas Processing and Petrochemical Investment
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's strategy of increasing domestic value creation from hydrocarbons supports investment in gas processing, gas-to-liquids and petrochemical infrastructure rather than relying exclusively on raw natural-gas production. These assets create capital requirements but also increase exposure to emissions, energy efficiency and technology performance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan produced 44.6 bcm of natural gas in 2025, demonstrating the scale of the domestic resource base supporting downstream investment. Existing large-scale downstream infrastructure includes the Kandym Gas Processing Complex, Uzbekistan GTL and Ustyurt Gas Chemical Complex. Relevant indicators include gas-processing capacity and utilisation, processed gas volumes, downstream output, energy intensity and petrochemical CAPEX.

drivers.name: Foreign Capital and Technology for Hydrocarbon Modernisation
drivers.logic: Modernisation of complex upstream, gas-processing and downstream infrastructure requires capital and specialised technologies that may exceed the capabilities of domestic suppliers alone. Energy-sector reforms therefore create opportunities for foreign investors, international operators, technology providers and joint ventures.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's reform programme includes measures to attract private investment into energy-sector modernisation and reforms intended to improve the financial viability and investment attractiveness of the energy sector. The World Bank identifies tariff reform and wider private-sector participation as important mechanisms for mobilising investment in infrastructure modernisation. Relevant indicators include FDI, foreign participation in energy projects, private CAPEX, production-sharing and joint-venture investment.

drivers.name: Methane-Abatement Investment Opportunity
drivers.logic: Methane reduction creates a particularly strong investment opportunity for Uzbekistan because reducing leakage, venting and other operational emissions can simultaneously lower climate exposure and recover gas that would otherwise be lost.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan has committed to reducing methane emissions by 30% by 2030. Globally, the IEA estimates that approximately 70% of methane emissions from fossil-fuel operations can be reduced using existing technologies, while more than 35 Mt of methane emissions could be avoided globally at no net cost based on 2025 energy prices. The IEA estimates that reducing methane emissions from oil and gas operations could make nearly 100 bcm of natural gas annually available to markets globally. Relevant investment indicators include methane-abatement CAPEX, methane intensity, LDAR deployment, recovered gas and avoided emissions.

drivers.name: Domestic Gas-Supply and Energy-Security Investment
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's large domestic gas sector and continuing dependence on gas across electricity, heating and industry create sustained investment needs across upstream production, processing, storage and transmission. Declining production efficiency, infrastructure losses and supply constraints can therefore have significant economic and energy-security implications.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan produced 44.6 bcm of natural gas in 2025. Natural gas accounted for more than 70% of electricity generation according to the World Bank's assessment of the country's power system. This dependence increases the strategic value of investment in reliable gas production, processing and transmission infrastructure. Relevant indicators include gas production, processing capacity, infrastructure utilisation, storage capacity and supply reliability.

drivers.name: Energy Efficiency and Loss-Reduction Investment
drivers.logic: High energy losses and inefficient infrastructure create investment opportunities in efficient compressors and turbines, digital monitoring, advanced metering, process optimisation and infrastructure rehabilitation. For hydrocarbon assets, these investments can reduce both operating costs and emissions intensity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank estimates that the new 1,580 MW Syrdarya 2 CCGT plant will achieve thermal efficiency of more than 60%—approximately twice that of Uzbekistan's ageing thermal fleet. The project is expected to save approximately 1.5–1.7 bcm of natural gas annually, equivalent to up to 3.5% of national annual gas consumption, while reducing emissions by up to 2.8 MtCO₂ annually in its initial years. Separately, projected unrepaired transmission-network gas losses could reach 1.75 bcm by 2030. These figures demonstrate the scale of potential economic and emissions benefits from efficiency and loss-reduction investments.

drivers.name: CCUS and Low-Carbon Industrial Technology Potential
drivers.logic: Concentrated CO₂ emissions from gas processing, refining, GTL and petrochemical facilities could create longer-term demand for carbon-management technologies. However, unlike methane abatement and efficiency, CCUS should currently be treated as an emerging investment potential rather than an established Uzbekistan investment pipeline.
drivers.evidenceKpi: A 2025 Uzbekistan-specific academic assessment estimated potential annual CO₂ storage and utilisation resources of approximately 1,171 MtCO₂, substantially exceeding the country's current annual CO₂ emissions. However, the study also notes that Uzbekistan's existing green-economy strategies do not yet incorporate CCUS as an established technology pathway. Therefore, the driver reflects longer-term resource and technology potential rather than confirmed near-term deployment. Relevant indicators include identified storage capacity, CO₂ capture capacity, concentrated industrial emissions and CCUS project CAPEX.

drivers.name: Water Scarcity and Declining Water Availability
drivers.logic: Water constraints can disrupt gas processing, refining, cooling, drilling and other water-dependent operations. Competition with agriculture and municipalities can increase operating costs and constrain expansion of water-intensive facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's water availability is projected to decline 30–40%, while irrigation demand could increase 25% as climate change reduces glacier-fed flows and increases evapotranspiration and drought frequency. Agriculture already accounts for around 90% of national water consumption, increasing competition for industrial water.

drivers.name: Transboundary Water Stress
