drivers.logic: Oil & gas assets are exposed not only to local water availability but also to upstream changes in the Amu Darya and Syr Darya. Reduced river flows can constrain industrial water supply and increase competition among sectors.
drivers.evidenceKpi: By 2050, water resources are projected to decline by around 5% in the Syr Darya basin and up to 15% in the Amu Darya basin. Only around 9% of the 123 km³ of water resources of the Aral Sea Basin originate within Uzbekistan, highlighting substantial transboundary dependence.

drivers.name: Extreme Heat and Heat Stress
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures can reduce worker productivity and increase health and safety risks, while also affecting compressor, processing, refining and other equipment and increasing cooling requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's average temperature has been increasing by approximately 0.27°C per decade (1950–2013). ADB projects average temperature increases of 1.8–3.3°C by 2050. (Asian Development Bank) World Bank modelling indicates that labour supply in Uzbekistan could decline by up to 2% under 1.5°C warming, 5% under 2°C and 10% under 3°C by 2100. (World Bank)

drivers.name: Drought and Reduced Industrial Water Reliability
drivers.logic: More frequent droughts can create temporary or seasonal shortages of water needed for processing, refining, cooling and other operations, increasing the probability of production interruptions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADB identifies increasing frequency and severity of droughts and a growing seasonal and absolute water supply-demand gap in Uzbekistan. (Asian Development Bank) ADB estimates Uzbekistan's current water deficit at around 3 bcm, potentially increasing to 7 bcm by 2030 and 15 bcm by 2050. (Asian Development Bank)

drivers.name: Flooding and Extreme Rainfall
drivers.logic: Intense rainfall and flash flooding can damage pipelines, roads, compressor stations, processing facilities and other linear or fixed infrastructure, disrupting production and transportation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank identifies rainfall volatility and flooding among Uzbekistan's material climate risks. (World Bank) ADB similarly identifies increasing risks from floods and other extreme events. (Asian Development Bank)

drivers.name: Climate-Driven Infrastructure Damage
drivers.logic: Repeated heat, drought, flooding and other extreme events can accelerate degradation of pipelines, roads, storage and processing infrastructure, increasing maintenance and replacement expenditure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank estimates Uzbekistan may require approximately $340 billion by 2060 for replacing ageing energy infrastructure and decarbonisation measures.

drivers.name: Gas Supply Stress from Declining Domestic Production
drivers.logic: Climate change is not the only physical risk: declining domestic gas production combined with rising demand increases the vulnerability of the gas system to supply disruptions and makes infrastructure efficiency increasingly important.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's natural gas production fell from 53.8 bcm in 2021 to 44.6 bcm in 2024 according to World Bank project documentation. (World Bank) Official statistics report 41.5 bcm in 2024, versus 53.8 bcm in 2021. (SIAT) IEA estimates gas demand could reach 65 bcm by 2030, around 30% above the level at the time of its assessment. (IEA)
drivers.keySources: World Bank; IEA; Uzbekistan Statistics Agency

drivers.name: Climate Transition and Hydrocarbon Demand Risk
drivers.logic: Global decarbonisation can reduce long-term demand for hydrocarbons and increase the risk of stranded or underutilised upstream, processing, refining and transportation assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's energy sector accounts for approximately 75% of national GHG emissions, while the World Bank identifies reducing dependence on depleting natural gas reserves as important for long-term energy security.

drivers.name: Ageing Gas Transmission Infrastructure and Leakage
drivers.logic: Ageing pipelines, compressors, valves and metering infrastructure increase dependence on maintenance, replacement equipment and specialised contractors while creating physical supply-chain disruption and methane risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank estimates that without intervention, cumulative gas losses from Uzbekistan's ageing transmission system could reach 1.75 bcm by 2030, equivalent to approximately $228 million in lost revenue. A 2023 pilot identified around 700 million m³/year of currently unaccounted-for gas. (World Bank)

drivers.name: Dependence on Specialised Oil & Gas Equipment and Technology
drivers.logic: Upstream production, gas processing and transmission require specialised compressors, valves, pumps, drilling equipment, metering, SCADA, leak-detection and processing technologies. Limited domestic supply can create import, lead-time and supplier-concentration risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA identifies modernisation of gas pipelines, compressor stations and the gas transportation system as an important investment requirement. Uzbekistan's gas infrastructure is ageing and requires modernisation. (IEA)

drivers.name: Critical Spare Parts and Maintenance Supply Risk
drivers.logic: Extended lead times for compressors, turbines, valves, control systems and other critical components can increase downtime when infrastructure is ageing and maintenance requirements rise.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank's gas network project specifically targets deteriorating infrastructure and major leaks, while IEA identifies pipeline and compressor modernisation as a significant requirement. (World Bank)

drivers.name: Domestic Gas Supply–Demand Imbalance
drivers.logic: Declining domestic production alongside high and growing gas demand increases dependence on the reliability of upstream producers, transmission infrastructure and alternative supply arrangements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Domestic production declined from 53.8 bcm in 2021 to 44.6 bcm in 2024 in World Bank project documentation, while IEA previously projected demand to reach 65 bcm by 2030. (World Bank)

drivers.name: Gas Network Reliability and Transmission Losses
drivers.logic: The oil & gas sector is dependent on reliable transmission and distribution infrastructure. Technical losses and failures can interrupt supply, reduce revenues and increase methane emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's gas transmission system could lose 1.75 bcm annually/cumulatively by 2030 without intervention, with the World Bank estimating $228m of lost revenue. The 2023 pilot found around 700m m³/year of unaccounted-for gas. (World Bank)

drivers.name: International Methane MRV and Market-Access Requirements
drivers.logic: International buyers and financial institutions increasingly require reliable methane measurement, reporting and verification. Weak methane data can increase market-access, financing and reputational risks for gas producers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Under the EU Methane Regulation, importers must report methane intensity of imported oil, gas and coal from 2028 and demonstrate compliance with a methane-intensity limit for relevant contracts from 2030. Uzbekistan has committed to reduce methane emissions by 30% by 2030. (IEA)

drivers.name: Methane Leakage Across the Supply Chain
drivers.logic: Methane emissions occur throughout production, gathering, processing, transmission and distribution. Leakage therefore creates both environmental liabilities and loss of saleable gas.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA estimates that around 80% of oil & gas methane emissions globally occur upstream, while downstream operations account for the remaining ~20%. (IEA) Uzbekistan's fugitive emissions are particularly associated with gas leakage from corroded pipelines and outdated equipment. (World Bank)

drivers.name: Flaring and Gas Utilisation Efficiency
drivers.logic: Flaring represents both an environmental risk and a loss of potentially saleable gas. Suppliers and operators with high flaring intensity may face increasing investor, lender and buyer scrutiny.
drivers.evidenceKpi: A recent World Bank low-carbon pathway assessment reports that Uzbekistan has historically flared around 1 bcm of natural gas annually on average. (World Bank)

drivers.name: International Supply and Pipeline Connectivity
drivers.logic: Cross-border pipeline dependence creates exposure to geopolitical events, transit constraints, contractual changes and regional gas-market volatility.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA notes that reliance on pipeline-imported gas can create energy-security risks because gas is transported through fixed infrastructure over long distances. (IEA)

drivers.name: Oil / Petroleum Product Import and Logistics Exposure
drivers.logic: Refining and downstream operations may depend on imported crude, petroleum products, catalysts, chemicals and other inputs, exposing companies to international logistics disruption and supplier concentration.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA identifies oil and petroleum-product trade as an important part of Uzbekistan's energy system and notes the country's ongoing refinery and petrochemical modernisation needs. (IEA)

drivers.name: Climate-Resilient Supplier and Logistics Network
drivers.logic: Suppliers, roads, railways, pipelines, warehouses and ports/terminals can themselves be exposed to heat, drought, flooding and water scarcity, creating indirect disruption to oil & gas operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank identifies water scarcity, drought, extreme heat and rainfall volatility as material country-wide risks. By 2030, at least 8 million people are expected to live in very high climate-risk areas, while climate impacts could make Uzbekistan's economy 10% smaller by 2050 without adaptation. (World Bank)

drivers.name: National GHG Reduction Requirements and Decarbonisation Direction
drivers.logic: National climate commitments increase pressure on oil & gas operators to reduce operational emissions, improve energy efficiency, deploy low-carbon technologies and demonstrate credible emissions-reduction pathways. The oil & gas sector is particularly material because of its contribution to national emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE NDC 3.0 targets a 47% reduction in GHG emissions by 2035 vs. 2019, from 196.3 MtCO₂e to 103.5 MtCO₂e. Coverage includes CO₂, CH₄, N₂O and F-gases. (IEA) KPIs: Scope 1 & 2 tCO₂e; tCO₂e/boe; absolute emissions; emissions-reduction %; energy intensity.

drivers.name: Environmental Permitting and EIA for Oil & Gas Projects
drivers.logic: Oil & gas exploration, drilling, production and other projects with environmental impacts are subject to environmental approval and, where applicable, EIA requirements. This creates regulatory requirements around impact assessment, mitigation and environmental monitoring before/throughout project operation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Environmental permit/EIA required for applicable projects; EIA must include mitigation and monitoring measures. Federal framework requires environmental monitoring and reporting. (IEA) KPIs: % projects with valid environmental permits; EIA compliance; environmental incidents; mitigation actions closed on time.
drivers.keySources: UAE Federal Law No. 24 of 1999; Cabinet Resolution No. 37 of 2001

drivers.name: Air Emission Limits and Monitoring
drivers.logic: Oil & gas facilities must control atmospheric emissions from combustion, production and other activities. This creates compliance requirements for emission measurement, prevention of uncontrolled releases and monitoring against applicable limits.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Federal Law Article 48 requires air pollutants to remain within permissible limits; Article 55 requires measures to prevent leakage/emission of pollutants. (UAE Legislation) KPIs: NOx, SOx, VOCs, PM; emission concentrations; number of exceedances; % monitored sources; corrective actions.
drivers.keySources: UAE Legislation – Federal Law No. 24 of 1999; Cabinet Decree No. 12 of 2006

drivers.name: Oil & Gas Emissions Control and Measurement
drivers.logic: Petroleum activities are subject to specific environmental controls covering exploration, drilling, extraction and production. Operators must take measures to reduce emissions and maintain emissions records, making emissions measurement a compliance issue rather than only an ESG disclosure practice.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA identifies requirements for emissions from exploration, drilling, extraction and production, including registration of fuel-combustion and flaring emissions and maintenance of emissions measurement records. (IEA) KPIs: Scope 1 emissions; flaring emissions; emissions registry completeness; emissions exceedances; monitoring coverage.
drivers.keySources: IEA policy database; UAE Federal Law No. 24 of 1999

drivers.name: Petroleum Resource Conservation and Prevention of Waste
drivers.logic: UAE petroleum regulation has historically required conservation of petroleum resources and restricted practices that result in unnecessary loss or waste of hydrocarbons. This supports regulatory pressure to minimise flaring, leakage and inefficient resource use.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The UAE's NDC identifies Law No. 8 of 1978 as having banned routine flaring and prevented air and water pollution in oil & gas operations. (IEA) KPIs: routine flaring; flaring intensity; vented gas; fugitive losses; hydrocarbon recovery.
drivers.keySources: UAE NDC 3.0; Abu Dhabi petroleum-resource legislation

drivers.name: Methane Emissions Reduction and MRV
drivers.logic: Methane is a high-priority component of the UAE's oil & gas decarbonisation agenda. The NDC explicitly promotes near-zero upstream methane emissions, recognised measurement/reporting frameworks and improved monitoring across the sector.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE NDC 3.0 supports near-zero upstream methane by 2030, zero routine flaring by 2030 and use of internationally recognised MRV frameworks such as OGMP 2.0. (UNFCCC) KPIs: methane intensity; CH₄ t/year; % assets covered by LDAR; % emissions measured; OGMP reporting level.

drivers.name: Emissions Reduction and Climate MRV
drivers.logic: For operators in Abu Dhabi—the UAE's largest oil & gas producing emirate—the climate strategy creates additional pressure to reduce emissions from the energy sector and strengthen emissions measurement, reporting and verification.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Abu Dhabi targets a 22% reduction in total emissions by 2027 vs. 2016. The strategy covers 77 strategic projects and includes development of environmental-data reporting to support an MRV programme aligned with the Paris Agreement. (Department of Energy) KPIs: Scope 1–2 emissions; emissions intensity; MRV coverage; reported environmental data; reduction vs. 2016 baseline.
drivers.keySources: Abu Dhabi DoE / Environment Agency Abu Dhabi

drivers.name: CCUS Deployment and Industrial Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Carbon capture is explicitly embedded in Abu Dhabi's climate strategy as a mitigation pathway. For carbon-intensive oil & gas and associated industrial operations, this increases expectations around identification of technically and economically viable CCUS opportunities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Abu Dhabi climate strategy includes expanding carbon capture and storage as a core mitigation pillar. (Department of Energy) At operator level, ADNOC has increased its target to 10 MtCO₂/year capture capacity by 2030. (Adnoc) KPIs: tCO₂ captured/stored; capture capacity; % emissions covered by CCUS; CCUS investment.
drivers.keySources: Abu Dhabi Climate Change Strategy; ADNOC

drivers.name: Gas Infrastructure Safety, Efficiency and Environmental Compliance
drivers.logic: The 2025 Executive Regulation establishes detailed requirements for the design, construction, operation and maintenance of gas systems in Abu Dhabi. For oil & gas companies and gas infrastructure operators, compliance extends across technical, operational, safety and environmental requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Regulation applies to natural gas, LPG and other gas systems and provides for inspections, compliance and penalties. (Department of Energy) KPIs: regulatory compliance rate; gas-system incidents; inspection findings; maintenance compliance; equipment certification.
drivers.keySources: Abu Dhabi DoE – Regulations and Laws

drivers.name: Standardisation of Gas-System Technical and Environmental Requirements
drivers.logic: The Unified Gas Code is being established as a comprehensive framework for gas systems, standardising requirements for design, installation, operation and maintenance. This is particularly relevant to gas-processing, transmission and distribution infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Applies across natural gas, LPG and other fuel-gas systems and is intended to create a single reference framework for gas-related activities. (Department of Energy) KPIs: % assets compliant; certified equipment; inspection findings; gas losses; operational incidents.

drivers.name: Petroleum Products Licensing, Storage and Transportation Compliance
drivers.logic: Petroleum-product trading, transport, storage and related activities require regulatory permits, creating compliance requirements across downstream oil & gas value chains.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Abu Dhabi DoE states that entities involved in petroleum-product trading, storage or transport must obtain the relevant permits; activities include import, manufacturing, storage and transportation. (Department of Energy) KPIs: % facilities with valid permits; permit breaches; storage/transport incidents; inspection findings.
drivers.keySources: Abu Dhabi DoE; Federal Law No. 14/2017; Abu Dhabi Law No. 5/2023

drivers.name: Water Pollution and Industrial Wastewater Management
drivers.logic: Oil & gas production, processing and refining can generate contaminated water and wastewater. Federal environmental legislation requires protection of water resources and controls on pollution, while emirate-level permits impose additional conditions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Federal Law No. 24/1999 establishes controls on water pollution and protection of marine and inland water environments. (UAE Legislation) KPIs: produced-water volume; discharge quality; oil & grease; COD/BOD where applicable; water reuse %; environmental exceedances.
drivers.keySources: UAE Federal Law No. 24 of 1999; local environmental authorities

drivers.name: Hazardous Materials and Waste Management
drivers.logic: Oil & gas operations generate hazardous wastes including used chemicals, contaminated materials, drilling wastes and other industrial waste streams. Environmental legislation therefore creates requirements for handling, treatment, storage and disposal.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Federal Law No. 24/1999 and its executive regulations establish controls for dangerous materials and waste. (IEA) KPIs: hazardous waste generated; % recycled/recovered; compliant disposal rate; spills; waste intensity.
drivers.keySources: UAE Federal Law No. 24 of 1999; Cabinet Resolution No. 37 of 2001

drivers.name: Industrial Energy and Water Efficiency
drivers.logic: Abu Dhabi's energy and water efficiency agenda increases regulatory and policy pressure to reduce energy and water consumption, supporting efficiency improvements across energy-intensive oil & gas operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Abu Dhabi's updated strategy targets 22% lower electricity consumption and 32% lower water consumption by 2030 versus the 2013 BAU baseline. (Department of Energy) KPIs: GJ/boe; electricity consumption; water withdrawal/consumption; water intensity; efficiency savings.

drivers.name: Operational GHG Intensity Reduction
drivers.logic: ADNOC's targets create an important benchmark for operators and contractors in Abu Dhabi's oil & gas ecosystem, even though the target itself should not be classified as a statutory UAE requirement.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 25% reduction in operational emissions intensity by 2030 vs. 2019; ADNOC reported 24.6 MtCO₂e upstream GHG emissions and 7 kgCO₂e/boe intensity in 2024. (Adnoc) KPIs: kgCO₂e/boe; Scope 1–2; absolute GHG emissions; reduction vs. 2019.

drivers.name: Near-Zero Methane and Zero Routine Flaring
drivers.logic: ADNOC's methane and flaring targets set a high operational benchmark for UAE oil & gas producers and suppliers. They are especially relevant for companies seeking to operate within ADNOC's value chain.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC reported 22% methane reduction in 2024, with upstream methane intensity below 0.15%, and an 8% reduction in routine flaring. Target: near-zero methane and zero routine flaring by 2030. (Adnoc)

drivers.name: Operational Electrification and Clean Power Procurement
drivers.logic: Electrification of oil & gas facilities can reduce Scope 1 emissions from gas-fired power generation and is becoming a major decarbonisation pathway in UAE upstream operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC's $3.8bn subsea transmission project is expected to reduce offshore emissions by at least 5 MtCO₂e/year once completed. ADNOC already sources grid electricity for onshore operations from nuclear and solar power. (ADNOC) KPIs: % operations electrified; % electricity from clean sources; Scope 1 reduction; tCO₂e avoided.

drivers.name: Transition & Decarbonisation Financing
drivers.logic: UAE oil & gas companies face growing pressure to demonstrate credible allocation of capital toward emissions reduction, energy transition and climate-aligned technologies. Demonstrated decarbonisation investment can improve access to sustainability-linked / green financing and reduce transition-financing constraints.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC increased its allocation to decarbonisation and low-carbon solutions to $23bn; 2025 upstream GHG intensity was 7.0 kgCO₂e/boe; cumulative savings from emission-reduction initiatives reached $242m since 2022. KPIs: decarbonisation capex ($); % capex aligned with transition plan; tCO₂e avoided; GHG intensity.

drivers.name: Sustainable / Green Financing for Oil & Gas Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Availability of labelled financing creates a direct capital-market incentive for oil & gas companies to develop eligible emissions-reduction projects and robust ESG frameworks. Credible use-of-proceeds and impact reporting increasingly determine access to this financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC signed its first green financing facility of $3bn with JBIC in 2024 to support decarbonisation and energy-transition initiatives. KPIs: green/sustainability-linked financing ($); financing cost vs conventional debt; % proceeds allocated to eligible projects; tCO₂e financed/avoided.

drivers.name: Climate-Related Financing & Disclosure Expectations
drivers.logic: UAE financial-sector requirements increasingly require banks and other financial institutions to integrate climate risks into financing, investment, due diligence and risk-management decisions. This increases the importance of oil & gas borrowers demonstrating credible climate-risk management, transition plans and measurable targets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CBUAE's Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation (C8/2025) is in force. UAE climate-finance principles require climate considerations to be incorporated into financing, investment, underwriting and due-diligence decisions. KPIs: climate-risk assessment coverage; financed emissions; transition-plan milestones; climate scenario analysis; ESG data availability.
drivers.keySources:
CBUAE Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation;
CBUAE Principles for Climate Transition Planning (Rulebook)

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Production & Market Valuation
drivers.logic: Carbon intensity is becoming an increasingly relevant differentiator for oil & gas assets as investors and buyers assess the relative transition exposure of hydrocarbon producers. Lower operational emissions intensity can support competitiveness and reduce the relative climate risk attributed to reserves and production.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC reported 7.0 kgCO₂e/boe upstream GHG intensity in 2025, among the lowest levels in the industry. Its target is a 25% reduction in operational emissions intensity by 2030. KPIs: kgCO₂e/boe; Scope 1+2 intensity; methane intensity; carbon-adjusted production cost; emissions per barrel sold.

drivers.name: Methane Performance & Investor Risk
drivers.logic: Methane is a high-impact climate issue for oil & gas companies and increasingly affects investor assessment of operational emissions quality. Reliable measurement, disclosure and reduction of methane can therefore affect perceived transition risk and access to capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC reduced upstream methane emissions by 22% in 2024 vs 2023; 2025 upstream methane emissions were 24.6 kt and methane intensity was 0.05%. ADNOC targets near-zero methane from operations. KPIs: methane intensity (%); methane emissions (kt CH₄); % assets covered by OGMP 2.0; leak-detection coverage; flaring intensity.

drivers.name: Transition-Asset / Stranded-Asset Risk
drivers.logic: Accelerating global decarbonisation can reduce the expected economic life and valuation of high-emission oil & gas assets, increasing investors' focus on reserve life, project economics, carbon intensity and compatibility with alternative demand scenarios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA estimates that under a pathway consistent with 1.5°C, the value of today's private oil & gas companies could be ~60% lower; even if national climate goals are achieved, value could be ~25% lower. IEA also estimates that more than 7 mb/d of oil production could be pushed out before the end of its technical lifetime by 2040 in a 1.5°C pathway.
drivers.keySources: IEA – The Oil and Gas Industry in Net Zero Transitions (IEA)

drivers.name: Gas/LNG Transition Investment Risk
drivers.logic: LNG and gas infrastructure can attract capital as a lower-carbon alternative to coal and oil, but long-lived infrastructure also creates transition risk if gas demand, carbon constraints or methane requirements tighten faster than expected. Investors therefore increasingly need to assess both the ESG opportunity and asset-life risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC Gas plans $15bn of capex over five years; Ruwais LNG will increase operated LNG capacity from 6 mtpa to >15 mtpa, with total Ruwais capacity of 9.6 mtpa. IEA expects global gas demand to grow into the 2030s under current-policy scenarios but decline more rapidly under net-zero pathways. KPIs: LNG capacity (mtpa); project life; utilisation; methane intensity; lifecycle GHG intensity; scenario-adjusted NPV.
drivers.keySources:
ADNOC Gas – Ruwais LNG; 
IEA – World Energy Outlook 2025 (ADNOC Gas)

drivers.name: Extreme Heat & Heat Stress
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures and humidity increase occupational heat stress and cooling requirements and can reduce equipment efficiency, constrain outdoor work and increase operational costs at upstream, processing, refining and logistics facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP identifies UAE as exposed to significant compounded heat risk and provides CMIP6 projections under multiple warming scenarios. KPIs: extreme-heat days; maximum wet-bulb temperature; cooling-energy demand; heat-related incidents; heat-related downtime; productivity loss.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – UAE Compounded Heat Risks

drivers.name: Water Stress & Water Availability
drivers.logic: The UAE's arid climate and water-stressed operating environment create long-term risks for oil & gas processes requiring water for cooling, firefighting, drilling, processing and reservoir management. Increasing water demand and climate stress can increase reliance on desalination and water-treatment infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC identifies its Abu Dhabi operations as located in a water-stressed area. In 2025 ADNOC withdrew 5,373 million m³ of water, with 5,036m m³ (93.7%) seawater; freshwater withdrawal was reported as zero under its revised definition. KPIs: water withdrawal/boe; water consumption/boe; % non-freshwater sources; produced-water reuse; desalination energy intensity.

drivers.name: Sea-Level Rise & Coastal Asset Exposure
drivers.logic: A substantial share of UAE oil & gas infrastructure is located along the coast, including offshore production, ports, terminals, LNG facilities and export infrastructure. Sea-level rise can increase chronic inundation, storm-surge exposure, corrosion and disruption risks, creating adaptation capex and potential asset downtime.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP provides UAE-specific CMIP6 sea-level projections through 2100 under multiple SSP scenarios. KPIs: % assets within coastal/flood-risk zones; projected sea-level rise; storm-surge exposure; adaptation capex; expected annual loss; downtime.

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall & Flash Flooding
drivers.logic: Although the UAE is arid, intense rainfall events can cause flash flooding that disrupts roads, pipelines, substations, production facilities, storage sites, ports and supply routes. Oil & gas facilities can face both direct physical damage and operational interruptions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP provides UAE-specific historical and CMIP6 projections for extreme precipitation for 2025, 2050, 2075 and 2085. KPIs: maximum 1-day/5-day precipitation; flood-exposed assets; drainage capacity; weather-related downtime; repair costs; business-interruption losses.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – UAE Extreme Precipitation Events (climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org)

drivers.name: Marine & Coastal Ecosystem Vulnerability
drivers.logic: Offshore oil & gas operations can be exposed to climate-driven changes in marine ecosystems and coastal habitats, while infrastructure development can compound pressures on mangroves, coral and other sensitive ecosystems. This can increase permitting, biodiversity-management and restoration requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC reported that 36% of its concession/operational areas overlapped protected areas in 2025, covering 13 protected areas, up from 25%/9 in 2024. KPIs: protected-area overlap; habitat affected/restored; biodiversity incidents; ecological monitoring coverage; restoration expenditure.

drivers.name: Global Oil Demand Transition
drivers.logic: Global climate policy, electrification and energy-efficiency improvements can reduce long-term oil demand and therefore affect production volumes, reserve economics, project utilisation and the value of UAE upstream assets. This creates transition risk even where individual UAE projects have low operating emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA's 2025 outlook projects global oil demand to reach a plateau of around 105.5 mb/d by 2030; EVs alone are expected to displace 5.4 mb/d of oil demand by 2030. IEA's 2025 WEO also sees oil demand peaking around 2030 under stated policies.
drivers.keySources:
IEA – Oil 2025;
IEA – World Energy Outlook 2025 (IEA)

drivers.name: Carbon-Intensive Asset Transition Risk
drivers.logic: UAE oil & gas companies can face increasing economic pressure on long-lived upstream, refining, LNG and associated infrastructure as climate policies tighten. Projects with high emissions, high breakeven costs or long payback periods are particularly exposed to reduced demand and carbon constraints.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA estimates that under a 1.5°C pathway oil & gas company valuations could be up to 60% lower than under current-policy expectations, while more than 7 mb/d of oil production could be retired before the end of its technical life by 2040. KPIs: reserve life; project breakeven; carbon intensity; remaining asset life; NPV under climate scenarios; percentage of capex exposed to transition scenarios.
drivers.keySources: IEA – The Oil and Gas Industry in Net Zero Transitions (IEA)

drivers.name: Supplier GHG & Climate Performance Requirements
drivers.logic: Oil & gas companies increasingly need visibility over suppliers' GHG emissions and climate performance because purchased goods, services, equipment and logistics contribute to the value-chain emissions footprint. Supplier ESG screening and emissions data therefore become increasingly important for procurement decisions and Scope 3 management.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC has established supplier sustainability requirements and integrates ESG considerations into its supply-chain processes. KPIs: % strategic suppliers screened on ESG; % suppliers reporting GHG emissions; Scope 3 Category 1/2 emissions; supplier emissions intensity; % procurement spend covered by ESG requirements.

drivers.name: Methane Measurement & Verification Across the Supply Chain
drivers.logic: Methane performance is increasingly becoming a supply-chain requirement because buyers, financiers and regulators seek greater assurance over the emissions intensity of oil and gas throughout the production and supply chain. Suppliers providing equipment, measurement, leak detection and certification services increasingly need to support accurate methane quantification.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC reported 24.6 kt methane emissions in 2025 and methane intensity of 0.05%; ADNOC participates in OGMP 2.0 and targets near-zero methane from its operations. KPIs: methane intensity (%); supplier methane data coverage; % assets covered by measurement/LDAR; OGMP reporting level; verified methane emissions.

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Crude & Product Traceability
drivers.logic: Increasing differentiation between hydrocarbons based on lifecycle emissions creates demand for reliable emissions measurement, certification and traceability across the oil & gas value chain. Suppliers and logistics providers may therefore need to provide emissions data to substantiate the carbon intensity of UAE crude and products.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC reported 7.0 kgCO₂e/boe upstream GHG intensity in 2025 and targets a 25% reduction in operational GHG intensity by 2030. KPIs: kgCO₂e/boe; lifecycle GHG intensity; % barrels with verified carbon-intensity data; supplier emissions-data coverage; certified low-carbon volumes.

drivers.name: Local Content & Sustainable Supplier Development
drivers.logic: UAE industrial policy encourages oil & gas operators to develop domestic supply chains, increasing demand for local manufacturing and service providers. From an ESG perspective, localisation can strengthen supply-chain resilience while creating opportunities to embed sustainability, HSE, workforce and responsible-business requirements into the domestic supplier base.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC's In-Country Value (ICV) programme aims to drive greater economic value into the UAE; ADNOC has stated an ambition to retain AED 178bn of additional value in the UAE between 2023–2028 through its ICV programme. KPIs: % procurement spend retained locally; local supplier share; ICV score; local manufacturing spend; SME participation; supplier ESG compliance.

drivers.name: Supplier HSE & Responsible Procurement Standards
drivers.logic: Oil & gas supply chains involve high-risk activities, including drilling, construction, transportation, maintenance and industrial services. Operators therefore impose supplier HSE, labour, ethics and responsible-business requirements to manage operational, social and reputational risks embedded in the supply chain.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC's supplier requirements include health, safety, environment and responsible-business expectations. KPIs: % suppliers assessed; supplier HSE incident rate; lost-time injury frequency; fatalities; corrective-action closure; % strategic suppliers subject to ESG audits.

drivers.name: Climate-Resilient Supply Chain & Logistics
drivers.logic: Increasing heat, flooding and extreme-weather events can disrupt suppliers, ports, roads, logistics routes and delivery of critical equipment. Oil & gas companies therefore need climate-risk screening and contingency planning for strategically important suppliers and logistics corridors.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE climate projections indicate increasing exposure to extreme heat and extreme precipitation. KPIs: % critical suppliers assessed for physical climate risk; % critical suppliers with business-continuity plans; weather-related supply disruptions; supplier downtime; logistics interruption days; climate adaptation expenditure.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – UAE Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Circularity & Resource-Efficient Procurement
drivers.logic: Oil & gas operations require large volumes of metals, equipment, chemicals, packaging and other materials. Increasing emphasis on resource efficiency and circularity can drive procurement requirements for recycled content, equipment reuse, waste reduction and material recovery, reducing environmental impacts across the supply chain.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC has set sustainability objectives covering waste and resource efficiency. KPIs: % waste diverted from landfill; recycled/reused materials; recycled-content procurement; material intensity; supplier waste-management compliance; hazardous-waste recovery rate.

drivers.name: Critical Equipment & Technology Supply Resilience
drivers.logic: Dependence on specialised equipment can become an ESG issue where climate transition and emissions-reduction targets require access to specific low-carbon technologies, methane-monitoring systems, electrification equipment and CCUS components. Supply constraints can delay decarbonisation projects and increase transition risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC's decarbonisation programme includes $23bn allocated to lower-carbon solutions and decarbonisation and a target of 10 MtCO₂/year CCUS capacity by 2030, increasing demand for specialised low-carbon technologies. KPIs: critical technology supplier concentration; equipment lead times; % critical suppliers with climate-risk plans; decarbonisation-project delays; local manufacturing capacity.

drivers.name: Saudi Arabia Second NDC – 2035/2040 Emissions Reduction
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's updated NDC establishes a new national emissions-reduction pathway that increases expectations for mitigation across the economy, including the hydrocarbon sector. For oil & gas companies, this increases the importance of emissions management, abatement technologies, energy efficiency and credible emissions data.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia submitted its Second NDC on 31 December 2025. The new NDC sets a 335 MtCO₂e annual emissions-reduction target for 2040, compared with the previous 278 MtCO₂e target for 2030; the target is expressed against a baseline scenario. KPIs: Scope 1–2 emissions; tCO₂e/boe; emissions reduction achieved; abatement capacity; % facilities covered by mitigation programmes.

drivers.name: Net Zero 2060
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's commitment to achieve net zero emissions by 2060 creates a long-term policy direction for decarbonisation of oil & gas operations and requires companies to manage the emissions trajectory of long-lived hydrocarbon assets and new investments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia announced its net-zero ambition for 2060 in 2021, to be achieved through the Circular Carbon Economy approach. Aramco separately targets net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions across wholly owned and operated assets by 2050. KPIs: Scope 1–2 emissions; emissions intensity; transition capex; renewable electricity share; abatement/removal capacity; progress against interim targets.
drivers.keySources:
Saudi Ministry of Finance – Green Financing Framework 
Aramco Sustainability Report 2025

drivers.name: Environmental Permitting & Environmental Impact Assessment
drivers.logic: Oil & gas projects in Saudi Arabia are subject to environmental permitting requirements under the Environmental Law. New and expanded upstream, processing, refining and infrastructure projects therefore need environmental assessment, permits and compliance monitoring, creating direct ESG requirements throughout the asset lifecycle.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's Executive Regulation for Environmental Permits for Establishing and Operating Activities establishes the environmental permitting framework. KPIs: % projects with valid environmental permits; EIA completion; permit conditions breached; environmental incidents; compliance expenditure; corrective actions.
drivers.keySources: Umm Al-Qura – Executive Regulation for Environmental Permits (Uqn)

drivers.name: Air Emissions & Industrial Emission Limits
drivers.logic: Saudi environmental regulation establishes mandatory limits and monitoring requirements for emissions from stationary sources. This directly affects refineries, gas-processing plants, petrochemical facilities, combustion equipment and other oil & gas installations, requiring investment in emissions controls and monitoring systems.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Executive Regulation for Air Quality prohibits exceeding specified stationary-source emission limits and establishes activity-specific standards. KPIs: NOx; SOx; VOCs; particulate matter; CO; emissions against permitted limits; continuous monitoring coverage; exceedances.
drivers.keySources: Umm Al-Qura – Executive Regulation for Air Quality (Uqn)

drivers.name: Fugitive VOC Emissions & Leak Detection
drivers.logic: Saudi air-quality regulation specifically requires oil refineries and certain natural-gas activities to establish approved programmes for detecting, controlling and repairing fugitive organic emissions. This creates a direct regulatory driver for LDAR, equipment maintenance and emissions monitoring in oil & gas.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Regulation requires fugitive-emission detection and repair programmes for oil refining and natural-gas processing activities exceeding 700,000 m³/day. Operators must maintain inventories, monitoring, management plans and records; records must generally be retained for at least five years. KPIs: % equipment covered by LDAR; leaks detected/repaired; VOC emissions; repair time; monitoring frequency.
drivers.keySources: Umm Al-Qura – Executive Regulation for Air Quality (Uqn)

drivers.name: Flaring & Emission-Control Requirements
drivers.logic: Regulation of flaring creates a direct operational ESG requirement for oil & gas facilities because flaring contributes to GHG and air emissions. Compliance requires flare monitoring, continuous flame detection, flow measurement and plans to minimise emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi air-quality regulation requires high-VOC flares to operate with continuous flame monitoring, digital recording and flare-flow monitoring; operators must prepare plans to reduce flaring to the minimum possible level and submit monthly reports on the quantity and estimated composition of gases flared. KPIs: flaring intensity (scf/boe); flared gas volume; flare events; flare efficiency; % flares monitored; GHG emissions from flaring.
drivers.keySources: Umm Al-Qura – Executive Regulation for Air Quality (Uqn)

drivers.name: Methane & Oil/Gas Emissions Management
drivers.logic: Although Saudi Arabia's national methane policy is less directly prescriptive than some jurisdictions, methane management is increasingly embedded in Saudi oil & gas environmental performance and national decarbonisation objectives. Regulatory and policy pressure therefore increases the need for measurement, leak detection and reduction of methane emissions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco reported 0.04% upstream methane intensity in 2025, within the OGCI aspiration of well below 0.20%; it also uses continuous/AI-enhanced optical gas imaging for leak detection at gas facilities. KPIs: methane intensity; methane emissions (kt CH₄); LDAR coverage; leak repair rate; continuous monitoring coverage.

drivers.name: Circular Carbon Economy & CCUS Deployment
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's Circular Carbon Economy approach explicitly supports reducing, reusing, recycling and removing carbon emissions. This creates a policy driver for carbon capture, utilisation and storage and other carbon-management technologies in hard-to-abate oil & gas and industrial operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia has announced a major CCUS hub intended to capture 44 MtCO₂e by 2035, equivalent to around 15% of the Kingdom's then-current NDC target. The Ministry of Energy continues to promote CCU/CCUS as part of the pathway to net zero 2060. KPIs: CO₂ captured/stored; MtCO₂/year capture capacity; capture rate; storage capacity; tCO₂ avoided; CCUS investment.
drivers.keySources:
Saudi Ministry of Economy & Planning – Carbon Capture and Utilization Challenge;
Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs – MGI (Ministry of Economy and Planning)

drivers.name: Water Pollution & Produced-Water Management
drivers.logic: Oil & gas activities can affect marine and freshwater environments through produced water, wastewater, spills and discharges. Saudi environmental regulation establishes requirements for protecting aquatic media, creating compliance obligations for offshore production, terminals, refineries and processing facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia has a dedicated Executive Regulation for Protecting Aquatic Media from Pollution under the Environmental Law. KPIs: produced-water discharge; oil-in-water concentration; wastewater treated/reused; spills; discharge exceedances; water recycling rate.
drivers.keySources: Umm Al-Qura – Executive Regulation for Protecting Aquatic Media from Pollution (Uqn)

drivers.name: Marine & Coastal Environmental Protection
drivers.logic: Offshore oil & gas production, pipelines and coastal terminals create potential impacts on marine and coastal ecosystems. Saudi Arabia's environmental framework therefore creates requirements for managing impacts on marine environments, making biodiversity and marine pollution relevant ESG compliance issues for offshore assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia adopted an Executive Regulation for Sustainable Management of the Marine and Coastal Environment under the Environmental Law. KPIs: marine spills; affected habitat; biodiversity incidents; offshore environmental monitoring; restoration expenditure; protected-area overlap.
drivers.keySources: Umm Al-Qura – Executive Regulation for Sustainable Management of Marine & Coastal Environment (Uqn)

drivers.name: Climate-Aligned Capital Allocation
drivers.logic: Saudi oil & gas companies operate with very large and long-lived capital programmes, increasing investor focus on whether capital allocation remains resilient under different climate and energy-transition scenarios. The ESG quality of capex increasingly depends on emissions intensity, abatement potential and resilience to changes in energy demand and policy.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco reported $52.2bn of capital investment in 2025 and guided to $50–55bn for 2026.

drivers.name: Gas Transition Investment & Jafurah Development
drivers.logic: Gas can support Saudi Arabia's energy transition by replacing higher-emission liquid fuels in domestic power generation, but large long-lived gas assets also create exposure to methane regulation, carbon constraints and future changes in gas demand. Investors therefore need to assess both the transition opportunity and asset-level climate risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco targets approximately 80% growth in sales-gas production capacity by 2030 vs. 2021. Jafurah is expected to reach 2 bcfd of sales gas by 2030 and 550,000 bpd of ethane/NGLs by 2030.

drivers.name: CCUS & Carbon-Management Investment
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's Circular Carbon Economy approach creates a substantial investment pipeline in carbon capture, transport, utilisation and storage. For oil & gas companies, CCUS can reduce emissions from hard-to-abate operations while creating new infrastructure and technology investment requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco and partners are developing a CCUS hub with planned capacity of up to 9 MtCO₂/year by 2027; Saudi Arabia's broader CCUS ambition is much larger. KPIs: MtCO₂ captured/year; storage capacity; capture rate; $/tCO₂; % emissions covered by CCUS; CCUS capex.

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Oil Competitiveness & Valuation
drivers.logic: As customers and investors increasingly distinguish hydrocarbons by their emissions intensity, lower-carbon production can reduce relative transition exposure and support the competitiveness and valuation of Saudi oil assets. This makes operational carbon intensity a capital-markets consideration rather than solely an environmental KPI.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco reported 10.0 kgCO₂e/boe upstream carbon intensity in 2025. It also reported upstream methane intensity of 0.04%. KPIs: kgCO₂e/boe; methane intensity; flaring intensity; lifecycle emissions; emissions-adjusted production cost; % production covered by verified emissions data.

drivers.name: Methane Performance & Investor Risk
drivers.logic: Methane is a particularly material ESG issue for oil & gas because relatively small changes in methane leakage can materially affect the climate footprint of gas and oil production. Investors increasingly assess methane measurement, leakage reduction and verification when evaluating the transition exposure of hydrocarbon producers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco reported 0.04% upstream methane intensity in 2025, significantly below the 0.20% OGCI ambition. KPIs: methane intensity; methane emissions (kt CH₄); % facilities covered by LDAR; leak detection/repair rate; independently verified methane data.

drivers.name: Transition & Stranded-Asset Risk
drivers.logic: Long-lived upstream, gas, refining and LNG assets are exposed to changes in global oil and gas demand under different climate pathways. Investors may therefore apply higher transition-risk premiums to projects with high emissions, long payback periods or weak economics under lower-demand scenarios.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA estimates that in a 1.5°C pathway, the value of today's private oil & gas companies could be around 60% lower than under current-policy expectations. KPIs: reserve life; asset life; breakeven price; emissions intensity; NPV under APS/NZE scenarios; percentage of reserves exposed to demand decline.
drivers.keySources: IEA – The Oil and Gas Industry in Net Zero Transitions

drivers.name: Climate-Related Financing & Disclosure Expectations
drivers.logic: Banks, institutional investors and debt markets increasingly incorporate physical and transition climate risks into financing and investment decisions. Saudi oil & gas companies therefore face growing importance of climate-risk governance, emissions disclosure, scenario analysis and credible transition plans in maintaining access to capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Exchange ESG Disclosure Guidelines provide a framework for listed companies to disclose material ESG information, including climate-related indicators. KPIs: Scope 1–3 emissions; climate-risk assessment; scenario analysis; ESG disclosure coverage; climate targets; assurance of ESG data.

drivers.name: Sustainable & Transition Finance
drivers.logic: The development of sustainable and transition-finance markets creates potential financing channels for oil & gas companies undertaking measurable emissions-reduction projects. Access depends on credible transition strategies, eligible use of proceeds and measurable environmental outcomes.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia issued its Green Financing Framework; Aramco has also developed sustainable-finance and decarbonisation financing activities. KPIs: green/transition financing raised; financing cost; % eligible capex financed; tCO₂e avoided per $ financed; external verification.
drivers.keySources: Saudi National Debt Management Center – Green Financing Framework

drivers.name: Extreme Heat & Heat Stress
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures and extreme heat can increase worker health and safety risks, cooling requirements and equipment stress across upstream, gas-processing, refining and petrochemical operations. Heat can also reduce outdoor productivity and constrain maintenance and construction activities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia already experiences very high temperatures, and World Bank CMIP6 projections provide country-specific changes in extreme temperature indicators under different SSP scenarios. KPIs: number of extreme-heat days; maximum temperature; wet-bulb temperature; cooling-energy demand; heat-related incidents; heat-related downtime; productivity losses.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Saudi Arabia Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Water Stress & Scarcity
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's extremely arid climate creates structural water constraints for oil & gas processing, refining, cooling and industrial operations. Climate change can increase water demand while reducing the reliability of natural water resources, increasing dependence on desalination, recycling and water-treatment infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia is one of the world's most water-stressed countries. World Bank data provide country-specific projections for water availability and climate variables. Aramco reported over 99% of its water withdrawals came from non-freshwater sources in 2025, highlighting the sector's dependence on seawater, treated wastewater and other non-freshwater sources. KPIs: freshwater withdrawal/consumption; total water withdrawal; m³/boe; % non-freshwater sources; water reuse/recycling rate; desalination energy intensity.
drivers.keySources:
World Bank – Saudi Arabia CCKP;
Aramco Sustainability Report 2025

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall & Flash Flooding
drivers.logic: Despite its arid climate, intense rainfall events can produce flash floods that disrupt roads, pipelines, well sites, power systems, processing facilities and logistics. Flooding can cause direct physical damage as well as business interruption and supply-chain disruption.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP provides Saudi Arabia-specific historical and CMIP6 projections for extreme precipitation, including changes in maximum 1-day and 5-day precipitation under different scenarios. KPIs: maximum 1-day/5-day rainfall; flood-exposed assets; drainage capacity; weather-related downtime; repair costs; business-interruption losses.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Saudi Arabia Extreme Precipitation Events

drivers.name: Sea-Level Rise & Coastal Asset Exposure
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's oil & gas value chain has substantial exposure to coastal and offshore infrastructure, particularly in the Eastern Province and along the Red Sea. Sea-level rise, storm surges and coastal flooding can affect offshore platforms, terminals, ports, refineries, pipelines and other critical infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP provides Saudi Arabia-specific sea-level projections through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios. KPIs: % critical assets in coastal zones; projected sea-level rise; high-tide/storm-surge exposure; coastal flood probability; adaptation capex; expected annual physical loss; downtime.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Saudi Arabia Sea-Level Projections

drivers.name: Sand & Dust Storms
drivers.logic: More frequent or severe dust and sand storms can reduce visibility, disrupt transportation and logistics, damage or foul equipment, increase maintenance requirements and affect outdoor worker safety. The risk is particularly relevant for large desert-based upstream, pipeline and processing operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia is highly exposed to dust and sand storms due to its arid environment. WMO identifies dust storms as a significant hazard across the Arabian Peninsula. KPIs: dust-storm days; PM10/PM2.5 concentrations; weather-related transport disruptions; equipment-maintenance costs; production/logistics downtime; worker exposure.
drivers.keySources: World Meteorological Organization – Sand and Dust Storms

drivers.name: Marine Heat & Coastal Ecosystem Stress
drivers.logic: Rising sea temperatures and other climate-driven marine changes can affect offshore oil & gas operations and sensitive coastal ecosystems. This can increase environmental-management, biodiversity, permitting and restoration requirements around offshore platforms, pipelines and terminals.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia has extensive Red Sea and Arabian Gulf coastlines. Climate-driven marine heat and ecosystem degradation can increase pressure on sensitive coral and coastal habitats. KPIs: sea-surface temperature; marine heatwave days; biodiversity incidents; habitat affected/restored; offshore environmental incidents; protected-area overlap; ecosystem restoration expenditure.
drivers.keySources:
IPCC – AR6 WGII;
World Bank – Saudi Arabia CCKP

drivers.name: Oil & Gas Demand Transition
drivers.logic: Global climate policy, electrification, energy efficiency and substitution away from fossil fuels can reduce long-term oil demand, affecting Saudi production volumes, reserve economics and the valuation of long-lived upstream assets. This is the principal transition-risk driver for the Saudi oil & gas sector.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA's Oil 2025 forecasts global oil demand reaching around 105.5 mb/d by 2030, with demand growth slowing sharply. EV deployment is expected to displace around 5.4 mb/d of oil demand by 2030. Under a 1.5°C pathway, IEA estimates substantially greater risk of under-utilised or stranded oil & gas assets. KPIs: oil demand by scenario; reserve life; project breakeven; utilisation; asset impairment; NPV under climate scenarios; % reserves exposed to declining demand.
drivers.keySources:
IEA – Oil 2025; 
IEA – The Oil and Gas Industry in Net Zero Transitions

drivers.name: Supplier GHG & Climate Performance Requirements
drivers.logic: Oil & gas companies increasingly need visibility into suppliers' environmental performance because purchased equipment, materials, construction and services contribute to the value-chain emissions footprint. Supplier ESG screening and emissions data therefore become increasingly important for procurement and Scope 3 management.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco's sustainability approach includes supplier sustainability requirements and ESG considerations in its supply chain. KPIs: % strategic suppliers ESG-screened; % suppliers reporting GHG emissions; Scope 3 Category 1/2 emissions; supplier emissions intensity; % procurement spend covered by ESG requirements.

drivers.name: Methane Measurement & Verification Across the Supply Chain
drivers.logic: Methane performance is becoming increasingly important in oil & gas procurement and customer assessments. Suppliers of equipment, services and technologies increasingly need to support methane measurement, leak detection, quantification and verification across upstream and gas operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Aramco reported 0.04% upstream methane intensity in 2025, compared with the OGCI ambition of below 0.20%.
IEA estimates global oil & gas methane intensity needs to decline toward ~0.2% by 2030 in the NZE pathway.
drivers.keySources:
Aramco – Sustainability Report 2025;
IEA – Global Methane Tracker 2025

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Crude & Product Traceability
drivers.logic: As crude and petroleum products become increasingly differentiated by lifecycle emissions, customers may require reliable emissions data and traceability to substantiate the carbon intensity of hydrocarbons. This increases requirements for suppliers, logistics providers and service companies to provide consistent emissions data.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco reported 10.0 kgCO₂e/boe upstream carbon intensity in 2025 and 0.04% upstream methane intensity. KPIs: kgCO₂e/boe; lifecycle GHG intensity; % production with verified emissions data; emissions-data coverage across logistics/suppliers; certified low-carbon volumes.

drivers.name: Local Content & Sustainable Supplier Development
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's localisation agenda increases demand for domestic manufacturing and services across the oil & gas value chain. For ESG, localisation can strengthen supply resilience while allowing operators to embed environmental, HSE, labour and responsible-business standards into the domestic supplier base.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco's iktva programme targets 70% localisation of supply-chain spend by 2025. Aramco reported that the programme had reached approximately 70% localisation in 2025. KPIs: local-content share; % procurement spend localised; domestic manufacturing capacity; SME participation; supplier ESG compliance; supplier-development expenditure.

drivers.name: Supplier HSE & Responsible Procurement Standards
drivers.logic: Oil & gas supply chains involve high-risk drilling, construction, transportation, maintenance and industrial activities. Suppliers therefore need to meet environmental, health & safety, labour, ethics and responsible-business requirements to reduce operational, social and reputational risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco applies supplier qualification and performance requirements covering areas such as HSE and responsible business. KPIs: % suppliers assessed/audited; supplier HSE incident rate; LTIFR; fatalities; environmental incidents; corrective-action closure; % high-risk suppliers subject to ESG audits.

drivers.name: Climate-Resilient Supply Chain & Logistics
drivers.logic: Physical climate risks such as extreme heat, flooding and dust storms can disrupt suppliers, transportation routes, ports and delivery of critical equipment. Oil & gas operators therefore need climate-risk screening and business-continuity measures for critical suppliers and logistics corridors.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia is highly exposed to extreme heat and other climate hazards. KPIs: % critical suppliers assessed for physical climate risk; % critical suppliers with continuity plans; weather-related disruption days; logistics downtime; critical-equipment lead time; climate adaptation expenditure.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Saudi Arabia Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Technology & Equipment Supply Resilience
drivers.logic: Decarbonisation programmes require specialised technologies such as carbon capture, methane-monitoring systems, electrification equipment and energy-efficiency technologies. Concentration of suppliers or long lead times can delay emissions-reduction projects and increase transition risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia is developing large-scale CCUS infrastructure, including an initial up to 9 MtCO₂/year CCUS hub planned for 2027. Aramco also has extensive emissions-reduction and methane-monitoring programmes. KPIs: supplier concentration; equipment lead time; % critical technologies sourced domestically; decarbonisation-project delays; technology supplier ESG assessment.

drivers.name: Circularity & Resource-Efficient Procurement
drivers.logic: Oil & gas projects require significant quantities of steel, metals, chemicals, equipment and other materials. Increasing emphasis on resource efficiency and circularity can create procurement requirements for reuse, recycling, waste reduction and responsible material sourcing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Aramco reports material use, waste generation and waste diversion as part of its environmental performance. KPIs: waste generated; % waste diverted from landfill; recycled/reused materials; recycled-content procurement; hazardous-waste recovery; supplier waste-management compliance.

drivers.name: Paris Agreement & Net-Zero Transition
drivers.logic: The global transition toward limiting warming to well below 2°C and pursuing 1.5°C increases pressure on mining and metals companies to reduce operational emissions, decarbonise energy-intensive processing and align long-lived capital expenditure with lower-carbon pathways.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Paris Agreement temperature goal: well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C. KPIs: Scope 1–3 GHG emissions; tCO₂e/t metal; emissions intensity; renewable electricity share; low-carbon energy share; decarbonisation capex; progress against science-based targets.

drivers.name: Critical Minerals Demand from the Energy Transition
drivers.logic: Electrification, renewable generation, grids, batteries and energy storage increase structural demand for minerals such as copper, lithium, nickel, graphite and rare earths. This creates growth opportunities for miners but also increases expectations that new supply be developed responsibly.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, energy technologies drove around 75% of demand growth across key energy minerals. Lithium demand increased around 25% p.a. on average over the previous two years; battery demand exceeded 1.5 TWh in 2025. KPIs: production growth; reserves/resources; clean-energy demand exposure; % production qualifying as critical minerals; new capacity; responsible-mining investment.

drivers.name: Critical Mineral Supply Security & Concentration
drivers.logic: Concentration of mining and especially refining in a small number of countries creates geopolitical, trade and supply-disruption risks. This increases the strategic value of diversified producers and creates pressure for resilient, traceable and responsibly sourced mineral supply chains.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, the top refining country held ~70% average share across key energy minerals; the leading suppliers accounted for more than three-quarters of refined supply growth in 2023–25. IEA also reports that one country is the dominant refiner for 19 of 20 strategic energy minerals, with an average share of around 70%. KPIs: country concentration; supplier concentration; % production from high-risk jurisdictions; geographic diversification; traceable production.

drivers.name: Responsible Mineral Supply Chains & Human Rights Due Diligence
drivers.logic: Mining and mineral supply chains can be associated with human-rights abuses, conflict financing, corruption and environmental harm, particularly in conflict-affected and high-risk areas. Buyers and regulators therefore increasingly expect risk-based due diligence, traceability and remediation across mineral supply chains.
drivers.evidenceKpi: OECD framework requires a 5-step risk-based due-diligence process covering management systems, risk assessment, mitigation, independent audit and public reporting. KPIs: % suppliers/mines covered by due diligence; high-risk suppliers; audit coverage; traceability rate; identified human-rights incidents; remediation completion.

drivers.name: Human Rights, Indigenous Peoples & Community Relations
drivers.logic: Mining projects can significantly affect land, livelihoods, cultural heritage, Indigenous Peoples and local communities. Increasing expectations for meaningful engagement, respect for rights and effective grievance/remediation mechanisms can affect project approvals, operating continuity, reputation and access to capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: % projects with community engagement plans; grievance cases and resolution rate; resettlement/compensation; agreements with Indigenous/local communities; human-rights impact assessments; incidents involving Indigenous Peoples.
drivers.keySources:
OECD – Responsible Business Conduct in the Extractive Sector;
Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management (OECD)

drivers.name: Occupational Health & Safety
drivers.logic: Mining remains a high-risk industry because of underground operations, heavy machinery, blasting, haulage, tailings and exposure to hazardous substances. Stronger expectations for worker safety, contractor management and fatality prevention make occupational health and safety a core social ESG driver.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: fatalities; fatality frequency rate; TRIFR/LTIFR; lost days; high-potential incidents; contractor injury rate; occupational disease cases; % workers covered by H&S management systems.

drivers.name: Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
drivers.logic: Mining can cause land-use change, habitat loss, fragmentation and ecosystem degradation. The GBF increases global expectations for avoiding, minimising and restoring biodiversity impacts and for integrating biodiversity into corporate planning and investment decisions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: GBF Target 3 calls for at least 30% of terrestrial/inland-water and marine/coastal areas to be effectively conserved by 2030; Target 2 calls for at least 30% of degraded ecosystems to be under effective restoration by 2030. KPIs: hectares disturbed/restored; % sites in biodiversity-sensitive areas; habitat loss; restoration success; biodiversity net impact; protected-area overlap.
drivers.keySources: Convention on Biological Diversity – Kunming-Montreal GBF (Convention on Biological Diversity)

drivers.name: Nature-Related Dependencies, Impacts & Financial Risk
drivers.logic: Mining depends heavily on ecosystem services such as water, land, soil and ecosystem stability while creating material impacts on nature. Investors increasingly expect companies to identify nature-related dependencies, impacts, risks and opportunities and assess their financial implications.
drivers.evidenceKpi: TNFD provides 14 recommended disclosures across governance, strategy, risk and impact management, and metrics/targets. KPIs: assets in biodiversity-sensitive locations; water dependencies; nature-related impacts; restoration; nature-related risk exposure; % sites assessed using LEAP/TNFD approach.

drivers.name: Water Stewardship & Water Stress
drivers.logic: Mining and mineral processing can require significant water while many deposits are located in water-stressed regions. Competition for water can increase operating costs, regulatory constraints and conflict with communities and other users.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank reports that 70% of mining projects operated by the six largest mining companies were located in water-stressed regions in its climate-smart mining analysis. KPIs: m³ water withdrawn/tonne ore; m³/t metal; freshwater withdrawal; water consumption; % recycled/reused; sites in high-water-stress areas; community water dependence.

drivers.name: Mining & Metals Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Mining and metals production is energy-intensive, while metals such as steel and aluminium also have significant process emissions. Decarbonisation therefore creates pressure for electrification, renewable power, energy efficiency, hydrogen, low-carbon processing and, where applicable, CCUS.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Iron and steel account for around 7% of energy-system CO₂ emissions and about 8% of final energy demand. IEA's transition pathway for steel sees near-zero-emission iron production reaching 95% by 2050 and secondary steel's share of metallic inputs rising to 48%. KPIs: tCO₂e/t product; Scope 1–2 emissions; renewable electricity; energy intensity; electrification; low-carbon hydrogen use; CCUS capacity.
drivers.keySources:
IEA – Iron & Steel;
IEA – Steel & Aluminium (IEA)

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Metals & Product Carbon Footprint
drivers.logic: Customers increasingly seek lower-embedded-carbon metals, particularly in sectors such as automotive, construction, batteries and clean energy. This creates product differentiation based on emissions intensity and increases demand for credible product-level carbon accounting and certification.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: kg/t or tCO₂e/t metal; Scope 1–3 product footprint; renewable electricity share; recycled content; % production with verified product carbon footprint; low-carbon product volumes. IEA projects near-zero-emission production to become increasingly important in steel and aluminium markets.

drivers.name: Carbon Pricing & Border Carbon Measures
drivers.logic: Carbon pricing increases the cost of emissions-intensive production and can affect the competitiveness of metals exported to carbon-regulated markets. Border measures also increase demand for accurate embedded-emissions data and lower-carbon production.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EU CBAM covers iron & steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. From 2026, the definitive CBAM regime applies, linking imported products to embedded emissions and the EU carbon price. KPIs: tCO₂e/t product; carbon cost/t; CBAM-covered exports; embedded emissions; % verified emissions data; carbon-price exposure.
drivers.keySources: European Commission – CBAM (Taxation and Customs Union)

drivers.name: Circular Economy & Mineral Recycling
drivers.logic: Increasing use of secondary materials can reduce demand for primary extraction, energy consumption, waste and environmental impacts. At the same time, recycling creates new competition and opportunities for mining and metals companies as secondary supply becomes increasingly important.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IEA reports that in 2025 battery demand exceeded 1.5 TWh and recycling is increasingly important to mineral security. For copper, IEA projects secondary supply and reuse to reach 8.7 Mt by 2040 under STEPS versus 4.4 Mt in 2024. KPIs: recycled content; secondary production; recovery rate; recycling capacity; material efficiency; % revenue from recycled/secondary materials.
drivers.keySources:
IEA – Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026;
IEA – Copper (IEA)

drivers.name: Tailings & Mine Waste Management
drivers.logic: Tailings failures can create catastrophic environmental, social, financial and reputational liabilities. Global expectations increasingly require independent governance, risk assessment, monitoring, emergency preparedness, disclosure and lifecycle management of tailings facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management contains 6 topic areas, 15 principles and 77 auditable requirements, including zero tolerance for human fatalities and requirements covering design, operation, closure, emergency response and public disclosure. KPIs: number of TSFs; consequence classification; GISTM conformance; independent reviews; critical controls; incidents; closure liabilities.
drivers.keySources: Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management (Global Tailings Review)

drivers.name: Mine Closure, Rehabilitation & Post-Closure Liabilities
drivers.logic: Mining creates long-lived environmental and social liabilities that can persist after production ends. Increasing expectations for progressive rehabilitation, financial provisioning and post-closure monitoring make closure planning a material ESG and financial-risk issue.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: closure liability ($); % closure provision funded; hectares rehabilitated; rehabilitation success rate; progressive rehabilitation (% disturbed area); post-closure monitoring period; closure plan coverage.

drivers.name: ESG Disclosure & Investor Decision-Usefulness
drivers.logic: Investors increasingly require consistent information on financially material sustainability risks and opportunities. Mining companies therefore face growing expectations to disclose climate, water, biodiversity, social, safety and other sustainability risks in a way that connects them to enterprise value and financial performance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IFRS S1 requires disclosure of sustainability-related risks and opportunities that could reasonably be expected to affect cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital. KPIs: material ESG risks; financial effects; governance; metrics/targets; scenario analysis; sustainability-related financial effects.

drivers.name: Climate-Related Financial Disclosure
drivers.logic: Climate-related physical and transition risks can affect mining assets, production costs, capital expenditure and asset values. IFRS S2 increases expectations for consistent disclosure of climate risks, opportunities, governance, strategy, metrics and targets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: Scope 1–3 emissions; climate targets; carbon intensity; transition risks; physical-risk exposure; climate scenario analysis; climate resilience; climate-related capital expenditure.

drivers.name: Science-Based Decarbonisation Targets for Steel
drivers.logic: SBTi's steel-sector guidance provides sector-specific approaches for companies in steel production to establish science-based emissions-reduction targets. This is relevant to metals companies with steel exposure and demonstrates increasing expectations for sector-specific decarbonisation pathways in emissions-intensive materials industries.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Relevant to steel producers,  integrated steel/mining groups, and iron ore producers

drivers.name: Mining-Specific Sustainability Reporting Expectations
drivers.logic: Mining's distinctive environmental and social impacts create demand for sector-specific reporting on emissions, water, biodiversity, waste, tailings, communities, labour and human rights beyond generic sustainability reporting.
drivers.evidenceKpi: GRI 14 Mining Sector 2024 identifies likely material topics and sector-specific disclosures; the latest V1.1 was published in January 2026 and aligns with revised GRI climate and energy standards. KPIs: GHG emissions; energy; water; waste; tailings; biodiversity; community impacts; human rights.

drivers.name: Sustainability Disclosure and Cost of Capital
drivers.logic: Comprehensive, comparable and reliable sustainability disclosure can reduce a company’s cost of capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Empirical research from the University of Oxford found that ‘90% of the studies on the cost of capital show that sound sustainability standards lower the cost of capital for companies.
drivers.keySources: University of Oxford and Arabesque Partners, ‘From the Stockholder to the Stakeholder: How Sustainability Can Drive Financial Outperformance,’ March 2015.

drivers.name: Sustainability Information and Earnings Stability
drivers.logic: Sustainability information can be a strong signal of share price volatility.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Based on historical data, Bank of America Global Research found that companies in the top quintile of sustainability performance experienced the lowest volatility in earnings per share (EPS) in a subsequent five-year period. By contrast, ‘companies with the worst environmental, social and governance records averaged 92% volatility.

The researchers also found that sustainability information was the only reliable signal for predicting EPS volatility, providing better insight than traditional measures such as return on equity.
drivers.keySources: Bank of America, ‘Equity Strategy Focus Point,’ 18 December 2016.

drivers.name: Sustainable Bond Market Development
drivers.logic: The continued growth of sustainable bond markets increases demand for ESG strategies, sustainability frameworks, transparent disclosures, and impact reporting. Companies issuing sustainable bonds are expected to align with internationally recognized market principles and demonstrate the environmental and/or social use of proceeds or sustainability performance commitments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2026: Total sustainable bond issuance reached USD 357.6 billion. Green bonds remained the largest segment, with USD 229.2 billion issued (64.08% of total issuance), followed by Sustainability bonds with USD 60.3 billion (16.88% of total issuance).

drivers.name: Carbon Neutrality Strategy 2060
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's legally approved long-term carbon-neutrality strategy creates a structural policy direction for decarbonising energy-intensive industries, including mining and metallurgy. Companies face increasing pressure to modernise production, reduce energy-related emissions, electrify processes and redirect investment toward lower-carbon technologies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Carbon neutrality by 2060. Strategy estimates approximately US$610bn of net investment in low-carbon technologies through 2060, including US$10bn to 2030. KPIs: Scope 1–2 emissions; tCO₂e/t metal; energy intensity; low-carbon capex; renewable electricity; electrification; emissions trajectory.
drivers.keySources: Presidential Decree No. 121 / Carbon Neutrality Strategy (Leap)

drivers.name: NDC 3.0 – Industrial Emissions Reduction
