drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's updated NDC strengthens the national emissions pathway and explicitly identifies industry, energy efficiency and low-emission technologies as mitigation priorities. This increases pressure on emissions-intensive mining and metallurgical operations to contribute to national reductions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2030: 15% GHG reduction unconditionally and up to 25% with international support vs. 1990. 2035: 17% unconditional and 25% conditional. NDC 3.0 also prioritises energy efficiency, low-emission technologies, hydrogen and carbon capture. KPIs: Scope 1–2; tCO₂e/t metal; emissions reduction vs. baseline; decarbonisation capex; technology adoption.

drivers.name: Kazakhstan ETS / Carbon Pricing
drivers.logic: The KAZ ETS places a compliance obligation on covered installations and makes GHG emissions financially relevant for large industrial emitters. This creates incentives to improve emissions intensity and manage exposure to future carbon-cost changes.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KAZ ETS covered approximately 50% of Kazakhstan's CO₂ emissions in 2024, covering 229 installations across power, heating, extractive industries and manufacturing. Phase 6 runs 2026–2030. KPIs: tCO₂e; allocated vs. verified emissions; allowance surplus/deficit; carbon cost; tCO₂e/t metal; ETS-covered production.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Carbon Pricing Dashboard: Kazakhstan ETS (Carbon Pricing Dashboard)

drivers.name: Comprehensive Environmental Permits & BAT
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's transition to integrated environmental permitting makes Best Available Techniques a direct compliance and technology-modernisation driver for the largest and most environmentally significant industrial facilities. This is particularly material for mining, beneficiation and metallurgy.
drivers.evidenceKpi: From 1 January 2025, Category I facilities must obtain comprehensive environmental permits based on BAT. OECD notes that facilities with gross emissions of 1,000 tonnes or more require an integrated permit. BAT non-compliance can trigger increasing environmental fines. KPIs: BAT compliance; permit status; emissions vs. BAT levels; energy/resource intensity; environmental capex; number of Category I facilities covered.
drivers.keySources:
Kazakhstan Environmental Code – Adilet; 
OECD – Kazakhstan RBC (Adilet)

drivers.name: Mining & Metallurgy BAT Standards
drivers.logic: Sector-specific BAT reference documents establish technical benchmarks for reducing emissions, resource consumption and environmental impacts in mining and metallurgical processes. This creates a direct technology-upgrade and environmental-performance driver.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan has approved 20 sector-specific BAT reference documents covering major industries. Mining-specific documents include non-ferrous ore extraction and beneficiation, while BAT materials also cover energy efficiency and other industrial processes. KPIs: BAT adoption; pollutant emissions; energy intensity; water use; waste generation; resource efficiency; technology-modernisation capex.
drivers.keySources:
Adilet – BAT for Non-Ferrous Ore Extraction & Beneficiation; 
International Green Technologies & Investment Projects Center (Adilet)

drivers.name: Environmental Impact Assessment & Environmental Permitting
drivers.logic: Mining and metallurgical projects with significant environmental impacts are subject to environmental assessment and permitting requirements covering emissions, waste, water, soil and other impacts. This can affect project design, operating conditions, timelines and environmental expenditure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Category I objects have significant negative environmental impact; construction and operation of Category I and II facilities require environmental permits. Permits establish environmental conditions and monitoring requirements. KPIs: EIA status; permit conditions; emissions limits; waste limits; water/soil monitoring; environmental compliance incidents; remediation expenditure.

drivers.name: Mining Waste & Tailings Management Requirements
drivers.logic: Mining waste, tailings and waste-storage facilities create significant environmental risks, particularly through water contamination, dust, instability and long-term liabilities. Kazakhstan's Environmental Code requires dedicated mining-waste management programmes and controls throughout operation and closure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Mining-waste programmes must aim to prevent/reduce waste generation and increase recovery/reuse, and must incorporate BAT. Operators must assess and control leachate, protect surface/groundwater and manage post-closure monitoring. KPIs: tonnes of mining waste; tailings volume; % waste reused/recovered; water contamination incidents; tailings-storage facilities; monitoring coverage; closure liabilities.

drivers.name: Mine Closure, Rehabilitation & Financial Security
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan requires mining operators to address the environmental consequences of subsoil use and provides financial-security mechanisms for closure and rehabilitation. This makes closure liabilities a direct regulatory and financial ESG issue rather than a discretionary sustainability activity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Subsoil users must mitigate the consequences of subsoil operations; financial security is required for applicable liquidation obligations. For Category I facilities, financial security must cover estimated closure-related costs and is recalculated every seven years. KPIs: closure liability; financial security; hectares rehabilitated; progressive closure; reclamation cost; post-closure monitoring.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Subsoil Code – Adilet Environmental Code – Article 147 (Adilet)

drivers.name: Water Use & Pollution Controls
drivers.logic: Mining and metallurgy depend on water for extraction, beneficiation, cooling and processing. Kazakhstan's water legislation regulates special water use and wastewater discharge, creating requirements around abstraction, discharge quality and protection of water resources.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Special water use requires permits for relevant surface/groundwater abstraction and discharge. KPIs: m³ water withdrawn/t ore or metal; freshwater withdrawal; water reuse/recycling %; wastewater discharge; pollutant load; sites in water-stressed basins; water-related incidents.

drivers.name: Industrial Waste Recycling & Circularity Targets
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's green-transition policy is increasing expectations for industrial waste recovery and recycling. This is particularly material to mining and metallurgy because of the very large volumes of mineral, metallurgical and processing waste generated by the sector.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan targets 50% industrial-waste recycling by 2030. The 2024–2030 Green Economy Action Plan also provides for full compliance of Category I enterprises with waste recycling/monitoring requirements by 2030. KPIs: % industrial waste recycled; tonnes waste recovered; secondary raw materials; tailings reprocessing; waste intensity/t metal.
drivers.keySources:
OECD – Critical Raw Materials Governance in Central Asia 
Prime Minister of Kazakhstan (OECD)

drivers.name: Critical Minerals & Value-Added Processing Policy
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan is positioning itself as a supplier of critical raw materials and increasingly promotes exploration, processing and higher-value products. This creates incentives for responsible development of critical minerals while increasing expectations around environmental performance, sustainable processing and supply-chain resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan reports capacity to supply finished products derived from 20 of 60 USGS critical minerals. The Kazakhstan–EU partnership focuses on exploration, processing and higher-value products; the 2025–2026 Roadmap supports critical raw-material projects. KPIs: critical-mineral reserves/production; processing capacity; % minerals processed domestically; exploration expenditure; environmental performance of critical-mineral projects.
drivers.keySources: Government of Kazakhstan – Critical Minerals Kazakhstan–EU Critical Raw Materials Cooperation (Government of Kazakhstan)

drivers.name: Renewable Energy & Low-Carbon Electricity Transition
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's renewable-energy targets create an increasingly relevant pathway for mining and metallurgical companies to reduce Scope 2 emissions through renewable procurement, PPAs and cleaner electricity. This is particularly material for electricity-intensive metallurgy.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan targets 15% renewable electricity by 2030 and 50% by 2050. NDC 3.0 also targets at least 35% of total electricity generation from renewable and nuclear sources by 2035. KPIs: renewable electricity share; Scope 2 tCO₂e; renewable PPAs; clean-power capacity; electricity emissions factor.

drivers.name: Energy Efficiency Requirements
drivers.logic: Mining and metallurgy are among Kazakhstan's most energy-intensive industrial activities. Mandatory energy-management and audit requirements for large energy consumers increase pressure to identify efficiency opportunities and reduce energy intensity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Entities consuming ≥1,500 tonnes of conventional fuel equivalent/year are subject to mandatory energy audits at least once every five years, with action plans required based on audit results. KPIs: GJ/t metal; kWh/t product; energy intensity; audit completion; identified savings; realised energy savings; energy-efficiency capex.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Law on Energy Saving & Energy Efficiency – Adilet (Adilet)

drivers.name: EU CBAM – Embedded Carbon Requirements
drivers.logic: EU CBAM creates an external carbon-cost and emissions-data requirement for Kazakh exporters of covered metals. This increases pressure to measure product-level embedded emissions and reduce carbon intensity, particularly for iron, steel and aluminium producers exporting to the EU.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CBAM definitive regime applies from 1 January 2026 and covers iron & steel and aluminium, among other sectors. EU importers above the 50-tonne annual threshold generally require authorised CBAM-declarant status. KPIs: tCO₂e/t product; embedded emissions; CBAM-covered exports; carbon cost; % verified emissions data; CBAM certificate exposure.
drivers.keySources: European Commission – CBAM Definitive Regime (Taxation and Customs Union)

drivers.name: Sustainable Finance Access for Mining & Metallurgy
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's developing sustainable-finance market creates opportunities for mining and metals companies to access capital specifically for environmental projects, while alignment with the national Green Taxonomy increasingly determines whether projects qualify as green. This can diversify funding sources and potentially improve financing terms for eligible investments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's sustainable-finance market had issued approximately USD 2.5bn of bonds and loans cumulatively by end-2025; AIFC-supported transactions represented approximately 70% of Kazakhstan's green bonds and loans. KPIs: green/sustainability-linked financing raised; % eligible capex; financing cost vs. conventional debt; taxonomy-aligned investment; external-review coverage.

drivers.name: Mining-Specific Green & Sustainability-Linked Financing
drivers.logic: Mining companies can use labelled debt to finance energy efficiency, water recycling, emissions reduction and other environmental improvements. Kazakhstan already has a mining-specific precedent, demonstrating that ESG performance can be directly incorporated into financing structures.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's first green bond for mining activities was issued by Tau-Ken Samruk in 2021 for KZT 18.4bn (~USD 40m); the bond included coupon adjustments linked to water recycling and energy-efficiency targets. KPIs: labelled bond/loan volume; sustainability-linked KPIs; coupon step-up/down; water recycling; energy intensity; emissions reduction.

drivers.name: Transition Finance for Emissions-Intensive Metallurgy
drivers.logic: Much of Kazakhstan's metals sector cannot immediately reach near-zero emissions because of coal-based electricity, high-temperature processes and process emissions. Transition finance therefore creates a capital-market opportunity for modernisation while investors increasingly assess whether transition investments have credible emissions-reduction pathways.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: transition capex; tCO₂e avoided; emissions intensity/t metal; coal replacement; electrification; renewable PPAs; transition-finance volume; % capex aligned with decarbonisation pathway. Kazakhstan's Carbon Neutrality Strategy estimates approximately US$610bn of net low-carbon investment needs through 2060 across the economy.

drivers.name: Critical Minerals Investment & Financing
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's critical-minerals potential is attracting targeted public and private financing. Development of extraction and processing capacity creates investment opportunities while ESG performance becomes increasingly relevant because international investors and customers are concerned with responsible sourcing, environmental impacts and supply security.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Development Bank of Kazakhstan launched a USD 1bn financing programme for 2025–2030 for extraction and processing of rare, rare-earth and critical materials. Minimum financing amount: KZT 5bn, with terms up to 20 years. KPIs: critical-minerals FDI; project pipeline; financing volume; reserves/resources; processing capacity; % value-added processing; ESG-screened projects.

drivers.name: Metallurgical Modernisation & Environmental Capex
drivers.logic: Decarbonisation, BAT implementation, pollution control, energy efficiency and resource efficiency require substantial capital expenditure. For listed and debt-financed producers, the scale and effectiveness of this capex increasingly affects long-term competitiveness, operating costs and access to capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: environmental/decarbonisation capex; BAT-related capex; energy intensity; emissions intensity; pollution-control investment; water-reuse capex; % capex allocated to ESG transition.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Environmental Code; Carbon Neutrality Strategy

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Metals & Product Competitiveness
drivers.logic: International buyers and investors increasingly distinguish metals by embedded carbon. Lower-carbon production can protect market access and potentially command a premium, while high-carbon production can face higher financing, customer and trade costs.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: tCO₂e/t metal; product carbon footprint; renewable electricity share; low-carbon product volumes; green premium; share of exports to carbon-sensitive markets; CBAM exposure.

drivers.name: Carbon-Cost Exposure & Asset Valuation
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's ETS makes emissions financially relevant for covered mining and metallurgical assets. As carbon costs and allocation rules evolve, companies with high emissions intensity may face higher compliance costs and greater capital requirements, affecting cash flows and valuation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KAZ ETS covered approximately 50% of national CO₂ emissions and 229 installations in 2024. KPIs: tCO₂e; allowance deficit/surplus; carbon cost; carbon cost/t metal; emissions intensity; future carbon-price sensitivity; ETS-covered EBITDA exposure.

drivers.name: Critical Minerals Financing & Energy-Transition Supply Chains
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's role in critical-mineral extraction and processing is creating financing demand for exploration, mine development, processing, infrastructure and higher-value mineral supply chains. Dedicated public financing for critical and rare-earth materials increases access to long-term capital for projects aligned with the global energy transition.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Development Bank of Kazakhstan launched a USD 1bn financing programme for 2025–2030 for projects involving rare, rare-earth and critical materials. Financing starts from KZT 5bn, with maturities of up to 20 years. Eligible materials include lithium, cobalt, tungsten, germanium, gallium, graphite and rare-earth elements. The EBRD has also identified critical raw materials and mining modernisation as strategic investment areas in Kazakhstan.

drivers.name: Water Scarcity & Drought
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's mining and metallurgical operations are exposed to declining and increasingly variable water availability. Climate change is already affecting freshwater storage in eastern, southern and central Kazakhstan, while higher temperatures increase evaporation and water demand. This creates risks for ore processing, beneficiation, cooling and other water-dependent operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank identifies declining terrestrial freshwater storage in eastern, southern and central Kazakhstan and expects higher temperatures to accelerate drying of major water bodies, including Lake Balkhash. Kazakhstan also receives around half of its water from sources originating outside the country, increasing exposure to transboundary water availability. KPIs: m³ water/t ore; m³/t metal; freshwater withdrawal; water consumption; % water recycled/reused; site-level water stress; production exposed to water shortages.

drivers.name: Extreme Heat
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures and more frequent heat extremes can affect worker health and productivity, increase cooling requirements and reduce operating efficiency at Kazakhstan's open-pit mines and processing facilities. Heat also increases evaporation and therefore compounds water stress.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan is projected to experience substantial warming; under high-emissions scenarios, warming could reach approximately 5.3°C by the 2090s relative to the historical baseline. KPIs: extreme-heat days; maximum temperature; heat-index days; heat-related incidents; lost working hours; cooling energy; heat-related downtime.

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall & Flooding
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's mining assets can be exposed to intense spring flooding, which can disrupt mines, roads, railways, processing facilities and water-management infrastructure. Floodwater can also mobilise contaminants from mining waste and tailings facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The 2024 spring flood was Kazakhstan's most devastating flood event in ~80 years, with more than 200,000 people displaced and reported economic losses exceeding US$440m. Kazakhstan's climate projections indicate increasing precipitation intensity and flood risk. KPIs: mining assets in flood-prone areas; flood return period; extreme precipitation; production downtime; repair costs; drainage capacity; adaptation capex.

drivers.name: Climate Risk to Tailings & Mining Waste Facilities
drivers.logic: Changes in precipitation, flooding, drought and temperature can affect the stability and water balance of tailings-storage facilities. Because tailings failures can create severe environmental and social consequences, climate-related changes in hazard conditions can increase financial and liability exposure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: TSFs exposed to flood/extreme-rainfall risk; consequence classification; freeboard; precipitation extremes; water balance; dam-safety incidents; climate stress tests; adaptation capex; GISTM alignment.
drivers.keySources: ICMM / Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management; World Bank climate-risk data

drivers.name: Climate Risk to Transport & Export Infrastructure
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan has a large legacy and active inventory of tailings facilities, and changing precipitation, spring flooding, temperature and water conditions can affect tailings water balances, seepage and structural stability. This creates potentially material environmental, safety, remediation and financial liabilities for mining companies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Recent Kazakhstan-specific research identified approximately 120 TSFs nationally and found that spring flooding and changing weather conditions can exacerbate overtopping and seepage risks. A detailed Kazakhstan case study found the tailings water pond and wet-tailings area were responsive to precipitation and temperature variability, with increased vulnerability during spring floods. KPIs: TSFs exposed to flood risk; water balance/freeboard; seepage; overtopping incidents; precipitation extremes; consequence classification; climate stress tests; adaptation capex.

drivers.name: Drought & Hydrological Variability
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's continental climate creates substantial interannual variability in precipitation and river flows. Longer or more severe droughts can reduce water available to mines and metallurgical plants, increase competition with agriculture and communities, and increase operating costs for water-intensive processing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank identifies drought and declining water availability as significant Kazakhstan climate risks. The country has particularly high exposure because ~90% of current water use is for irrigation, increasing competition for available water resources. KPIs: drought frequency/duration; basin water availability; water allocation; production exposed to drought; water-storage capacity; freshwater cost; emergency water sourcing.

drivers.name: Freeze–Thaw & Extreme Winter Conditions
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's highly continental climate exposes mining infrastructure to large seasonal temperature swings. Changing freeze–thaw conditions can affect roads, railways, pipelines, water infrastructure, foundations and tailings facilities, while severe winter conditions can disrupt production and transportation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan case-study research identifies temperatures ranging from approximately −30°C to +30°C at a representative mining site and finds that temperature variability affected tailings water conditions. KPIs: freeze–thaw cycles; days below critical temperature; infrastructure failures; maintenance costs; winter downtime; pipeline/water-system failures.

drivers.name: Compound Climate Hazards
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's mining infrastructure can be exposed to technological accidents triggered or amplified by natural hazards such as floods, landslides and extreme precipitation. For tailings and other hazardous mining-waste facilities, climate change can therefore convert physical climate hazards into environmental contamination and industrial-safety events.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UNECE identifies Kazakhstan as exposed to Natech risks involving mining/tailings facilities and notes that changing weather patterns and more extreme events can aggravate these risks. KPIs: mining facilities exposed to natural hazards; climate-triggered incidents; spill/release events; emergency-response time; contaminated area; adaptation investment.

drivers.name: EU CBAM Exposure
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's exporters of covered metals face direct pressure to measure, verify and reduce embedded carbon emissions to preserve competitiveness in the EU market. This is particularly material for aluminium, ferroalloys, iron and steel exporters.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CBAM entered its definitive regime in January 2026. The EU accounted for approximately 44% of Kazakhstan's exports in 2025, while more than 50% of Kazakhstan's aluminium exports went to the EU. A 2026 ITC–QazTrade assessment estimates potential CBAM obligations of around €114m annually for four key Kazakhstan export categories, including aluminium and ferrochrome. KPIs: EU export value; tCO₂e/t product; verified embedded emissions; CBAM certificates/cost; % exports covered by CBAM.
drivers.keySources:
EU Delegation to Kazakhstan — CBAM readiness assessment;  
Kazakhstan Ministry of Trade — CBAM impact on exporters

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Metal Customer Requirements
drivers.logic: International buyers increasingly require product-level emissions information to manage their own Scope 3 emissions. For Kazakhstan's energy-intensive metals producers, carbon intensity can therefore become a commercial differentiator and a condition for maintaining access to international customers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: tCO₂e/t metal; product carbon footprint; % production with verified PCF; % customers requesting emissions data; low-carbon product share; renewable electricity share. Kazakhstan's CBAM-readiness assessment specifically recommends stronger emissions data collection and engagement with EU buyers.
drivers.keySources:
EU Delegation to Kazakhstan — CBAM readiness assessment; 
GHG Protocol — Scope 3 Standard

drivers.name: Responsible Mineral Sourcing & Traceability
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's growing role in critical-mineral supply chains increases expectations for responsible sourcing, due diligence, transparency and traceability. International investors and customers increasingly assess whether minerals can be demonstrated to originate from responsible operations and whether environmental, social and governance risks are being managed.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan became an OECD adherent to the Minerals Guidance in 2017 and has a national responsible-business-conduct framework. OECD reports that Kazakh mining companies are already implementing supply-chain due diligence: Kazzinc was assessed against the Copper Mark Joint Due Diligence Standard in 2023, while Kazzinc and Kazakhmys participate in international responsible-sourcing systems. KPIs: % production traceable; supplier due-diligence coverage; high-risk suppliers; audit findings; corrective actions; chain-of-custody coverage.
drivers.keySources:
OECD — Responsible Mineral Supply Chains; 
OECD — Critical Raw Materials Governance in Central Asia

drivers.name: Critical Minerals Supply Security
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's substantial critical-mineral endowment creates an opportunity to become a diversified supplier to international markets seeking more secure and geographically diversified mineral supply. This increases the strategic importance of reliable production, processing capacity and ESG-compliant supply chains.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan reports the ability to supply finished products from 20 of the 60 critical minerals on the USGS list. Kazakhstan and the US signed a critical-minerals MOU in 2025 focused on processing capacity, technology transfer and market access. KPIs: reserves/resources; production; processing capacity; export concentration; customer concentration; long-term offtake agreements; share of critical minerals processed domestically.
drivers.keySources: Government of Kazakhstan — Critical Minerals Ministerial; OECD — Critical Raw Materials Governance in Central Asia

drivers.name: Supply-Chain Emissions & Logistics Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's mining sector is geographically dispersed and export-oriented, making transportation a material part of the value-chain carbon footprint. International customers increasingly need emissions data covering transport and other Scope 3 categories, creating pressure to improve logistics efficiency and emissions measurement.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: kgCO₂e/t-km; tCO₂e/t metal transported; rail/road share; logistics emissions; route distance; % shipments with verified emissions data; emissions per tonne exported. Kazakhstan-specific assessment should prioritise major export corridors and EU-facing supply chains.
drivers.keySources: GHG Protocol — Scope 3 Standard; EU Delegation to Kazakhstan — CBAM readiness assessment

drivers.name: Domestic Processing & Value-Chain Development
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan is seeking to move from extraction toward greater domestic processing and production of higher-value critical-mineral products. This changes supply-chain requirements by increasing demand for processing technologies, infrastructure and ESG performance across the domestic value chain.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's critical-minerals cooperation with the US explicitly includes development of processing capacities and technology transfer. KPIs: % minerals processed domestically; processing capacity; share of exports consisting of processed products; domestic value added; downstream investment; processing yield.
drivers.keySources: Government of Kazakhstan — Critical Minerals Ministerial; OECD — Critical Raw Materials Governance in Central Asia

drivers.name: Circularity & Secondary Metals
drivers.logic: Increasing use of recycled metals by downstream customers can reduce dependence on primary extraction and associated energy and environmental impacts. For Kazakhstan's metals industry, greater recycling and secondary production can therefore become a customer requirement as well as a competitiveness opportunity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: recycled input %; secondary metal production; recovery rate; scrap utilisation; recycled content; energy/t metal; GHG emissions/t secondary metal.

drivers.name: Law on Subsoil (2024)
drivers.logic: The new Subsoil Law modernises the legal framework for exploration and extraction and introduces a more structured framework for mineral-resource development. For mining companies, this creates requirements around legal access to resources, licensing, resource use and compliance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Law No. ZRU-987 adopted 31 October 2024. KPIs: mining/exploration licences; exploration expenditure; licence compliance; resource/reserve reporting; violations; rehabilitation obligations.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Ministry of Mining & Geology — Law on Subsoil

drivers.name: Environmental Impact Assessment & Environmental Expertise
drivers.logic: Mining and metallurgical projects must demonstrate environmental acceptability before implementation. The strengthened EIA framework increases requirements to identify, assess and mitigate environmental and social impacts, including emissions, water impacts and waste from mining and processing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Law No. ZRU-1036 adopted 24 February 2025. EIA/environmental expertise includes assessment of environmental risks, resource-use efficiency and proposed mitigation measures; public environmental expertise is also recognised. KPIs: EIA approvals; environmental conditions; emissions/discharges; waste; mitigation capex; environmental violations; public consultations.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Government — Environmental Expertise Law No. 1036

drivers.name: NDC 3.0 / Industrial Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's higher climate ambition creates an economy-wide direction toward lower emissions intensity, directly affecting energy-intensive mining and metallurgy. Companies face increasing pressure to improve energy efficiency, reduce GHG intensity and integrate lower-carbon power.
drivers.evidenceKpi: NDC 3.0 raises the target from 35% GHG-intensity reduction by 2030 to 50% by 2035, relative to 2010. The target is measured as GHG emissions per unit of GDP. KPIs: Scope 1–2; tCO₂e/t metal; energy intensity; renewable electricity share; decarbonisation capex.

drivers.name: National Green Economy Taxonomy
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's Green Taxonomy determines which investments can be classified as green and therefore creates a regulatory framework for directing capital toward resource-efficient and low-carbon activities. This is directly relevant to mining projects seeking green financing or state financial support.
drivers.evidenceKpi: National Green Taxonomy adopted 25 October 2023. It covers water/raw-material efficiency, air and soil quality, energy efficiency and renewable energy. For industrial/technical uses, the taxonomy targets 40% reduction in freshwater consumption; it also targets at least 20% GHG reduction and 80% recycling of collected secondary raw materials.

drivers.name: Mining & Geological Sector Development / Responsible Resource Development
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan is moving from predominantly raw-resource extraction toward exploration, processing, technology and higher-value mineral production. This policy direction increases expectations for efficient resource utilisation, technological upgrading and domestic value addition.
drivers.evidenceKpi: More than 1,650 new deposits identified over seven years; direct foreign investment in the mining/geology sector reached US$3.6bn. KPIs: exploration expenditure; resource replacement; processing rate; value added; technology investment; resource efficiency.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Ministry of Mining & Geology — Mineral Resources & Geological Sector

drivers.name: Critical Minerals Development
drivers.logic: Government policy is actively prioritising exploration, extraction, processing and higher-value production of critical/rare minerals. For mining companies, this creates both development opportunities and increasing expectations around efficient extraction, processing and technology transfer.
drivers.evidenceKpi: More than 30 critical-metal deposits identified. 76 projects covering 28 rare minerals planned over three years with total investment of US$2.6bn. KPIs: critical-mineral production; processing capacity; resource efficiency; recovery rates; investment; value-added output.

drivers.name: Ferrous Metallurgy Development Strategy to 2030
drivers.logic: The government's metallurgy strategy promotes expansion and technological modernisation of ferrous metallurgy. For producers, this creates pressure to improve production efficiency, technology and environmental performance as capacity expands.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Strategy adopted pursuant to Presidential Decree PF-16 of 30 January 2025, with a 2030 horizon. KPIs: steel capacity/output; energy intensity; emissions intensity; modernisation capex; scrap utilisation; production efficiency.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Ministry of Mining & Geology — Ferrous Metallurgy Strategy 2030

drivers.name: Resource Efficiency & Mining Waste Management
drivers.logic: Mining and beneficiation generate substantial waste and consume water, energy and raw materials. Uzbekistan's environmental framework increasingly requires rational resource use and control of pollution from extraction, blasting, enrichment and waste-storage facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: water consumption/t ore; energy/t metal; waste generated/t ore; tailings volume; recovery rate; recycled materials; land rehabilitated; pollution incidents. Uzbekistan's environmental requirements explicitly cover pollution and depletion associated with extraction, blasting, waste storage, dumps and mining/enrichment activities.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Government — Water, Land & Underground Resources Environmental Requirements

drivers.name: ESG-Linked Access to International Capital
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's mining sector is increasingly being prepared for international capital markets, with ESG ratings, international resource valuation and Eurobond issuance explicitly being considered as part of the transformation of mining companies. Better ESG data and performance can therefore facilitate access to international investors and debt markets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In December 2024, Uzbekistan's Ministry of Mining and Geology held discussions with Sustainable Fitch, London Stock Exchange and international financial institutions regarding ESG ratings and Eurobond issuance as part of mining-company transformation. KPIs: ESG rating; international debt raised; investor participation; cost of debt; Eurobond issuance; ESG disclosure coverage.

drivers.name: Green & Sustainable Finance Eligibility
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's National Green Taxonomy creates an increasingly concrete pathway for mining and metallurgical companies to finance eligible environmental investments through green bonds, loans and other sustainable-finance instruments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Green Taxonomy adopted in 2023; green-project classification is being applied to green bonds, loans and other financing. State-supported companies' capital expenditures are subject to taxonomy classification. KPIs: taxonomy-aligned capex; green loans/bonds; eligible project volume; financing cost; external verification.

drivers.name: Green Bond & Sustainable Bond Market Development
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan is developing its sustainable debt market, creating a potential funding channel for mining companies investing in energy efficiency, renewable power, water efficiency and other eligible projects. This makes ESG project eligibility increasingly relevant to financing strategy.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan has issued sovereign green and SDG bonds and maintains annual allocation/impact reporting. The Ministry of Economy and Finance reported a US$1bn mobilisation of green investments through sustainable/green bonds issued by partner banks on the London Stock Exchange. KPIs: green/SDG bond issuance; mining-related eligible proceeds; green capex; impact metrics; financing cost.
drivers.keySources:
Uzbekistan Ministry of Economy & Finance; 
Uzbekistan Government - US$1bn Green Financing Mobilisation

drivers.name: Critical Minerals Investment
drivers.logic: Government prioritisation of critical minerals is attracting capital toward exploration, extraction and processing. The scale of planned projects makes ESG performance increasingly relevant to investors assessing long-duration mining assets and processing projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 76 projects covering 28 rare minerals; US$2.6bn planned investment over three years. More than 30 critical-metal deposits have been identified. KPIs: mining FDI; exploration capex; project pipeline; processing capacity; ESG-screened investment; project-level environmental capex.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan - Critical Minerals Development

drivers.name: Mining FDI & ESG Investor Due Diligence
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's mining reforms are attracting international investors, increasing the relevance of environmental, social and governance due diligence for project financing and strategic investment. International investors can increasingly assess environmental permitting, resource governance, ESG ratings and operational risks before committing capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Mining/geology sector FDI reached US$3.6bn; major investors from France, Japan, China and other countries have entered the sector. KPIs: mining FDI; foreign-investor share; ESG due-diligence coverage; environmental/social conditions attached to financing; ESG rating.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Ministry of Mining & Geology - Mineral Resources & Geological Sector

drivers.name: Large-Scale Metallurgical Modernisation Capex
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's expansion of copper, gold and ferrous-metals processing creates substantial capital requirements. For investors, the ESG quality of these projects—energy intensity, emissions, water use, waste and technology—affects long-term operating costs and transition resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Current projects include a US$2.7bn copper processing complex at Almalyk with capacity to process 60m tonnes of ore/year and produce approximately 900,000 tonnes of copper concentrate/year. A new metallurgical complex is planned with 300,000 tonnes/year of copper cathode capacity. KPIs: capex; energy intensity; tCO₂e/t metal; water use; renewable electricity; waste/tailings; BAT/clean-technology investment.
drivers.keySources:
Uzbekistan Government - Copper Processing Plant No. 3; 
President of Uzbekistan - Industrial Development Programme

drivers.name: Transition Finance & Decarbonisation Investment
drivers.logic: Energy-intensive mining and metallurgy require capital for energy efficiency, electrification, renewable power, water efficiency and pollution control. Uzbekistan's sustainable-finance policy increasingly creates channels for financing these investments.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan State Programme — Green Finance & Investment Requirements

drivers.name: Water Scarcity & Declining Water Availability
drivers.logic: Water scarcity is a material physical risk for Uzbekistan's mining and metals sector because ore processing, beneficiation, metallurgy and cooling can require substantial water. Declining river flows and rising demand can increase competition for water, operating costs and potentially constrain production.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank estimates that climate change could reduce water availability by 30–40% while increasing irrigation demand by 25%. KPIs: m³/t ore; m³/t metal; freshwater withdrawal; water consumption; % recycled/reused water; sites in water-stressed basins; production exposed to water constraints.
drivers.keySources: World Bank — Uzbekistan irrigation and water availability; World Bank — Uzbekistan CCDR

drivers.name: Drought & Hydrological Variability
drivers.logic: More frequent and severe drought can reduce water availability for mining and processing while increasing competition between industrial, agricultural and municipal users. This can create production, cost and social-licence risks for water-intensive mines and metallurgical plants.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's climate assessment identifies droughts and reduced glacier-fed flows as major climate risks. KPIs: drought frequency/severity; river inflows; reservoir levels; water availability per site; production downtime; water procurement cost.
drivers.keySources: World Bank — Uzbekistan CCDR; World Bank — Water Availability

drivers.name: Extreme Heat
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures can reduce worker productivity and increase occupational-health risks, while also increasing cooling requirements and thermal stress on mining and metallurgical equipment. Heat can therefore affect both production costs and operational continuity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank identifies extreme heat as a major climate vulnerability for Uzbekistan; by 2030, at least 8 million people are projected to live in very high climate-risk areas. KPIs: maximum temperature; number of extreme-heat days; heat-related incidents; lost work hours; cooling energy; heat-related downtime.

drivers.name: Rainfall Volatility & Flash Flooding
drivers.logic: Increasing rainfall variability and intense precipitation can damage mine roads, rail links, drainage systems, processing facilities and tailings infrastructure. For mines located in mountainous areas, runoff and flash flooding can be particularly disruptive.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank identifies rainfall volatility as one of Uzbekistan's key climate risks. KPIs: extreme precipitation events; flood-exposed assets; drainage capacity; downtime; repair costs; tailings facilities exposed to flood pathways.

drivers.name: Dust Storms & Land Degradation
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's arid climate and the ecological degradation associated with the Aral Sea region increase exposure to dust storms. Dust can disrupt mining and transport operations, reduce visibility, damage equipment and increase worker-health risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank specifically identifies dust storms and the Aral Sea ecological disaster as climate-related vulnerabilities. KPIs: dust-storm days; PM10/PM2.5; visibility-related disruptions; exposed sites; respiratory incidents; equipment maintenance costs.

drivers.name: Climate Stress on Energy Security
drivers.logic: Mining and metallurgy are electricity-intensive, while Uzbekistan's energy system is itself exposed to climate and water stress. Power shortages or increased cooling demand can therefore translate into production interruptions and higher operating costs for mines and processing plants.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Energy sector accounts for approximately 75% of Uzbekistan's GHG emissions, highlighting the scale and importance of the energy system. KPIs: kWh/t metal; outage hours; production lost from power interruptions; backup capacity; renewable electricity share; Scope 2 emissions.

drivers.name: Climate Risk to Tailings & Mine Waste Infrastructure
drivers.logic: Changes in extreme rainfall, runoff and water availability can increase physical risks to tailings storage and mine-waste facilities. Failure or uncontrolled discharge could create severe environmental, financial and social consequences.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: tailings facilities exposed to extreme rainfall/flood pathways; freeboard; water balance; consequence classification; extreme-rainfall design standard; adaptation capex; incidents.
drivers.keySources:
World Bank — Uzbekistan CCDR; 
Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management

drivers.name: Responsible Mineral Sourcing & Due Diligence
drivers.logic: International customers and investors increasingly expect mining companies to identify, prevent and mitigate environmental, human-rights, corruption and other ESG risks throughout mineral supply chains. This is increasingly relevant as Uzbekistan integrates into international critical-mineral supply chains.
drivers.evidenceKpi: OECD due-diligence framework applies across the entire minerals supply chain, from mines to end users. KPIs: % suppliers screened; % high-risk suppliers assessed; due-diligence coverage; corrective actions; ESG audits; supplier incidents.

drivers.name: Mineral Traceability & Chain of Custody
drivers.logic: As Uzbekistan develops critical-mineral exports and seeks international customers, demonstrating the origin and responsible production of minerals becomes increasingly important. Traceability can support customer due diligence, ESG claims and access to premium international markets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: OECD identifies supply-chain transparency and traceability as key implementation challenges for responsible mineral supply chains.
drivers.keySources:
OECD - Critical Raw Materials Governance in Central Asia; 
OECD - Responsible Mineral Supply Chains

drivers.name: Critical Mineral Supply Security
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's expansion of critical-mineral production creates opportunities to become a diversified international supplier, but customers will increasingly assess reliability, production continuity, processing capacity and concentration risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: More than 30 critical-metal deposits identified; 76 projects covering 28 minerals with planned investment of US$2.6bn. KPIs: production capacity; reserves/resources; export concentration; customer concentration; long-term offtake agreements; inventory days.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan — Critical Minerals Programme

drivers.name: Domestic Processing & Value-Added Supply Chains
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan is explicitly seeking to move from raw-material extraction toward processing and finished products. This creates more integrated domestic supply chains and increases requirements for reliable processing, technology, environmental performance and resource efficiency.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Government plans 76 projects covering 28 rare minerals, with emphasis on the chain from raw materials → processing → science/technology → finished products. KPIs: % minerals processed domestically; processing capacity; recovery rate; value-added output; downstream production.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan — Critical Minerals Programme

drivers.name: Product Carbon Footprint & Customer Emissions Data
drivers.logic: International customers increasingly need product-level emissions information to manage their own Scope 3 emissions and compare suppliers. For Uzbekistan's energy-intensive metals producers, lack of reliable product carbon data can become a barrier to international market access.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: tCO₂e/t metal; Scope 1–3; product carbon footprint; % products with verified PCF; % customers requiring emissions data; supplier emissions coverage.
drivers.keySources:
GHG Protocol - Product Standard; 
GHG Protocol - Scope 3 Standard

drivers.name: EU CBAM Exposure — Covered Metals
drivers.logic: Where Uzbek producers export CBAM-covered products to the EU, embedded-emissions measurement and carbon-cost management can become a direct supply-chain competitiveness issue. This driver should therefore apply only to companies/products with EU exposure, rather than to Uzbekistan's entire mining sector.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EU CBAM definitive regime began in 2026 and covers iron & steel and aluminium, among other sectors. KPIs: EU export value; tonnes exported; embedded tCO₂e/t product; verified emissions; CBAM certificates/cost.

drivers.name: Supply-Chain Climate Resilience
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's mining supply chains depend on water, electricity, transport and processing infrastructure that are increasingly exposed to heat, drought, water scarcity and rainfall volatility. Climate disruption at suppliers or logistics providers can therefore interrupt production even where the mine itself is resilient.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: % critical suppliers climate-screened; supplier sites in water-stressed areas; logistics routes exposed to flooding/heat; supplier disruption days; business-continuity coverage; dual sourcing.

drivers.name: Supply-Chain Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Mining companies face increasing pressure to reduce emissions beyond their own operations, including purchased electricity, fuel, transportation, equipment and processing. This is particularly relevant for Uzbekistan because its mining and metals industry is energy-intensive.
drivers.evidenceKpi: KPIs: Scope 3 tCO₂e; supplier emissions coverage; logistics tCO₂e/t-km; purchased-goods emissions; renewable electricity share; % suppliers with climate targets.
drivers.keySources: GHG Protocol — Scope 3 Standard; World Bank — Uzbekistan CCDR

drivers.name: UAE NDC 3.0 / National 2035 Emissions Target
drivers.logic: The UAE's updated national climate commitment strengthens the policy direction toward economy-wide emissions reduction. For energy-intensive metals production, particularly aluminium, iron and steel, this increases pressure to reduce operational emissions and align industrial investment with national decarbonisation objectives.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE committed to reduce GHG emissions 47% by 2035 compared with 2019 levels, reducing anticipated emissions from 196.3 MtCO₂e to 103.5 MtCO₂e. KPIs: Scope 1–2 emissions; tCO₂e/t aluminium or steel; renewable/clean electricity share; decarbonisation capex.

drivers.name: UAE Net Zero by 2050 Strategic Initiative
drivers.logic: The UAE's national net-zero objective creates a long-term transition framework for energy-intensive industrial sectors. Metals producers increasingly need to consider operational decarbonisation, electricity sourcing, technology upgrades and long-term asset resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Climate neutrality by 2050. KPIs: net-zero transition plan; Scope 1–3 emissions; tCO₂e/t metal; low-carbon electricity share; decarbonisation capex; residual emissions.
drivers.keySources: UAE National Framework for Sustainable Development

drivers.name: UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap
drivers.logic: This is the most directly relevant national policy driver for UAE metals. The Roadmap explicitly targets heavy-emitting industrial sectors including aluminium, iron and steel, creating a clear national decarbonisation pathway for production technologies, energy use and industrial investment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Targets cumulative industrial-sector CO₂ reductions of 5% by 2030, 63% by 2040 and 93% by 2050. The Roadmap aims to support a cumulative reduction of 2.9 GtCO₂ by 2050 and evaluates more than 50 decarbonisation technologies and solutions. KPIs: tCO₂e/t metal; emissions reduction vs. baseline; renewable electricity; technology deployment; decarbonisation capex.
drivers.keySources: UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap — MoIAT (Ministry of Interior Affairs)

drivers.name: Federal Regulation for Energy Management in Industrial Facilities
drivers.logic: The UAE has introduced a dedicated federal regulation for energy management in industrial facilities. This makes systematic energy management and consumption reduction increasingly relevant for energy-intensive aluminium and metals production.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Regulation is described by the UAE government as the first of its kind in the UAE industrial sector and supports operational energy management to reduce consumption and accelerate industrial decarbonisation. KPIs: energy intensity (GJ/t metal or kWh/t product); facility energy-management systems; energy savings; energy reduction projects; emissions avoided.
drivers.keySources: MoEI — Federal Regulation for Energy Management in Industrial Facilities (Ministry of Education)

drivers.name: National Energy & Water Demand Management Programme 2050
drivers.logic: Metals production is among the UAE's most energy-intensive industrial activities. National demand-management policy therefore creates a strong policy driver for industrial energy efficiency and more efficient resource use.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE programme targets a 40% reduction in energy demand by 2050 and explicitly identifies industry as one of the three largest energy-consuming sectors targeted for efficiency improvements. KPIs: kWh/t aluminium or steel; GJ/t product; energy savings; electricity demand; energy-management performance.
drivers.keySources: UAE National Energy and Water Demand Management Programme

drivers.name: Operation 300bn / Sustainable Industrial Production
drivers.logic: UAE industrial policy combines industrial expansion with advanced technology, resource efficiency, clean energy and reduced environmental footprint. For metals and advanced manufacturing, this creates policy support and increasing expectations for technological modernisation and sustainable production.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Operation 300bn targets increasing industrial-sector GDP contribution from AED133bn to AED300bn by 2031. The strategy promotes sustainable production cycles, reduced resource consumption, clean-energy deployment and lower industrial environmental footprints. KPIs: industrial output; technology investment; energy intensity; resource efficiency; environmental footprint; clean-energy share.

drivers.name: Circular Economy Policy & Resource Efficiency
drivers.logic: UAE industrial policy increasingly promotes resource efficiency, waste reduction and circular production. This is particularly relevant to metals because recycled input, scrap recovery and material efficiency can reduce both environmental impacts and energy requirements compared with primary production.
drivers.evidenceKpi: National policy framework seeks sustainable and efficient resource use, increased recycling and use of waste as manufacturing inputs, and reductions in water and energy consumption. KPIs: recycled input %; scrap utilisation; material recovery rate; waste/t metal; secondary metal production; energy intensity.
drivers.keySources:
UAE National Framework for Sustainable Development (UAE Legislation); 
Operation 300bn - UAE Government

drivers.name: Industrial Water Efficiency & Water Reuse
drivers.logic: The UAE has very limited natural freshwater resources, making efficient water management strategically important for industrial processing and metals production. National water-demand policy increasingly encourages lower water consumption and greater reuse.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE policy framework targets a 21% reduction in total water-resource demand by 2036 and, under the national demand-management programme, targets expanded water reuse of up to 95%. KPIs: m³/t metal; freshwater withdrawal; desalinated-water use; recycled/reused water %; wastewater discharge; water intensity reduction.
drivers.keySources: UAE National Energy & Water Demand Management Programme - UAE Legislation

drivers.name: Advanced & Clean Industrial Technology Adoption
drivers.logic: UAE industrial policy promotes advanced technologies and Industry 4.0 solutions to improve industrial productivity while reducing environmental footprints. For metals production, this supports digital energy management, process optimisation, predictive maintenance and lower-carbon technologies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap assessed more than 50 technologies and solutions for industrial decarbonisation. MoIAT's industrial strategy explicitly promotes advanced technology adoption to increase efficiency and reduce environmental impact. KPIs: technology adoption rate; energy savings; emissions avoided; process efficiency; digital monitoring coverage; capex in low-carbon technologies.
drivers.keySources: UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap - MoIAT (Ministry of Interior Affairs)

drivers.name: Strategic Investment in Aluminium & Downstream Metals
drivers.logic: Aluminium is a strategically important UAE industrial sector and a major component of the country's non-oil industrial base. Continued expansion of primary and downstream production creates capital requirements while increasing the importance of energy efficiency, emissions performance and long-term transition resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EGA reported an economic contribution of approximately AED23.49bn (US$6.4bn) in 2024. KPIs: aluminium production; downstream capacity; industrial capex; economic value added; energy intensity; tCO₂e/t Al.
drivers.keySources:
EGA 2025 Sustainability Report; 
ADNOC–EGA aluminium raw-material localisation agreement

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Aluminium Competitiveness
drivers.logic: Aluminium customers and investors increasingly differentiate producers based on carbon intensity because electricity and smelting technology materially determine aluminium's embedded emissions. Lower-carbon production can therefore support customer demand, long-term contracts, asset competitiveness and access to sustainability-focused capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EGA's 2025 GHG emissions intensity was reported as approximately 32% below the global industry average. EGA targets a 25% reduction in emissions intensity by 2030 versus 2020, covering Scope 1, Scope 2 and upstream Scope 3 emissions. KPIs: tCO₂e/t Al; product carbon footprint; renewable/low-carbon electricity share; low-carbon aluminium sales; verified product emissions.

drivers.name: Industrial Decarbonisation Capital Requirements
drivers.logic: UAE aluminium, iron and steel production will require substantial investment in lower-carbon electricity, process efficiency, electrification, hydrogen and other industrial decarbonisation technologies. Capital allocation increasingly needs to account for long-term carbon and technology risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap targets industrial CO₂ reductions of 5% by 2030, 63% by 2040 and 93% by 2050 and assessed more than 50 technologies and solutions. The Roadmap specifically covers aluminium, iron and steel. KPIs: transition capex; tCO₂e avoided; renewable electricity capacity; technology deployment; emissions intensity.
drivers.keySources: UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap - MoIAT (Ministry of Interior Affairs)

drivers.name: Green & Transition Finance for Heavy Industry
drivers.logic: UAE decarbonisation targets create demand for capital to finance projects that may reduce emissions but cannot be achieved through immediate zero-carbon substitution. Metals producers therefore increasingly need access to financing for energy efficiency, clean electricity, process innovation and emerging technologies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap provides a national investment framework for heavy-emitting sectors including aluminium and steel and evaluates more than 50 potential decarbonisation solutions. KPIs: green/transition financing volume; taxonomy-aligned capex; cost of capital; tCO₂e avoided per AED invested; transition capex as % of total capex.
drivers.keySources: UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap - MoIAT (Ministry of Interior Affairs)

drivers.name: Industrial Localisation & Supply-Chain Investment
drivers.logic: Localisation of industrial inputs and downstream processing can reduce supply-chain dependence and create new investment opportunities. ESG performance is relevant because local manufacturing projects increasingly need to demonstrate resource efficiency, energy performance and long-term resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, ADNOC and EGA announced a US$500m agreement to localise production of key raw material used in aluminium production. In 2026, the UAE also established a AED1bn National Industrial Resilience Fund to strengthen industrial supply chains, local manufacturing capacity and import substitution. KPIs: local procurement; domestic manufacturing capacity; local content; investment in localisation; supplier concentration; supply disruption exposure.
drivers.keySources:
ADNOC–EGA localisation agreement; 
UAE National Industrial Resilience Fund - MoIAT (Ministry of Interior Affairs)

drivers.name: Industrial Efficiency & Technology Modernisation Investment
drivers.logic: Advanced technologies, digitalisation and process optimisation can reduce energy use, emissions and operating costs in energy-intensive metals production. This creates an investment case where ESG improvements can simultaneously improve asset efficiency and financial resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap assessed 50+ technologies and solutions for industrial decarbonisation. KPIs: technology-modernisation capex; energy saved; kWh/t metal; GJ/t product; emissions avoided; operating-cost savings.
drivers.keySources: UAE Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap - MoIAT (Ministry of Interior Affairs)

drivers.name: Extreme Heat & Worker Heat Stress
drivers.logic: Extreme temperatures can affect outdoor mining activity, worker health and productivity, while increasing cooling requirements and thermal stress on industrial equipment. This is particularly material for large industrial facilities operating continuously in the UAE's hot climate.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP projects increasing exposure to extreme temperature and heat-index thresholds. Its UAE heat-risk analysis explicitly identifies risks to labour productivity, infrastructure, electricity systems and worker health. KPIs: days above 40°C/45°C; heat-index days; heat-related incidents; lost work hours; cooling energy; heat-related downtime.
drivers.keySources: World Bank CCKP - UAE Compounded Heat Risks (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Water Scarcity & Industrial Water Dependence
drivers.logic: The UAE's highly constrained natural freshwater resources create operational and cost risks for mineral processing, industrial cooling and associated supply chains. Rising temperatures also increase water demand across competing sectors.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE's National Climate Adaptation Plan identifies increased demand for water and electricity due to rising temperature and humidity as an urgent climate impact. KPIs: m³/t metal; freshwater withdrawal; desalinated-water dependence; recycled/reused water %; water cost; production exposed to water constraints.
drivers.keySources: UAE National Climate Adaptation Action Plan

drivers.name: Sea-Level Rise & Coastal Industrial Exposure
drivers.logic: Much of the UAE's major industrial, export and logistics infrastructure is concentrated along the coast. Rising sea levels can increase exposure of ports, industrial zones, warehouses and export infrastructure to coastal flooding and disruption.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP provides UAE-specific projections of rising sea levels under all future emissions pathways and projected increases in high-tide flooding thresholds. KPIs: coastal assets exposed; metres of projected sea-level rise; high-tide flooding days; port disruption; flood protection capex; insured/uninsured losses.
drivers.keySources: World Bank CCKP - UAE Sea-Level Projections (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall & Flash-Flood Exposure
drivers.logic: Although the UAE is arid, intense rainfall events can create severe local flooding because industrial drainage, roads, logistics infrastructure and urban systems may be exposed to high volumes of precipitation over short periods. This can disrupt industrial sites, transport corridors and port access.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP provides UAE-specific extreme precipitation projections for future periods through the end of the century. KPIs: extreme rainfall events; flood-exposed facilities; logistics disruption days; production downtime; repair costs; drainage capacity.
drivers.keySources: World Bank CCKP - UAE Extreme Precipitation Events (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Climate Risk to Electricity Supply & Cooling Demand
drivers.logic: Aluminium smelting is exceptionally electricity-intensive, making reliable electricity supply a critical operational dependency. Rising temperatures can increase cooling demand, strain electricity networks and reduce the efficiency of energy infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank's UAE heat-risk assessment explicitly identifies strained grids and potential outages due to increased cooling demand and reduced power-generation efficiency as climate-related risks. EGA's 2025 Scope 1 emissions were 21 MtCO₂e, illustrating the scale of energy dependence in UAE aluminium production. KPIs: kWh/t Al; outage hours; production lost due to power interruptions; peak electricity demand; cooling load; low-carbon electricity share.
drivers.keySources:
World Bank CCKP - UAE Compounded Heat Risks; 
EGA - Net Zero FAQs (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Climate Risk to Transport, Ports & Export Logistics
drivers.logic: UAE metals production depends heavily on ports and international logistics for raw-material imports and aluminium and metal exports. Heat, coastal flooding and extreme rainfall can therefore create indirect operational and revenue risks through disrupted transport infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE's National Climate Adaptation Plan specifically identifies trade and logistics and infrastructure as sectors requiring climate-risk assessment and adaptation. KPIs: logistics disruption days; port downtime; delayed shipments; tonnes of production affected; alternative-route capacity; supply-chain losses.
drivers.keySources: UAE National Climate Adaptation Action Plan

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Aluminium Demand & Product Carbon Data
drivers.logic: Global automotive, construction, packaging and manufacturing customers increasingly seek lower-carbon aluminium to reduce value-chain emissions. UAE producers' competitiveness therefore increasingly depends on the ability to measure, verify and communicate product-level carbon intensity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EGA reported aluminium emissions intensity of 10.4 tCO₂e/t Al in 2025. KPIs: product carbon footprint (tCO₂e/t Al); % production covered by verified product-level emissions data; low-carbon aluminium sales; customer requirements for carbon data; renewable/low-carbon electricity share.

drivers.name: Localisation of Critical Aluminium Inputs
drivers.logic: Local production of strategically important inputs can reduce import dependence, shorten supply chains and improve resilience against international trade and logistics disruptions. For UAE aluminium production, localisation is particularly relevant where key carbon materials have historically been imported.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADNOC and EGA signed a US$500m five-year agreement for up to 1.5 Mt of calcined petroleum coke. The agreement is expected to supply at least 30% of EGA's calcined petcoke requirements, reducing import dependence. KPIs: % critical inputs locally sourced; import dependency; supplier concentration; inventory days; supply disruptions.

drivers.name: Local Procurement & In-Country Value
drivers.logic: UAE industrial policy increasingly promotes local procurement and supplier development. For metals producers, this creates incentives to expand domestic sourcing while also strengthening supply-chain resilience and local economic value creation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EGA spends more than AED8bn annually on goods and services from UAE suppliers, representing more than 40% of its total global procurement spend. Nationally, industrial procurement under the UAE ICV Program reached AED168bn in 2025, while cumulative local spending reached AED347bn by the end of 2024. KPIs: local procurement %; ICV contribution; spend with UAE suppliers; number of local suppliers; supplier development expenditure.

drivers.name: Critical Raw-Material Supply Security
drivers.logic: UAE aluminium production remains dependent on internationally sourced materials such as bauxite and alumina, while other inputs such as carbon materials are increasingly being localised. Geographic concentration and disruption of upstream suppliers can therefore affect production continuity, costs and inventory requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The calcined-petcoke agreement illustrates that EGA historically depended significantly on imports and is now securing 30% of this requirement domestically. KPIs: import dependency by critical input; supplier/country concentration; inventory days; alternative supplier capacity; supply disruption days; raw-material price volatility.

drivers.name: Responsible Mineral Sourcing & Supplier ESG Due Diligence
drivers.logic: International customers, investors and downstream manufacturers increasingly expect metals producers to identify and manage environmental, human-rights and governance risks in upstream mineral supply chains. This is particularly relevant where UAE metals producers source internationally.
drivers.evidenceKpi: OECD guidance applies across the entire mineral supply chain and recommends risk-based due diligence covering environmental and social impacts, human rights and other ESG risks. KPIs: % suppliers subject to ESG due diligence; high-risk suppliers identified; supplier audits; corrective-action completion; responsible-sourcing coverage.
drivers.keySources: OECD Responsible Mineral Supply Chains Guidance

drivers.name: Mineral & Metal Traceability
drivers.logic: Traceability is increasingly important for demonstrating the origin and ESG characteristics of minerals and metals. Better traceability can support responsible-sourcing claims, product carbon-footprint disclosure and customer due diligence.
drivers.evidenceKpi: OECD and IEA published dedicated analysis on traceability in critical-mineral supply chains in 2025, reflecting increasing policy and market attention to mine-to-market information. KPIs: % material volume traceable; chain-of-custody coverage; % suppliers providing origin data; traceability-system coverage; verified material flows. (OECD)
drivers.keySources: OECD/IEA — The Role of Traceability in Critical Mineral Supply Chains

drivers.name: Supply-Chain Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Aluminium's value-chain footprint extends beyond smelting to purchased raw materials, electricity, transport and other upstream activities. Customers and investors increasingly assess these value-chain emissions, creating pressure to obtain emissions data and engage suppliers in decarbonisation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EGA's net-zero approach includes Scope 1, Scope 2 and upstream Scope 3 emissions, making upstream supply-chain emissions financially and commercially relevant. KPIs: Scope 3 emissions; supplier emissions coverage; tCO₂e/t material purchased; logistics emissions; % strategic suppliers with decarbonisation targets.

drivers.name: Mining Investment Law: Environmental & Social Licensing Requirements
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's Mining Investment Law integrates ESG requirements directly into mining licensing. Mining and small-mine licence applicants must assess environmental and social impacts and establish environmental management, rehabilitation and closure plans, making ESG performance a condition of project development rather than a voluntary consideration.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Mining licences require an Environmental and Social Impact Study, Environmental Management Plan and approved rehabilitation and closure arrangements. KPIs: number of permits; environmental/social impact assessments completed; compliance incidents; rehabilitation obligations; environmental capex.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Arabia Mining Investment Law (Ministry of Interior)

drivers.name: Mine Rehabilitation, Closure & Financial Assurance
drivers.logic: Saudi mining regulation requires operators to plan and financially provide for mine rehabilitation and closure, increasing long-term environmental liabilities and making closure costs material to project economics and capital allocation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Exploitation licence holders must provide a financial guarantee for reclamation and closure. The guarantee may only be released following approval and verification of compliance with the reclamation plan. KPIs: closure provision; rehabilitation liability; financial guarantee; hectares disturbed/restored; closure-cost coverage.
drivers.keySources: Mining Investment Law - rehabilitation and closure requirements (Ministry of Interior)

drivers.name: Water Protection & Water-Use Permitting
drivers.logic: Water scarcity makes water management a material ESG and regulatory issue for Saudi mining and mineral processing. Mining operators must protect water resources, while groundwater extraction and industrial water use are subject to licensing and conditions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Mining law requires protection of water resources from hazardous waste and environmental damage. Current groundwater rules specifically apply to mining projects and crushers, requiring conditions such as demonstrating that treated water is unavailable and specifying required daily water quantities. KPIs: m³ water/t ore or metal; groundwater withdrawal; treated/recycled water share; discharge volumes; water permits; water-related compliance incidents.

drivers.name: Environmental Protection, Pollution & Waste Management
drivers.logic: Mining and mineral-processing expansion increases exposure to environmental permitting, hazardous materials, waste, soil and water pollution. Regulatory compliance therefore increasingly affects operating costs, project timelines and environmental liabilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Mining regulations require environmental impact management and engineering/environmental measures for mineral-processing facilities, waste and hazardous materials. KPIs: environmental permits; waste generated; hazardous waste; tailings/waste-management incidents; soil contamination; emissions; environmental penalties.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Mining Investment Law and Executive Regulations (UQN)

drivers.name: Vision 2030 Mining Sector Expansion & ESG Capacity
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's strategy to develop mining as a major economic pillar accelerates exploration and mine development, increasing the importance of managing cumulative environmental and social impacts as the number and scale of projects expand.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, Saudi Arabia had 2,925 valid mining licences, up from 2,401 in 2024. Mining-sector investments reached SAR189.4bn, while the sector contributed SAR138bn to GDP. KPIs: licensed area; environmental permits; disturbed land; rehabilitation area; water use; mining-related employment and local-community impacts.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Press Agency - 2025 industry and mining results

drivers.name: Critical Minerals & Responsible Resource Development
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's expansion into copper, zinc, nickel, rare earths and other strategic minerals increases pressure to demonstrate responsible extraction because these minerals enter international energy-transition and advanced-manufacturing supply chains. ESG performance can therefore affect project attractiveness, downstream market access and international partnerships.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's estimated mineral wealth reached approximately SAR9.4tn in 2025. KPIs: critical-mineral production; exploration licences; environmental footprint/t mineral; water intensity; emissions intensity; responsible-sourcing coverage; rehabilitation performance.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Press Agency - mining sector achievements (Saudi Press Agency)

drivers.name: Local Content & Community Development Requirements
drivers.logic: Saudi mining regulation links project development with local economic and social value. Mining licence applications must demonstrate contributions to nearby communities and support for local content, making social licence and domestic value creation part of mining project requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Mining and small-mine licence applicants must include in feasibility studies the project's contribution to development of local communities and support for local content. KPIs: local procurement %; Saudi workforce %; local supplier spend; community investment; local employment; community grievances.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Mining Investment Law - community and local-content requirements (Ministry of Interior)

drivers.name: Industrial Localisation & Domestic Mineral Processing
drivers.logic: Vision 2030 seeks to capture more value domestically through mineral processing and downstream manufacturing. This creates ESG-relevant investment requirements around energy efficiency, emissions, water use and environmental performance of new processing capacity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Mining-sector investment reached SAR189.4bn in 2025, reflecting the scale of industrial expansion. KPIs: domestic processing capacity; % minerals processed locally; downstream value added; energy intensity; tCO₂e/t product; water intensity; local-content contribution.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Press Agency - industry and mining achievements (Saudi Press Agency)

drivers.name: National Net-Zero 2060 & Industrial Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's national net-zero objective creates a long-term transition context for energy-intensive mining and metals operations. Electricity, fuel use and processing technologies increasingly need to be assessed against future emissions-reduction and energy-transition pathways.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia targets net-zero emissions by 2060. PIF's current green-finance framework also references the national NDC objective of reducing annual CO₂ emissions by 278 Mt by 2030 compared with 2019. KPIs: Scope 1–2 emissions; tCO₂e/t metal; energy intensity; renewable electricity share; decarbonisation capex; emissions avoided.
drivers.keySources: PIF Green Finance Framework (Public Investment Fund)

drivers.name: Environmental Remediation & Contaminated-Site Management
drivers.logic: Legacy environmental impacts and mine-site degradation can create material liabilities for mining companies. Saudi environmental regulation provides specific requirements and licensing mechanisms for remediation and rehabilitation, increasing the importance of managing contaminated land throughout the mine life cycle.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The National Center for Environmental Compliance provides an environmental licensing service for implementation of approved remediation and rehabilitation plans. KPIs: contaminated land area; remediation capex; rehabilitation progress; closure liabilities; environmental incidents; compliance status.
drivers.keySources: Saudi environmental remediation licensing service (My Government)

drivers.name: Sustainable Debt Framework for Mining
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's formal sustainable-debt framework creates a capital-market channel for mining companies to finance projects with positive environmental or social impacts, or to link financing terms to sustainability performance. This is relevant to capital-intensive mining and mineral-processing projects requiring long-term funding.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi CMA approved its Green, Social, Sustainable and Sustainability-Linked Debt Instruments Guidelines on 27 May 2025.
