The framework covers green, social, sustainable and sustainability-linked debt and is intended to encourage local issuance and deepen Saudi Arabia's debt market. The CMA also reported that 94 Saudi listed companies disclosed sustainability practices in 2024, up from 81 in 2023.

drivers.name: Green Financing for Mining Decarbonisation
drivers.logic: Mining and metals production are energy- and resource-intensive, creating financing opportunities for renewable electricity, energy efficiency, water efficiency, waste management and recycling. Saudi sustainable-finance frameworks provide an established basis for financing these types of investments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: PIF's Green Finance Framework identifies renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable water management, waste management and recycling as eligible green categories. PIF's October 2025 green bond raised €1.65bn, with orders exceeding €10bn, making it more than 6× oversubscribed.
drivers.keySources: PIF Green Finance Framework / Green Bond

drivers.name: International ESG Investor Access
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's growing sustainable-debt market can improve access to international institutional capital for mining companies that can demonstrate credible environmental performance and alignment with recognised sustainable-finance frameworks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: PIF's €1.65bn euro-denominated green bond in October 2025 attracted orders exceeding €10bn and was more than six times oversubscribed, with participation from a wide range of global institutional investors.

drivers.name: Sukuk-Based Mining Financing
drivers.logic: Sukuk is a particularly relevant financing channel for Saudi mining because major mine-development, processing and downstream projects require substantial long-term capital and Saudi Arabia has a deep Shariah-compliant financing market.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Ma'aden priced its first international senior unsecured sukuk in February 2025 for US$1.25bn, comprising US$750m five-year and US$500m ten-year tranches. The issue was more than 9.2× oversubscribed, with orders exceeding US$11.5bn.

drivers.name: Mining Investment & Capital Requirements
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's rapid development of mining as a third economic pillar is generating substantial requirements for exploration, mine development, processing and downstream mineral projects, increasing the importance of diversified financing sources.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi mining-sector investment reached SAR189.4bn in 2025. The sector contributed SAR138bn to GDP, while Saudi Arabia's mineral wealth was estimated at approximately SAR9.4tn. The number of valid mining licences increased from 2,401 in 2024 to 2,925 in 2025.

drivers.name: Extreme Heat & Mining Productivity
drivers.logic: Extreme heat is a material physical climate risk for Saudi mining operations, affecting outdoor workers, heavy equipment, mine productivity and energy requirements for cooling and ventilation. The exposure is particularly relevant for open-pit operations and surface infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's World Bank climate-risk data provide country-specific projections for temperature extremes, including thresholds of 35°C, 40°C and 45°C, across future climate periods.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Water Scarcity & Mining Water Security
drivers.logic: Water availability is a structural ESG constraint for Saudi mining because mineral processing and beneficiation require water while the Kingdom operates in an extremely water-stressed environment. Increasing water constraints can raise operating costs and limit production expansion.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia is one of the world's most water-stressed countries and relies heavily on groundwater and desalination for water supply. The World Bank identifies water scarcity and drought as material climate risks for the country.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall & Mine Infrastructure Resilience
drivers.logic: Despite Saudi Arabia's predominantly arid climate, intense rainfall events can generate flash flooding that disrupts mine access, pits, processing facilities, tailings infrastructure, electricity and mineral logistics.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank provides Saudi-specific extreme-precipitation projections for future periods centred on 2025, 2050, 2075 and 2085 and highlights the potential for changes in extreme rainfall intensity.

drivers.name: Coastal Climate Exposure of Mineral Infrastructure
drivers.logic: As mining becomes more integrated with Saudi industrial and export infrastructure, coastal processing, storage, port and logistics assets may face exposure to sea-level rise and coastal flooding along the Red Sea and Arabian Gulf.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi-specific World Bank climate projections include sea-level-change assessments and future climate scenarios. Coastal exposure is relevant to mineral-processing and export infrastructure located within Saudi industrial and port areas.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Climate Change Knowledge Portal

drivers.name: Dust & Sandstorm Disruption
drivers.logic: Dust and sandstorms are particularly relevant to Saudi mining because they can reduce visibility, disrupt exploration and haulage, increase particulate exposure and accelerate wear on mining and processing equipment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's multi-hazard climate profile identifies sand and dust storms among the country's relevant environmental hazards.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Arabia Multi-Hazard Early Warning and Climate

drivers.name: Critical Minerals & Energy-Transition Exposure
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's mining strategy is increasingly focused on minerals needed for clean energy, advanced manufacturing and digital technologies. This creates growth opportunities for transition minerals but also exposes mining companies to changing technology demand, commodity prices and substitution risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's National Minerals Program aims to strengthen the supply of minerals needed for clean energy, digital technologies and other strategic industries, while reducing risks associated with mineral supply chains. Saudi mineral wealth is estimated at SAR9.4tn.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Press Agency – National Minerals Program

drivers.name: Critical Minerals Supply-Chain Development
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia is positioning mining as a strategic supplier for energy-transition and advanced-industrial value chains. Expansion of exploration and production increases the importance of developing reliable domestic supply of strategic minerals such as copper, zinc, gold and other critical minerals.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's mineral wealth is estimated at approximately SAR9.4tn, while mining investment reached SAR189.4bn in 2025. In 2025, Saudi Arabia increased valid mining licences to 2,925, from 2,401 in 2024.

drivers.name: Responsible Mineral Sourcing & Traceability
drivers.logic: As Saudi mining companies increasingly supply international manufacturers and participate in global mineral value chains, customer and investor expectations around traceability, responsible sourcing, human rights and environmental due diligence become increasingly relevant.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The OECD's Responsible Mineral Supply Chains framework covers mineral supply chains from mines to end users and identifies risks including human rights abuses, environmental impacts, corruption and financial crime. Saudi Arabia's growing integration into global mineral value chains increases the relevance of these requirements.

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Metals & Product Carbon Footprinting
drivers.logic: Saudi mining companies supplying international industrial customers may increasingly face requirements for product-level emissions data and lower-carbon materials. This makes carbon intensity and access to lower-carbon energy increasingly relevant to the competitiveness of Saudi metals.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia is seeking to expand its role in global mineral value chains, while international mineral supply chains face increasing demand for emissions transparency. Saudi mining investment reached SAR189.4bn in 2025, increasing the scale of future production potentially exposed to downstream carbon requirements.

drivers.name: Domestic Mineral Processing & Downstream Value Addition
drivers.logic: Saudi Arabia's mining strategy is shifting from extraction toward integrated mineral value chains, creating demand for domestic beneficiation, refining, smelting and downstream manufacturing. This increases ESG exposure to energy use, emissions, water consumption and waste across processing operations.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi policy seeks to position mining as a third pillar of the national economy and increase integration into global value chains. Saudi Arabia's mineral wealth is estimated at SAR9.4tn, while mining contributed SAR138bn to GDP in 2025.

drivers.name: Strategic Mineral Supply-Security & Geopolitical Risk
drivers.logic: Growing global competition for critical minerals and concentration of mineral production in a limited number of countries increase supply-security risks. Saudi Arabia is therefore seeking to secure strategic mineral supplies, reduce supply-chain gaps and strengthen international partnerships.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's National Minerals Program explicitly aims to ensure sustainable mineral raw-material supplies and reduce risks associated with foreign mining investments. The Kingdom has also expanded exploration opportunities for strategic minerals, including copper, zinc, gold and silver.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Press Agency – National Minerals Program / Mining Exploration

drivers.name: Mining Equipment & Technology Localisation
drivers.logic: Rapid expansion of exploration and mining increases demand for specialised equipment, technology and mining services. Localisation can reduce import dependence and supply-chain disruption while supporting Saudi industrial-development and local-content objectives.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia had 2,925 valid mining licences at the end of 2025, including 1,018 exploration licences. In 2025, the Ministry issued 736 new mining licences, demonstrating continued expansion of the mining pipeline.
drivers.keySources: Saudi Press Agency / Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources

drivers.name: Mineral Export & Customer Diversification
drivers.logic: As Saudi Arabia expands mining production and integrates into global mineral value chains, companies become more exposed to commodity-price cycles, customer concentration and changing requirements across international markets. Diversifying end markets and customers can therefore improve resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Saudi Arabia's mining sector contributed SAR138bn to GDP in 2025, with mineral wealth estimated at SAR9.4tn. Government policy explicitly seeks to strengthen the Kingdom's position in global value chains and increase the competitiveness of national exports.

drivers.name: Paris Agreement & Net-Zero Buildings Transition
drivers.logic: The Paris Agreement and global net-zero transition increase pressure on developers, property owners and investors to reduce emissions across the building lifecycle. This increasingly affects development design, energy systems, construction materials, asset values and capital allocation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Operational carbon intensity (kgCO₂e/m²/year); embodied carbon (kgCO₂e/m²); Scope 1–3 emissions; % portfolio aligned with net-zero pathway; renewable-energy share; net-zero-certified floor area.
drivers.keySources: UNEP / GlobalABC — Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2025–2026

drivers.name: IFRS S1 — Sustainability-Related Financial Disclosure
drivers.logic: Material sustainability-related risks and opportunities can affect development costs, rental income, occupancy, insurance, asset values and access to capital. IFRS S1 provides an investor-focused framework for identifying and disclosing such financially material sustainability information.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Material sustainability risks/opportunities; financial effects; assets exposed; sustainability-related capex and opex; governance; metrics and targets.

drivers.name: IFRS S2 — Climate-Related Financial Risk
drivers.logic: Physical and transition climate risks can affect property values, development feasibility, operating costs, insurance and financing. IFRS S2 increases the importance of climate governance, scenario analysis and disclosure of climate-related financial effects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Scope 1–3 emissions; climate scenario analysis; % portfolio exposed to physical risk; transition-risk exposure; expected financial effects; adaptation and transition capex.

drivers.name: GRI Sustainability Reporting
drivers.logic: Developers and property companies face broad environmental and social impacts beyond climate, including energy, water, waste, labour, occupational safety, communities and biodiversity. GRI provides a widely used framework for reporting these impacts.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Energy consumption; GHG emissions; water withdrawal and consumption; waste; occupational injuries; employee indicators; community impacts.

drivers.name: GHG Protocol & Value-Chain Carbon Accounting
drivers.logic: Construction materials, contractor activities, purchased energy and tenant-related emissions can create significant building-related emissions. Standardised carbon accounting is therefore increasingly necessary to identify decarbonisation opportunities and respond to investor and customer requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions; kgCO₂e/m²; embodied-carbon emissions; supplier/material emissions; emissions by development project.

drivers.name: Science-Based Net-Zero Targets for Buildings
drivers.logic: SBTi Buildings Criteria establish sector-specific requirements for companies that own, develop, manage or finance buildings, covering both operational and upfront embodied emissions. This increases pressure on real-estate companies to align building portfolios, new developments and construction materials with science-based decarbonisation pathways.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Buildings account for >1/3 of global energy-related emissions; global floor area is expected to grow ~15% by 2030, with ~80% of growth in developing economies. SBTi requires targets addressing operational and embodied emissions and a commitment to stop new fossil-fuel installations by 2030 at the latest.

drivers.name: Building Operational Energy & Carbon Performance
drivers.logic: Buildings and construction remain a major source of global emissions and energy demand, making operational energy efficiency and decarbonisation a core ESG driver for property portfolios. Inefficient assets face higher operating costs and increasing transition risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Buildings and construction account for approximately 37% of global CO₂ emissions and nearly 50% of global material extraction. Global building energy intensity has fallen 8.5%, but further acceleration is required. KPIs: kWh/m²/year; kgCO₂e/m²/year; renewable-energy share; energy-cost intensity.
drivers.keySources: UNEP Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2025–2026

drivers.name: Embodied Carbon & Whole-Life Carbon
drivers.logic: A significant share of building lifecycle emissions occurs before and during construction through cement, steel, aluminium and other materials. Developers increasingly need to assess whole-life carbon and reduce emissions through material selection, design optimisation and reuse.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Embodied carbon (kgCO₂e/m²); whole-life carbon; % materials covered by environmental product declarations (EPDs); cement/steel/aluminium emissions intensity; % low-carbon or recycled materials. The buildings and construction sector accounts for nearly 50% of global material extraction, highlighting the importance of material efficiency.

drivers.name: Green Building Certifications & Asset Quality
drivers.logic: Green building certifications provide third-party evidence of environmental performance and increasingly support transparency for investors, lenders, tenants and occupiers. They can therefore influence asset attractiveness, development positioning and ESG benchmarking.
drivers.evidenceKpi: % certified floor area; certification level; number of certified assets; energy and water intensity; indoor environmental performance. GRESB explicitly recognises building certifications as an additional layer of transparency and accountability for ESG performance.

drivers.name: GRESB & Investor ESG Benchmarking
drivers.logic: Institutional investors increasingly use standardised ESG benchmarking to compare real-estate portfolios. GRESB makes environmental performance, resilience and management systems increasingly visible in investor engagement and capital allocation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: GRESB Score; GRESB Rating; peer percentile; energy/GHG/water/waste intensity; data coverage; green-building certification coverage. In 2025, 1,002 fund managers submitted 2,382 assessments to the GRESB Real Estate Assessment.

drivers.name: Net-Zero Target Implementation & Portfolio Transition
drivers.logic: Real-estate companies increasingly need to move from net-zero commitments toward asset-level implementation through retrofits, clean electricity, electrification and low-carbon development. The transition creates both capital requirements and competitive differentiation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: % portfolio with net-zero policy; % portfolio covered by targets; emissions reductions; transition capex; assets on/off pathway. In 2025, 81.5% of GRESB real-estate entities had net-zero policies and 66.4% had net-zero targets.

drivers.name: CRREM & Carbon-Stranding Risk
drivers.logic: Assets whose energy or carbon performance exceeds decarbonisation pathways may require significant retrofits or face increasing transition risk. This can affect future capital expenditure and potentially asset competitiveness and valuation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: % portfolio above CRREM pathway; projected misalignment year; kgCO₂e/m²/year vs pathway; kWh/m²/year vs pathway; retrofit capex; floor area at risk. CRREM provides 1,000+ pathways covering 40+ countries and major property types.

drivers.name: Physical Climate Resilience
drivers.logic: Heat, flooding, drought, storms, sea-level rise and other climate hazards can damage buildings, disrupt construction and increase cooling, maintenance, insurance and adaptation costs. Climate resilience is therefore increasingly material to site selection, design and portfolio management.
drivers.evidenceKpi: % assets exposed to physical hazards; expected annual loss; climate-related downtime; insurance cost; flood/heat exposure; adaptation capex; resilience investment.
drivers.keySources: IPCC AR6 Working Group II — Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability

drivers.name: Water Efficiency & Water Resilience
drivers.logic: Water stress can increase operating costs and constrain building operations and development. Water-efficient design, reuse and alternative water sources are increasingly important, particularly in water-stressed markets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Water consumption (m³/m²/year); potable-water intensity; recycled/reused water %; water-stressed assets %; water cost; leakage rates.

drivers.name: Circular Construction & Construction Waste
drivers.logic: Construction, renovation and demolition require large volumes of materials and generate substantial waste. Circular design and material recovery can reduce environmental impacts, resource costs and waste liabilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Construction and demolition waste (kg/m²); waste diversion rate; reuse/recycling %; recycled material content; material recovery rate; design-for-disassembly coverage.

drivers.name: Biodiversity & Nature-Related Development Risk
drivers.logic: Real-estate development can affect ecosystems, land and water resources. Developers increasingly need to identify biodiversity-sensitive sites and manage impacts through avoidance, mitigation, restoration and nature-positive design.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Hectares developed/restored; developments near biodiversity-sensitive areas; biodiversity impact assessments; green/open space; nature-related dependencies and impacts.

drivers.name: Sustainable Finance & Green Building Investment
drivers.logic: Decarbonisation, deep renovation and climate resilience require significant capital. Green loans, green bonds and sustainability-linked financing increasingly create incentives for projects that can demonstrate measurable environmental performance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Green/sustainable financing volume; green-building capex; retrofit investment; financing margin differential; tCO₂e avoided per US$ invested; energy savings. UNEP estimates that annual investment in building energy efficiency needs to reach US$5.9 trillion by 2030, more than double current levels.
drivers.keySources: UNEP Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2025–2026

drivers.name: Green Building Market Demand & Asset Competitiveness
drivers.logic: Tenants, investors, occupiers and buyers increasingly assess energy performance, environmental quality and building certifications. Strong ESG performance can therefore influence occupancy, operating costs and the competitive positioning of developments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Green-certified floor area; occupancy rate; tenant retention; rental premium; operating cost/m²; energy intensity; tenant demand for certified space. GRESB's real-estate framework specifically evaluates efficiency, resilience and environmental performance against peers.

drivers.name: Sustainability Disclosure and Cost of Capital
drivers.logic: Comprehensive, comparable and reliable sustainability disclosure can reduce a company’s cost of capital.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Empirical research from the University of Oxford found that ‘90% of the studies on the cost of capital show that sound sustainability standards lower the cost of capital for companies.
drivers.keySources: University of Oxford and Arabesque Partners, ‘From the Stockholder to the Stakeholder: How Sustainability Can Drive Financial Outperformance,’ March 2015.

drivers.name: Sustainability Information and Earnings Stability
drivers.logic: Sustainability information can be a strong signal of share price volatility.
drivers.evidenceKpi:
Based on historical data, Bank of America Global Research found that companies in the top quintile of sustainability performance experienced the lowest volatility in earnings per share (EPS) in a subsequent five-year period. By contrast, ‘companies with the worst environmental, social and governance records averaged 92% volatility.

The researchers also found that sustainability information was the only reliable signal for predicting EPS volatility, providing better insight than traditional measures such as return on equity.
drivers.keySources: Bank of America, ‘Equity Strategy Focus Point,’ 18 December 2016.

drivers.name: Sustainable Bond Market Development
drivers.logic: The continued growth of sustainable bond markets increases demand for ESG strategies, sustainability frameworks, transparent disclosures, and impact reporting. Companies issuing sustainable bonds are expected to align with internationally recognized market principles and demonstrate the environmental and/or social use of proceeds or sustainability performance commitments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 2026: Total sustainable bond issuance reached USD 357.6 billion. Green bonds remained the largest segment, with USD 229.2 billion issued (64.08% of total issuance), followed by Sustainability bonds with USD 60.3 billion (16.88% of total issuance).

drivers.name: Energy Efficiency Requirements for Buildings
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's energy-efficiency legislation establishes mandatory requirements for energy saving and energy efficiency in buildings, directly affecting the design and construction of new, reconstructed and renovated buildings.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Mandatory energy-efficiency requirements apply to buildings; energy-efficiency performance is assessed against normative values for heating and ventilation. Compliance is reflected through the building's energy-efficiency documentation and classification.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Law on Energy Saving and Energy Efficiency (Adilet)

drivers.name: Building Energy Performance Classes
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan has a formal A–G building energy-efficiency classification, creating a measurable regulatory benchmark for building performance. This allows developers and owners to compare actual/calculated building performance against a national standard.
drivers.evidenceKpi: A–G scale based on deviation from normative heating/ventilation energy performance: A <−51%, B −16% to −50%, C −6% to −15%, D −5% to +5%, E +6% to +15%, F +16% to +50%, G >+51%. Energy-efficiency class information for new buildings is valid for 5 years after commissioning; for existing buildings it is determined through energy audit and is also valid for 5 years.
drivers.keySources: Adilet – Rules for Determining Energy-Efficiency Classes (Adilet)

drivers.name: Post-Project Energy Performance Verification
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan has strengthened the link between design-stage energy performance and actual building performance through post-project analysis. This creates a risk for developers if completed assets fail to achieve their designed energy-efficiency performance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Post-project analysis of actual energy performance vs required energy-efficiency class; actual vs calculated heating/ventilation performance; compliance outcome. The requirement was introduced into the energy-efficiency framework and applies to qualifying buildings/structures/installations.
drivers.keySources: Adilet – Energy Saving and Energy Efficiency Law

drivers.name: Green Building / Green Project Taxonomy
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's Green Taxonomy creates a national framework for classifying projects eligible for green financing, including energy-efficient and green buildings. This links real-estate development directly to Kazakhstan's sustainable-finance framework.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Eligible project categories include green buildings and energy-efficient construction/modernisation. KPIs should include certified/eligible building area (m²), energy savings, water savings and certification level. Recognised green-building standards include LEED, BREEAM, EDGE, DGNB and OMIR.

drivers.name: Green Building Certification / Sustainable Construction
drivers.logic: Green-building certification is increasingly relevant to Kazakhstan developers because the national taxonomy provides a formal basis for recognising green buildings and linking them to sustainable finance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: LEED / BREEAM / EDGE / DGNB / OMIR certification; certified building area, m²; energy and water performance; percentage of project meeting green-building criteria.

drivers.name: Kazakhstan NDC 3.0 – 2035 GHG Reduction
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's latest NDC materially increases the national decarbonisation requirement during the period in which today's buildings will be designed, constructed and operated. Importantly for real estate, NDC 3.0 explicitly identifies buildings as a sector achieving greater mitigation through electrification and stronger energy-efficiency policies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 17% reduction in economy-wide net GHG emissions vs 1990 by 2035 unconditionally; up to 25% conditional on international support. Under the conditional pathway, net emissions reach approximately 287.9 MtCO₂e in 2035, ~32% below BAU. The NDC states that buildings, transport and industry achieve greater mitigation through electrification and stronger energy-efficiency policies.

drivers.name: Carbon Neutrality by 2060
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's legally adopted long-term carbon-neutrality strategy creates a transition driver for real estate because buildings are long-lived assets and can lock in energy consumption and emissions for decades.
drivers.evidenceKpi: National carbon-neutrality target: 2060. The strategy includes a 2030 interim target of −15% GHG emissions vs 1990 and identifies sectoral decarbonisation pathways. For real estate: kgCO₂e/m², operational energy intensity, renewable-energy share and embodied carbon are appropriate exposure indicators.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Strategy for Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060

drivers.name: Renewable Energy Expansion
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's rapid expansion of renewable electricity increases the feasibility of reducing buildings' electricity-related Scope 2 emissions through renewable electricity procurement, onsite generation and electrification of building systems.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, renewable sources generated 8.621 TWh, equal to 7% of Kazakhstan's total electricity generation. Kazakhstan had 162 renewable-energy facilities with 3.5 GW installed capacity; 9 new projects totalling 503.5 MW were commissioned in 2025.

drivers.name: Housing Construction Expansion
drivers.logic: Rapid growth in Kazakhstan's housing stock increases the scale of buildings exposed to future energy-efficiency, climate and environmental requirements. The predominantly private-developer-led construction pipeline makes this particularly relevant to real-estate developers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 20.099 million m² of housing commissioned in 2025, +5.1% YoY. 13.524m m² was multi-apartment housing. 90% / 18.099m m² of total housing was commissioned by private developers. 2,591 multi-apartment residential buildings / 185,800 apartments were commissioned. Construction work increased 15.9% to KZT 10.705tn.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Bureau of National Statistics – Housing 2025 (Kazakhstan Statistics Committee)

drivers.name: Environmental Impact Assessment for Development Projects
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's Environmental Code requires environmental assessment for projects falling within the applicable categories. For qualifying development projects, this creates requirements to identify, assess and mitigate environmental impacts before implementation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: EIA/screening status; environmental impact category; predicted emissions/discharges; waste; water use; biodiversity/land impacts; mitigation measures. The Environmental Code provides the legal framework for environmental assessment and post-project analysis.

drivers.name: Environmental Permitting and Compliance
drivers.logic: Development projects with relevant environmental impacts may be subject to environmental permitting and operating conditions, creating compliance exposure throughout construction and operation.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Environmental category; permit status; permitted emissions/discharges; environmental incidents; exceedances; regulatory non-compliance.

drivers.name: Inclusive / Accessible Built Environment
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's 2026 Construction Code strengthens the social dimension of development by embedding requirements for a safe, comfortable and accessible built environment, including accessibility for persons with reduced mobility.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Accessibility compliance; accessible entrances/routes/facilities; number of accessibility non-compliances; % of relevant buildings meeting accessibility requirements.

drivers.name: Growing Sustainable Finance Market
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's sustainable-finance market is becoming an established source of capital for companies and projects meeting green, social or sustainability criteria. This expands the financing options available to developers with eligible projects and strengthens investor expectations around ESG performance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Since the launch of Kazakhstan's sustainable-finance market, USD 2.5bn of sustainable bonds and loans had been issued/provided by end-2025. The AIFC Green Finance Centre reports that it supported approximately 70% of green bonds and green loans issued in Kazakhstan.

drivers.name: Green Bond Financing
drivers.logic: Green bonds provide developers and infrastructure companies with access to debt capital for eligible green projects, including energy-efficient buildings and other projects recognised under Kazakhstan's green-finance framework. Issuers must define eligible use of proceeds and obtain independent assessment under the applicable framework.
drivers.evidenceKpi: As of June 2026, KASE had 19 green bonds and 49 sustainable-finance instruments listed; total registered sustainable-finance issues reached KZT 1.8tn, with financing raised exceeding KZT 1.3tn.

drivers.name: Green Building Financing
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's Green Taxonomy provides a framework for financing green buildings and energy-efficient construction/modernisation. Developers that can demonstrate eligibility can therefore access a dedicated pool of sustainable capital rather than relying exclusively on conventional financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Eligible green-building projects; green-certified m²; energy savings; water savings; eligible project capex. Recognised certification systems include LEED, BREEAM, EDGE, DGNB and OMIR.

drivers.name: Real-Estate / Housing Sector Access to Bond Markets
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's housing sector already demonstrates substantial use of domestic bond markets, showing that capital-market financing is material to the sector. This creates an established financing channel that can increasingly incorporate ESG characteristics.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan Housing Company raised KZT 180bn through three bond issues in 2024, with maturities of 6–12 years and yields of 4.05–8.79%. In 2026, additional KHC bond programmes included KZT 50bn issues.
drivers.keySources:
KASE – Kazakhstan Housing Company (KASE); 
KASE – KHC 2026 (KASE)

drivers.name: ESG / Sustainable Bond Investor Demand
drivers.logic: The increasing integration of ESG bonds into Kazakhstan's exchange infrastructure creates a stronger incentive for issuers to demonstrate credible environmental and social performance. ESG-labelled financing requires defined use of proceeds, an appropriate framework and independent assessment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: From 1 September 2026, KASE's representative ESG bond index list contains 25 bonds. KASE's sustainable-finance universe includes green, social and sustainability bonds.

drivers.name: Green Finance External Verification
drivers.logic: Independent verification is becoming an important part of accessing Kazakhstan's sustainable-finance market. For developers, credible ESG data, building certification and impact reporting therefore become increasingly important for obtaining labelled financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: AIFC Green Finance Centre had completed 45 external reviews since 2020 by June 2025, including SPOs and verification reports; its supported sustainable-finance casebook represented >USD 650m across 18 projects.

drivers.name: Housing Investment / Construction Pipeline
drivers.logic: The scale of Kazakhstan's construction pipeline creates significant demand for real-estate capital. The large private-developer component makes access to financing particularly relevant to developers and investors.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 20.1m m² of housing commissioned in 2025, +5.1% YoY; 90% / 18.1m m² was delivered by private developers. Construction activity reached KZT 10.7tn, +15.9% YoY.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Bureau of National Statistics – 2025 Housing (Kazakhstan Statistics Committee)

drivers.name: ESG-Linked Cost / Financing Differentiation
drivers.logic: Sustainable-finance instruments can create differentiated financing opportunities for projects with credible environmental or social characteristics. However, I would frame this as a potential financing advantage, not claim a Kazakhstan-wide greenium unless transaction-level evidence exists.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Green vs conventional coupon/yield; financing spread; tenor; investor demand; oversubscription; external-review cost; eligible green capex.

drivers.name: Flood Risk
drivers.logic: Flooding is a material physical risk for Kazakhstan's residential, commercial and infrastructure assets. The scale of the 2024 event demonstrates that flood exposure can translate directly into property damage, reconstruction costs, displacement and public infrastructure expenditure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In the 2024 floods, commissions inspected 19,359 homes and cottages in affected regions. 5,767 residential homes were purchased, 9,156 houses were fully repaired, and 2,680 new private houses were constructed. KZT 54.7bn was allocated for housing assistance and repairs, while construction of replacement houses cost KZT 64bn.

drivers.name: Physical Climate Risk and Asset Valuation
drivers.logic: Increasing physical climate risks can affect property values through higher expected damage, insurance costs, operating costs, downtime and required adaptation capex. For listed developers, REIT-like portfolios and real-estate investment vehicles, climate exposure can therefore become a valuation and financing consideration.
drivers.evidenceKpi: % asset value exposed to high/medium physical climate risk; expected annual loss; insurance premiums/claims; adaptation capex; occupancy/downtime; property value at risk. Kazakhstan's 2024 floods provide direct evidence of material property damage and reconstruction costs.
drivers.keySources: World Bank Climate Risk Country Profile; Kazakhstan Government flood-recovery data

drivers.name: Extreme Heat / Rising Cooling Demand
drivers.logic: Increasing heat exposure can reduce thermal comfort, increase cooling-energy demand and stress electricity infrastructure. For developers, this increases the importance of passive design, shading, insulation, efficient cooling and heat-resilient materials.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank climate-risk analysis identifies increasing heat risk in Kazakhstan and shows that heat risk can expand geographically and intensify later in the century, particularly under higher-emissions scenarios. Relevant building KPIs: cooling degree days; days >35°C; peak temperature; cooling kWh/m²; peak cooling load.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Kazakhstan Compounded Heat Risks (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Extreme Temperature / Thermal Comfort
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's continental climate creates exposure to both high summer temperatures and severe winter conditions. Climate change can increase summer heat exposure while increasing variability and creating challenges for building thermal performance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Historical Kazakhstan climate profile identifies an average July maximum temperature of ~30°C and projects a significant increase in heatwave likelihood under higher-emissions pathways. Cooling/heating degree days; peak temperature; overheating days; indoor temperature exceedance should be tracked at asset level.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Kazakhstan Climate Risk Profile (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Water Scarcity / Water Stress
drivers.logic: Water availability is a growing physical climate risk for Kazakhstan and Central Asia. Water-intensive residential and mixed-use developments may face higher water costs, restrictions and infrastructure constraints, while landscaping and cooling requirements can increase exposure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank estimates that surface-water availability in parts of Europe and Central Asia could decline by up to 50% by 2050, while water demand could increase by up to 51%. Central Asia is identified as one of the world's most vulnerable regions to future water stress.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Water Security in Europe & Central Asia (World Bank)

drivers.name: Water Availability in Southern Kazakhstan
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's water risk is geographically differentiated. Southern Kazakhstan is particularly relevant because much of the region's water availability depends on transboundary river systems and competition for water is increasing across Central Asia. This can affect residential development, municipal infrastructure and asset operating costs.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank notes that most river runoff in Central Asia originates in the Kyrgyz and Tajik highlands, while substantial withdrawals occur in the irrigated plains of southern Kazakhstan and neighbouring countries.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Central Asia Water & Energy Program (World Bank)

drivers.name: Drought Risk
drivers.logic: Drought can increase water stress, affect landscaping and urban water availability and indirectly increase operating costs and infrastructure pressure. It is particularly relevant for large residential developments, mixed-use projects and water-intensive facilities.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank's Kazakhstan climate-risk profile identifies drought as a significant natural hazard, with Kazakhstan's drought hazard score of 5.0/10 versus 3.2 global average in the cited INFORM risk assessment.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Kazakhstan Climate Risk Profile (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Severe Winter / Heating Demand
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's cold continental climate makes heating a major determinant of building energy consumption and operating costs. Poor building envelopes and inefficient heating systems increase both energy-cost exposure and transition risk as Kazakhstan tightens energy-efficiency requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's building-energy framework assesses heating performance against normative consumption. Asset KPIs: heating kWh/m²/year; heating degree days; envelope U-values; peak heating demand; heating-system efficiency.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Building Green: Kazakhstan (World Bank)

drivers.name: Compound Climate Hazard Exposure
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's physical-risk profile is multi-hazard: floods, drought, heat and other natural hazards can affect the same asset portfolio. Developers therefore need location-specific climate-risk assessments rather than assessing hazards independently.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank identifies floods, drought, avalanches and landslides among Kazakhstan's key climate-related natural hazards. Asset-level KPIs: % assets exposed to high-risk zones; expected annual loss; hazard score; insured value; adaptation capex.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Kazakhstan Climate Risk Profile (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Climate-Resilient Building / Infrastructure Investment
drivers.logic: Increasing physical hazards create a need to incorporate climate resilience into site selection, design, construction and asset management. For developers, this can increase upfront capex but reduce expected damage, downtime and repair costs.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Adaptation capex; % assets with physical climate-risk assessment; % assets in high-risk zones; expected annual loss; insurance claims; business interruption days; resilience measures implemented.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Kazakhstan Climate Risk Resources (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Construction Material Supply Dependence
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan has a large domestic construction-material base, but developers remain exposed to imported materials and cross-border supply disruptions. This creates procurement, cost and delivery risks, particularly for materials where domestic production does not fully satisfy demand.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, domestic production accounted for 71.3% of Kazakhstan's construction-material market, leaving approximately 28.7% supplied by imports. For Jan–Jul 2025, construction-material imports reached USD 669.4m / 2.21m tonnes, with Russia 42.1%, China 30.3% and Uzbekistan 8.9% of imports by country.

drivers.name: Imported Material / Geographical Concentration Risk
drivers.logic: Dependence on a limited number of supplier countries exposes developers to trade restrictions, logistics disruptions, currency volatility and geopolitical shocks. This is particularly relevant where projects have fixed completion schedules and limited material substitution options.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 42.1% of construction-material imports came from Russia, 30.3% from China and 8.9% from Uzbekistan in Jan–Jul 2025 — together 81.3% of imports. Import volumes increased 21.6% YoY to 2.21m tonnes despite relatively stable import value.

drivers.name: Critical Material Availability – Thermal Insulation
drivers.logic: Domestic supply capacity is uneven across construction-material categories. Shortfalls in locally produced materials can increase developers' exposure to imports, lead times and foreign-exchange movements. Thermal insulation is particularly relevant because it is directly linked to building energy performance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2023, Kazakhstan produced only 91,000 tonnes of thermal-insulation materials against domestic demand of 154,000 tonnes, covering approximately 59% of demand and leaving a 41% supply gap.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Ministry of Industry and Construction (gov.kz)

drivers.name: Construction Material Production Scale / Procurement Exposure
drivers.logic: The scale of Kazakhstan's construction-material industry makes material procurement a material part of developers' cost and supply-chain exposure. Rapid growth in construction-material production also indicates increasing demand from the domestic construction pipeline.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan produced KZT 1,734.6bn of construction materials in 2025, +29.8% YoY. Portland cement production increased 17.2% to 14.378m tonnes; cement/concrete/stone tiles and slabs increased 16.1% to 6.978m tonnes; concrete construction products increased 14.7% to 10.091m tonnes.

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Construction Materials
drivers.logic: Developers face increasing pressure to reduce the embodied environmental footprint of buildings. Kazakhstan's Green Taxonomy explicitly recognises low-energy and low-carbon construction materials, including materials produced from recycled inputs, creating a Kazakhstan-specific basis for incorporating embodied-carbon criteria into procurement.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Green Taxonomy recognises low-energy / low-carbon materials, materials using recycled materials and waste, and allows certification/verification through EPDs or material-specific schemes such as Concrete Sustainability Council (CSC) certification.

drivers.name: Construction Material Environmental Certification / EPDs
drivers.logic: Environmental information on construction materials is increasingly relevant to green-building eligibility and investor requirements. Developers can therefore face demand for independently verified environmental performance information from material suppliers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: % key materials with EPDs; % suppliers with verified environmental data; kgCO₂e/material unit; % low-carbon materials. Kazakhstan's Green Taxonomy explicitly references verified EPDs under ST RK STB ISO 14025-2006 and certification schemes for cement, concrete, ceramics and steel.

drivers.name: Construction & Demolition Waste
drivers.logic: Large construction volumes create significant material-waste exposure. Kazakhstan's Environmental Code establishes specific restrictions on disposal of construction waste, increasing the importance of segregation, recovery and authorised waste management within development projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Kazakhstan's Environmental Code prohibits disposal of construction waste at landfills covered by the prohibited-waste provisions. Relevant KPIs: kg construction waste/m²; % reused/recycled; tonnes diverted from landfill; waste by material type.

drivers.name: Construction Waste Traceability / Digital Monitoring
drivers.logic: Construction waste management is becoming more traceable at the local level. This increases the need for developers and contractors to document waste generation, transportation and final destination rather than treating waste disposal as an informal contractor activity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In Astana, 414 illegal construction-waste dumps were identified in 2024. Since 13 May 2025, new municipal construction-waste management rules have applied; the Smart Waste system had recorded >1,000 waste-transport trips and >14,500 tonnes of construction waste transported under the system.
drivers.keySources: Government of Astana – Construction Waste Management (Government of Kazakhstan)

drivers.name: Circular Construction Materials / Recycled Content
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan's Green Taxonomy supports the use of secondary raw materials and recycling infrastructure, creating an opportunity to reduce virgin-material demand and construction waste through circular procurement.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The Green Taxonomy sets a minimum 30% secondary raw-material content for eligible production under the relevant circular-material category and recognises recycling/reuse of construction and demolition materials.

drivers.name: Supplier Environmental Compliance
drivers.logic: Environmental impacts from construction-material suppliers can become a developer's indirect environmental exposure through emissions, waste, water use and regulatory non-compliance. Supplier screening therefore becomes increasingly relevant for large projects and green-financed developments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: % critical suppliers screened; % suppliers with environmental permits/certification; supplier environmental incidents; % suppliers with environmental-management systems; corrective actions.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Environmental Code; Kazakhstan Green Taxonomy

drivers.name: Supply-Chain GHG / Embodied Carbon Data
drivers.logic: Cement, steel, aluminium, glass and other materials can represent a significant portion of a building's embodied carbon. Developers seeking green certification, credible Scope 3 inventories or low-carbon development strategies increasingly need supplier-level emissions data.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Scope 3 Category 1 emissions; kgCO₂e/m²; kgCO₂e/tonne of material; % procurement spend/material volume covered by supplier-specific emission factors; % key suppliers providing verified emissions data.
drivers.keySources: GHG Protocol – Scope 3; Kazakhstan Green Taxonomy

drivers.name: Construction Material Import Restrictions / Regulatory Supply Risk
drivers.logic: Kazakhstan has begun using trade-policy measures affecting construction-material imports, demonstrating that developers can face regulatory changes affecting the availability of imported materials.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In May 2026, Kazakhstan introduced a six-month ban on imports from third countries for specified construction materials, covering products including certain cement, concrete, stone, insulation and glass categories.
drivers.keySources: Kazakhstan Government – Import Regulation, 2026 (Government of Kazakhstan)

drivers.name: Building Energy-Efficiency Classification
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan has introduced a formal energy-efficiency classification system for buildings, making energy performance a measurable characteristic of the building stock and increasing the relevance of energy-efficient design and renovation for developers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: From 1 November 2024, buildings and structures with a useful area >200 m² are assigned energy-efficiency categories A–G, with A representing highest and G lowest efficiency. An electronic registry of energy passports and energy-audit reports was also planned.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Energy Efficiency Agency (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Energy Efficiency of the Building Stock
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's buildings are a major source of final energy demand, making building efficiency material to national energy security and creating increasing pressure for developers and owners to reduce energy consumption.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Buildings account for almost 50% of Uzbekistan's final energy consumption. The government has set a target to reduce economy-wide energy consumption by at least 20% by 2030, with a 15% reduction target for state entities and social organisations.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan – Energy Efficiency (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: High Energy Intensity of Existing Buildings
drivers.logic: A large share of Uzbekistan's building stock was constructed before modern energy-efficiency standards, creating a substantial retrofit opportunity and increasing the operating-cost and transition-risk exposure of inefficient assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Most buildings were constructed in the 1960s–1970s. Government data indicate that average annual thermal-energy consumption of public kindergartens, schools and hospitals is approximately 350 kWh/m², around 2.4× the European average, 3× Austria and 3.7× the Netherlands.
drivers.keySources: National Energy Efficiency Agency – 2025 (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Green Building Certification Framework
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan is developing a dedicated green-building policy and certification framework, creating a pathway for developers to differentiate energy- and resource-efficient projects and potentially access future incentives and green finance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In February 2026, the National Agency for Energy Efficiency and IFC agreed to develop a Green Buildings programme including a green-building certification system, financial/non-financial incentives and supporting regulatory procedures.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan / Energy Efficiency Agency & IFC (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Green Building Incentives / Green Mahallas
drivers.logic: Government policy is moving beyond energy efficiency toward integrated sustainable neighbourhoods, including resource efficiency and environmentally sustainable residential environments. This creates an emerging policy driver for developers of large residential and mixed-use projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The 2026 IFC-government programme includes development of Green Mahallas, with measures targeting energy efficiency, rational resource use and environmental sustainability.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan / IFC (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: NDC 3.0 – GHG Intensity Reduction
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's latest NDC materially increases the national decarbonisation trajectory during the operating life of buildings being developed today. Although the NDC is not itself a building-level compliance requirement, it creates policy pressure for lower-energy buildings and more efficient urban infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan commits to a 50% reduction in specific GHG emissions per unit of GDP by 2035 from 2010 levels. The NDC explicitly frames this as a national mitigation commitment for the period to 2035.

drivers.name: Carbon Neutrality by 2060
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's long-term transition toward carbon neutrality increases the relevance of energy-efficient, electrified and climate-resilient buildings because buildings constructed today may operate for several decades.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's climate strategy targets carbon neutrality by 2060. The World Bank estimates that the energy sector accounts for approximately 75% of national GHG emissions, making energy efficiency and electrification particularly important to the transition.

drivers.name: Public-Building Energy-Efficiency Retrofit
drivers.logic: The large identified energy-saving potential in public buildings demonstrates the scale of Uzbekistan's building-efficiency challenge and supports demand for retrofit technologies, efficient heating/cooling, insulation and energy-management solutions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank analysis identified >7,000 GWh/year potential energy savings across pre-schools, schools and healthcare facilities: approximately 6,810 GWh thermal + >240 GWh electricity. Heating represents approximately 70% of energy use in regional hospitals, 84% in pre-schools, 88% in rural clinics and 97% in public schools.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Uzbekistan Public Building Energy Efficiency (World Bank)

drivers.name: Energy-Efficiency Investment / Retrofit Subsidies
drivers.logic: Government financial support for energy efficiency increases the economic feasibility of retrofit projects and creates an expanding market for energy-saving technologies in residential and public buildings.
drivers.evidenceKpi: For 2026, the government reported UZS 150bn in subsidies and compensation for energy-efficiency improvements. More than 30,000 social facilities were identified as requiring energy-efficiency attention.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan – Energy Efficiency (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Green City / Sustainable Urban Development Requirements
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan is increasingly integrating climate resilience, water efficiency, waste management and green infrastructure into urban-development policy. This is particularly relevant to large master-planned residential and mixed-use developments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: A special environmental and urban-planning regime is planned for Samarkand, under which green-building requirements for new and reconstructed facilities include energy- and water-saving technologies, waste sorting/recycling and resource efficiency, with non-compliant facilities not eligible for commissioning.
drivers.keySources: Government of Uzbekistan – Green City / Samarkand (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Green Housing Financing
drivers.logic: Green-building performance is increasingly linked to access to housing finance, creating a direct incentive for developers to integrate energy- and resource-efficiency measures.
drivers.evidenceKpi: From 1 May 2025, financing mechanisms were introduced for multi-apartment housing constructed according to green standards. KPI: green-eligible projects; green financing volume; financing rate/spread.

drivers.name: Green Mortgage / Retrofit Market
drivers.logic: Green mortgages create demand for energy-efficient housing and financing for improvements to existing residential assets.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, UZS 111.6bn of mortgage loans were directed to green renovations. The Uzbekistan Mortgage Refinancing Company allocated UZS 2.2tn in total loans to nearly 9,000 citizens.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Ministry of Economy & Finance (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Green Building Certification & Incentives
drivers.logic: Development of a national green-building certification and incentive framework increases the potential for green buildings to become a distinct financing and investment segment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In February 2026, Uzbekistan's National Energy Efficiency Agency and IFC agreed to develop a green-building certification system, financial/non-financial incentives and concessional-financing mechanisms.
drivers.keySources: National Energy Efficiency Agency / IFC (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Climate-Linked Development Finance
drivers.logic: International development-finance institutions are providing capital to Uzbekistan's housing-finance system, supporting the expansion of sustainable housing finance.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, Uzbekistan Mortgage Refinancing Company raised USD 63m: USD 30m ADB, USD 20m IFC and USD 13m EBRD; additionally UZS 600bn was raised from the domestic capital market.
drivers.keySources: Uzbekistan Ministry of Economy & Finance (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Housing Market & Mortgage Growth
drivers.logic: Rapid expansion of housing transactions, construction and mortgage lending increases the addressable market for energy-efficient and climate-resilient real estate.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025: 319.5k real-estate transactions (+15.8%); UZS 21.2tn mortgage lending (+29%); 15.9m m² housing commissioned (+7.2%).

drivers.name: Sustainable Housing Development Pipeline
drivers.logic: Government housing policy is explicitly incorporating environmentally friendly products and energy-saving technologies into future residential development, increasing demand for green construction solutions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: By 2040, annual housing construction is targeted at 421,000 units, the mortgage portfolio at USD 56.7bn, and modern housing at 50% of the housing stock. New residential infrastructure is to use environmentally friendly products and energy-saving technologies.
drivers.keySources: President of Uzbekistan – Housing & Mortgage Development (President of Uzbekistan)

drivers.name: Energy Performance & Asset Operating Costs
drivers.logic: High building energy consumption makes energy performance financially material through utility costs, tenant affordability and asset competitiveness.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Buildings account for almost 50% of final energy consumption in Uzbekistan. KPI: kWh/m²; energy OPEX/m²; energy savings; occupancy; retrofit payback.

drivers.name: Climate Risk & Asset Investment Decisions
drivers.logic: Increasing physical climate risks can affect operating costs, insurance, adaptation capex and asset values, increasing the relevance of climate-risk assessment in real-estate investment and lending.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank projects 30–40% declines in water availability in some catchments by 2050 and annual water shortages potentially reaching 15bn m³ by 2050. KPI: asset value exposed; expected annual loss; adaptation capex; insurance cost.

drivers.name: Extreme Heat / Building Overheating
drivers.logic: Rising temperatures increase cooling demand, reduce thermal comfort and can increase peak electricity loads. For real estate, this creates higher operating costs and requires better insulation, shading, ventilation and efficient cooling systems.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank identifies extreme heat as a major climate risk for Uzbekistan and notes that heat stress already affects labour productivity. By 2030, at least 8 million people are expected to live in areas of very high climate risk. Asset KPIs: cooling degree days, days >35°C, peak cooling load, cooling kWh/m², overheating hours.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Uzbekistan CCDR (World Bank); World Bank – Heat Risk (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Heat Stress / Labour Productivity
drivers.logic: Extreme heat can affect construction-worker productivity and health during project delivery, while increasing cooling requirements during asset operation. This creates both construction-phase and operational exposure for developers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank estimates that by 2040, heat stress could produce a 0.07–0.13% labour-force shock, with potential job losses of 2–3.5% during 2041–2050.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Climate Co-Benefits Analysis (World Bank)

drivers.name: Water Scarcity / Reduced Water Availability
drivers.logic: Water scarcity is one of Uzbekistan's most material physical climate risks. Water availability affects urban development, municipal services, landscaping, cooling and operating costs, particularly for large residential and mixed-use projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank estimates that in some catchments water availability could decline by 30–40% by 2050, while irrigation-water demand could increase by 25%. Annual water shortage could rise to 7bn m³ by 2030 and 15bn m³ by 2050.

drivers.name: Drought Risk
drivers.logic: More frequent/severe drought can increase water scarcity, affect municipal water availability and raise adaptation and operating costs for developments, particularly in already water-stressed regions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank identifies drought as a major climate vulnerability alongside water scarcity, heat and rainfall volatility. Relevant KPIs: drought severity/frequency; water availability; water consumption m³/m²; water cost; % assets exposed to drought risk.

drivers.name: Flooding / Extreme Rainfall
drivers.logic: Climate-driven rainfall volatility and extreme precipitation can damage buildings, roads, drainage and utilities and increase downtime and repair costs. Urban expansion can increase exposure where drainage and infrastructure capacity are inadequate.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank identifies rainfall volatility and flooding among Uzbekistan's major climate risks. The current World Bank climate portal provides extreme-precipitation projections at country/subnational level. Asset KPIs: % assets in flood zones; precipitation intensity; drainage capacity; expected annual loss; flood-related downtime/claims.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Uzbekistan CCDR (World Bank); World Bank Climate Knowledge Portal (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Dust Storms / Air Quality
drivers.logic: Uzbekistan's exposure to dust storms, including impacts associated with the Aral Sea region, can reduce outdoor air quality and increase filtration, ventilation and maintenance requirements for buildings. It also creates health and occupant-comfort risks.
drivers.evidenceKpi: The World Bank identifies dust storms as a significant climate/environmental vulnerability. Uzbekistan's CCDR notes that fossil-fuel dependence also contributes to severe air pollution. Relevant KPIs: PM2.5; PM10; dust-event days; filtration energy; indoor-air-quality exceedances.

drivers.name: Climate-Sensitive Municipal Infrastructure
drivers.logic: Climate risk to water, sanitation, drainage, roads and energy infrastructure can constrain development and reduce asset resilience. This is particularly important because Uzbekistan's urban population and infrastructure needs are growing rapidly.
drivers.evidenceKpi: >50% of Uzbekistan's 37m population lives in cities, expected to exceed 60% by 2050. The World Bank identifies aging utility/social infrastructure and limited access to water, sanitation, roads and public spaces as constraints, while heat and floods intensify these pressures.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Livable and Productive Cities Program (World Bank)

drivers.name: Physical Climate Risk to Asset Location
drivers.logic: Climate risks are highly spatially differentiated. Developers therefore need location-specific climate-risk assessment during land acquisition, master planning and investment appraisal rather than relying on a national average.
drivers.evidenceKpi: By 2030, ≥8m people are expected to live in very high climate-risk areas. World Bank's CCKP provides subnational projections for heat and extreme precipitation. Relevant KPIs: % portfolio in high-risk zones; asset value exposed; expected annual loss; adaptation capex; insurance cost.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – Uzbekistan CCDR (World Bank); World Bank CCKP (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Climate Change Impact on Economic Activity / Asset Demand
drivers.logic: Physical climate risks can affect household incomes, employment, business activity and therefore demand for residential and commercial real estate. This creates a second-order financial risk beyond direct physical damage.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Without adaptation, Uzbekistan's domestic economy is projected to be 10% smaller by 2050 than under a scenario without climate impacts. This can affect employment, household income, real-estate demand and asset valuations.

drivers.name: Low-Carbon Construction Materials
drivers.logic: Cement, steel, glass and other materials are major sources of embodied emissions. Developers face increasing pressure to reduce embodied carbon through material selection and supplier requirements.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan produced 21.5 Mt of cement in 2025, with 42 cement plants and 40.5 Mt/year of installed capacity. KPI: kgCO₂e/m²; cement/steel embodied carbon; % low-carbon materials.

drivers.name: Energy-Efficient / Insulation Materials
drivers.logic: Demand for energy-efficient buildings increases demand for insulation, efficient glazing and other high-performance construction materials, creating an opportunity to reduce building energy consumption through the supply chain.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Uzbekistan's construction-materials sector produced 110m m² of gypsum board, 40m m² of construction glass and 50,000 tonnes/year of basalt insulation capacity through a new 2025–26 investment project. KPI: insulation R-value; U-value; % high-efficiency materials.

drivers.name: Local Sourcing / Supply-Chain Resilience
drivers.logic: Increasing domestic production of construction materials can reduce import dependence, logistics exposure and supply disruption while giving developers greater visibility over local suppliers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: 98% of materials required for new residential and industrial buildings are produced locally. The industry has grown to approximately UZS 53tn of output and USD 1.2bn exports. KPI: % locally sourced materials; import dependency; supplier concentration; lead time.
drivers.keySources: Digital Government of Uzbekistan – Construction Materials (O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Hukumat portali)

drivers.name: Construction Material Supply Capacity
drivers.logic: Rapid growth in construction creates pressure on the availability and capacity of cement, glass, ceramics, insulation and other materials, making supplier capacity and continuity important for project delivery.
drivers.evidenceKpi: In 2025, the construction-materials sector commissioned 353 projects worth USD 1.8bn; production included 21.5 Mt cement, 40m m² glass and 47m m² ceramic tiles. KPI: supplier capacity; material availability; lead-time variance; project delays.

drivers.name: Construction Waste & Circularity
drivers.logic: Large-scale construction increases demand for resource efficiency, material reuse and waste reduction. Circular procurement can reduce material costs and environmental impacts.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IFC identifies circularity, waste reduction and resource efficiency as key sustainability opportunities in construction-material supply chains. KPI: kg waste/m²; % recycled/reused materials; landfill diversion rate; recycled-content %.

drivers.name: Responsible Supplier Management
drivers.logic: Developers increasingly need visibility into suppliers' environmental, labour and safety practices, particularly where projects seek green certification or institutional financing.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IFC's Uzbekistan Green Building programme is developing a local green-building ecosystem and certification framework. KPI: % suppliers ESG-screened; ESG clauses; supplier incidents; % suppliers with certifications.

drivers.name: Green / Certified Construction Materials
drivers.logic: The emerging green-building ecosystem increases demand for materials with verified environmental performance and lower resource intensity.
drivers.evidenceKpi: IFC's EDGE system is being promoted in Uzbekistan; the programme specifically addresses reducing the resource intensity of building materials. KPI: % certified materials; EPD coverage; recycled content; embodied carbon kgCO₂e/m².

drivers.name: Material Price / Availability Risk
drivers.logic: Rapid construction growth and dependence on major material categories expose developers to price volatility, capacity constraints and supply interruptions. Local production reduces but does not eliminate this risk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Cement domestic demand reached 19.9 Mt in 2025, versus 21.5 Mt production; production covered 108% of domestic demand, compared with only 72.4% in 2018. KPI: material-price volatility; supplier concentration; inventory days; project delays.
drivers.keySources: Chamber of Accounts of Uzbekistan – Cement Industry (Hisob Palatasi)

drivers.name: UAE Green Building Standards
drivers.logic: UAE green-building standards establish sustainability requirements affecting building design, energy, water and materials.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE Green Building and Sustainable Building standards approved in 2010; application began for government buildings in 2011. The UAE Government estimates the initiative could save AED 10bn by 2030 and reduce carbon emissions by ~30%. KPI: compliance; energy/water intensity; certified m².

drivers.name: Dubai Al Sa'fat
drivers.logic: Dubai requires new buildings to meet minimum green-building performance, directly affecting development design and construction decisions.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Silver Sa'fa is mandatory for all new buildings; Golden and Platinum are optional. Al Sa'fat covers energy, water, materials and other sustainability requirements.

drivers.name: Abu Dhabi Estidama Pearl Rating
drivers.logic: Estidama creates mandatory sustainability requirements for Abu Dhabi developments, affecting energy, water, materials and building design.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Private projects require ≥1 Pearl; government-funded projects require ≥2 Pearls as a condition for building permits. In 2025, 304 projects were in design and 81 in construction that had met Estidama standards.
drivers.keySources: Abu Dhabi Municipality – Estidama (Dubai Ministry of Transport)

drivers.name: UAE Net Zero by 2050
drivers.logic: The national transition pathway increases long-term pressure on developers and asset owners to reduce operational and embodied emissions and improve building efficiency.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Net-zero target 2050; buildings are one of six priority sectors under the Net Zero 2050 Strategy, with programmes focused on efficiency and green-building practices.

drivers.name: Dubai Demand-Side Management
drivers.logic: Dubai's energy and water efficiency targets create continuing pressure on building efficiency, retrofits and efficient cooling.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Dubai DSM 2050 targets ≥30% savings by 2030 and 50% by 2050 versus BAU across electricity, water and fuel. The strategy includes new-build carbon-neutrality standards, building retrofits and cooling efficiency.

drivers.name: District Cooling / Cooling Efficiency
drivers.logic: Cooling is a major building-energy consideration in the UAE's hot climate; district cooling provides an efficiency pathway for large developments.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE Government states district cooling systems generally consume ~50% less energy than conventional cooling systems. KPI: cooling kWh/m²; district-cooling penetration; cooling cost/m².

drivers.name: Water Efficiency Requirements
drivers.logic: Water efficiency is embedded in UAE green-building frameworks and is financially material because buildings operate in a water-scarce, desalination-dependent environment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Estidama explicitly covers water as a sustainability category; Dubai DSM targets ≥30% reduction in water demand by 2030 and 50% by 2050 versus BAU. KPI: m³/m²; potable-water intensity; recycled-water %.

drivers.name: UAE Sustainable Finance Mobilisation
drivers.logic: The UAE's sustainable-finance agenda is creating a large pool of capital that can potentially finance green buildings, energy efficiency and sustainable infrastructure.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE banking sector target to mobilise AED 1 trillion (USD 272bn) in sustainable finance by 2030.
drivers.keySources: Central Bank of the UAE – Sustainable Finance (Central Bank of the UAE)

drivers.name: Green Bonds & Sukuk
drivers.logic: UAE and regional sustainable-debt markets provide financing channels for eligible green real-estate and infrastructure projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE Islamic banks' sustainable sukuk issuance facilitated increased from USD 2.6bn in 2022 to USD 6.9bn in 2023–24; UAE Islamic banks facilitated 19.24% of global sustainable sukuk issuance.
drivers.keySources: CBUAE Annual Report 2024 (Central Bank of the UAE)

drivers.name: Sustainable Debt Market Growth
drivers.logic: Rapid expansion of labelled sustainable debt increases the availability and visibility of climate-linked capital for qualifying real-estate and infrastructure projects.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Labelled sustainable debt issuance in MENA and emerging APAC reached USD 94bn, approximately 3× 2020 levels; UAE and Saudi Arabia accounted for 74% of MENA issuance since 2023.

drivers.name: Green / Sustainable Finance Frameworks
drivers.logic: UAE financial-centre frameworks increasingly formalise green funds, bonds, sukuk and ESG disclosures, improving the infrastructure for sustainable real-estate investment.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADGM has established a sustainable-finance framework covering funds, portfolios, bonds, sukuk and environmental instruments, including green and sustainability-linked bonds/sukuk.

drivers.name: Energy-Efficiency Investment & Retrofit Market
drivers.logic: High cooling loads and Dubai's demand-reduction targets create a large investment opportunity in efficient cooling, building retrofits and energy-management technologies.
drivers.evidenceKpi: Dubai DSM 2050 targets ≥30% savings by 2030 and 50% by 2050; the strategy explicitly includes building retrofits and cooling efficiency.

drivers.name: Green Building Financing Eligibility
drivers.logic: Green-building standards and sustainable-finance frameworks increasingly allow developers to position qualifying projects for green loans, bonds and sukuk.
drivers.evidenceKpi: ADGM's framework explicitly covers green and sustainability-linked bonds and sukuk; UAE sustainable-finance mobilisation target is AED 1tn by 2030. KPI: green financing; eligible capex; certified m²; financing spread.
drivers.keySources: CBUAE (Central Bank of the UAE); ADGM (ADGM)

drivers.name: Climate Risk in Financial Decision-Making
drivers.logic: UAE financial-sector climate-risk requirements increase the likelihood that lenders and investors will incorporate physical and transition risks into financing and investment decisions affecting real estate.
drivers.evidenceKpi: CBUAE's Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation (C8/2025) is in force and establishes requirements for financial institutions to identify and manage climate-related financial risks.

drivers.name: Extreme Heat
drivers.logic: Extreme heat increases cooling demand, affects occupant comfort and creates health/productivity risks for outdoor construction workers.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank CCKP tracks UAE exposure to 35°C, 40°C and 45°C daytime thresholds and 29°C nighttime temperatures, as well as heat-index thresholds up to 41°C. KPI: cooling-degree days; days >40°C; peak cooling load; kWh/m².
drivers.keySources: World Bank – UAE Compounded Heat Risks (Climate Knowledge Portal)

drivers.name: Water Scarcity
drivers.logic: Water scarcity and the UAE's highly water-intensive supply system make water efficiency and reliable supply material to building operations and development resilience.
drivers.evidenceKpi: UAE's freshwater withdrawals equal 1,510% of internal freshwater resources (2022), illustrating the country's extreme dependence on non-renewable/external water sources. KPI: m³/m²; potable-water intensity; recycled-water %; water-stress exposure.
drivers.keySources: World Bank – UAE Data (World Bank Open Data)

drivers.name: Coastal Flooding / Sea-Level Rise
drivers.logic: A large share of UAE real estate and infrastructure is concentrated along the coast, creating long-term exposure to sea-level rise and coastal flooding.
drivers.evidenceKpi: World Bank provides UAE-specific projections of sea-level rise and additional population exposed to annual coastal flooding in 2050 and 2100. KPI: % assets in coastal/flood zones; projected sea-level rise; expected annual loss; adaptation capex.

drivers.name: Extreme Rainfall / Urban Flooding
drivers.logic: Intense rainfall events can overwhelm drainage systems and disrupt buildings, roads and utilities despite the UAE's generally arid climate.
